# Adgent · The first multiplayer AI in the marketing vertical
URL: https://adgent.app/

The first multiplayer AI in the marketing vertical.
An AI marketing employee that learns your business and helps your team make better decisions. It joins your meetings with account intelligence, then carries that understanding into execution plans and completed work.

For agencies Network and holding-group agencies, brand by brand.

Good questions, answered plainly.
Pricing
Q: What is Adgent?
A: Adgent is an AI marketing employee for agencies and brands that run Meta and Google Ads. It learns your business from the context you confirm, joins your team's meetings with account intelligence, then carries the decisions into execution plans and account changes. A change is applied only after you approve it.
Q: Who is Adgent for?
A: Agencies first: network and holding-group agencies running Meta and Google Ads for many brands, where senior hours are the limit. Then the large brands themselves and the teams that run their spend. An agency switches between client brands and sees which one needs attention first.
Q: What does multiplayer mean here?
A: The agency and the client work through the same account analysis with Adgent. Both can add context, question a finding and direct the next step in the meeting. Confirmed decisions stay with the brand's work. Separate client logins and roles are not built yet. See the meeting workflow
Q: Is everything on this site live?
A: Adgent's AI employee runs across account analysis, reporting, account changes and team meetings. Features still on the plan are marked Coming. Every capability, and where each one stands
Q: What can I actually do from chat?
A: Ask about any campaign, ad set or ad and get the answer with its numbers. Ask for a dashboard, a media plan or a campaign draft. Describe an agent in a sentence and it is set up. Ask for a change and Adgent prepares the exact account move; ask to put one back and it prepares the inverse from the ledger.
Q: Which platforms does it cover?
A: Meta and Google Ads, through their own APIs. GA4, Search Console, Merchant Center and the Drive files you choose can add context. You can share store revenue, refunds or margin in Drive; Adgent can compare the account read with that file and name the gap. Shopify is planned, not connected today.
Q: Why not connect ChatGPT or Claude to our ad accounts ourselves?
A: For a one-off question, that can work. Adgent keeps day-level account data outside the chat, syncs it nightly, reads the creative and gives recurring specialists the same confirmed account context. The 28-day read, the 12-month audit and the next report stay on the same working record instead of starting over with each prompt.
Q: How do I know an agent won't spam me?
A: A condition has to hold for several checks before an agent fires, there is a cooldown after it does, and the number has to recover before the same alert can come back. A metric sitting on the line does not reach you twice an hour. Runs collect in your Outputs, where you mark each one seen or dismiss it.
Q: What does AI Visibility measure?
A: Whether ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Mode and AI Overviews name, list or recommend you, which sources they cite and who they recommend instead. AI Visibility
Q: We already have a dashboard. Why add another tool?
A: Adgent keeps the account's goals, constraints and past decisions with the data it reads. It ranks what needs attention, prepares the report or account change and carries the measured result into what happens next.
See how Adgent works with your growth team.

The questions people ask before getting started.
Q: What does Adgent actually do on day one?
A: Connect Meta and Google Ads and the first run sorts what Adgent finds into decisions, each with its evidence and an estimate of what it is worth a month, the costliest on top. On one live account the first run returned 53 decisions plus 6 on watch.
Q: What data does it read besides my ad accounts?
A: GA4, Search Console, Merchant Center and the Drive files you pick add business context beside Meta and Google Ads. Merchant Center answers in chat; it is not part of the daily analysis yet. Shopify is planned.
Q: What happens after the first account read?
A: Keep the decisions moving in chat, turn a recurring check into an agent, ask for a report or plan, or prepare the account change from the same working record.
Q: How can we start?
A: See Pricing to discuss your team's workflow.

# Why Adgent: agency and brand, working on the same answer
URL: https://adgent.app/why-adgent

Your agency and brand can work on the same answer.
When one person runs the AI conversation, everyone else's questions pass through them. Adgent lets the agency and brand question the same analysis together, then carries the agreed work into the next report, plan or account move.
Working alone with an AI conversation compared with agency and brand working together with Adgent
Moment in the work One person operating the AI Agency + brand with Adgent
A client questions the analysis
The operator relays the question and brings back the answer.
The client and agency question Adgent in the same meeting.
A brand constraint changes the plan
The operator adds it to the prompt and explains the revision.
The team confirms the brand context that shapes the next piece of work.
The room agrees what to do
Someone turns the answer into a separate brief.
Adgent carries the agreed work into a report, plan or account action.
The next client review starts
The operator gathers the conversation and the work it produced.
Confirmed brand memory, account history and past work inform the next review.
A comparison of working modes, not a claim that every AI tool works the same way.
Nobody decided to stop reading the accounts. It stopped fitting in the morning.
Once Three platforms, each grading its own homework.
Every day A dashboard, read before the stand-up.
Then Accounts per buyer outgrew the hours in a morning.
So Waste hid in the accounts nobody had read.
So The fix arrived after the money was gone.
Now A team of agents reads every account and brings you the move. You say go.
It looks first, then brings the move. Every change has a way back.
Both from live accounts: a build it questioned before drafting, and an account move put back from its recorded before-state.
One case, start to finish Hotel group, Meta, Aug 2026
The assumption "Page and pixel are connected. Set up a sales campaign."
The question it asked instead Not whether the pixel exists, but what it records.
The evidence 30 days: 65,042 custom events and 16,404 initiate-checkouts, but 4 purchases . Every live ad set optimised to a click with no value.
The decision A sales campaign could be built, but couldn't learn. The team chose initiate-checkout, knowing it carries no purchase value.
The output A full draft with that caveat written on the card and the reason under every field.

Touching the platform is easy. Knowing what to do is hard.
The shared conversation rests on the same account evidence and confirmed brand memory as the work in the app. These layers carry that context through to action.
Wrong data memory remembers a wrong number
No memory it re-suggests what you rejected
No judgment confident, and unfounded
L6 Operating surface The same Adgent in the app and your team's meetings
L5 Safe execution Your approval, and a way back for every change
L4 Judgment Root cause and a priced position
L3 Memory Your brand's rules, confirmed by you
Evidence informs the work above
L2 Audit What happened, and where
L1 Data correctness One comparable number
L0 Connectivity Google Ads, Meta, GA4, Search Console
Fair questions, short answers.
Q: Isn't this a dashboard with a chat box?
A: A dashboard shows a view. Adgent brings a position with a price on it: 53 decisions on one account's first run, each with the evidence and next move attached. Decisions
Q: Why use Adgent alongside the platform's own automation?
A: The platform is good at the auction, inside its own pixel and its own account. Adgent adds your margin, the other platform and the account's decision history.
Q: How is this different from an AI assistant on my ad accounts?
A: Adgent keeps the account's daily history, reads every account every day (including days you don't ask), reads the creative itself and carries the decision into reports, plans and account work.
Q: How much of this is built?
A: Daily reads, the Change Ledger, creative analysis and AI Visibility are live. Seven of 27 account-action types have run end to end so far. Every capability, with its status
The comparison you can check is your own account.
Discuss how Adgent fits alongside the tools your team already uses.

What to bring to the conversation.
An example of work that gets repeated is enough to start.
Q: What will we discuss?
A: How your team reviews accounts, which decisions need the client's input and what happens after the meeting. Together, we'll identify a useful starting workflow and the next step.
Q: Can our agency and client work with the same Adgent?
A: Yes, in the meeting: your team and the brand question the same analysis, and Adgent brings the account evidence and confirmed brand memory into the conversation, then carries the agreed work forward. Separate client logins and roles are not built yet. See Adgent in your meetings .
Q: Do we need to connect an account first?
A: No. Start by describing how your team works. We can discuss the relevant accounts and connections during the conversation.
Q: Can we discuss a specific account question?
A: Yes. Tell us what your team is trying to understand or decide. We can use that question to focus the conversation.

The daily verdict, plainly.
Further reading
Why Adgent leads with the verdict
How much ad budget is wasted
Q: When does it arrive?
A: Every connected account is read every day, on data through the last full day. You can also ask about any account in chat, any time.
Q: Where does the monthly amount come from?
A: The model's estimate from the account's own numbers, shown with the evidence. It ranks the work; it doesn't promise a saving. A finding gets no figure when the account evidence cannot support one.
Q: How is this different from a scheduled report?
A: A report tells you CPA is up 18% week on week. A verdict tells you what to change and what it is costing a month, with the evidence underneath, so you can disagree with a position instead of staring at a chart. Why Adgent
Q: I run a book of client accounts. Which one first?
A: Each account gets its own read. The workspace lets you switch between them and see which one needs attention first; the analysis never blends clients. For agencies
Q: Where does a decision go next?
A: A completed account move enters Being measured with its date and before-state. Once the result window closes, the outcome returns to the same chain and becomes context for the next read. Change Ledger
See how Adgent reads your accounts.
Talk to us about the daily account read and the decisions it returns, ranked by money.

# Trust Gate: initiative on numbers it can trust · Adgent
URL: https://adgent.app/trust-gate

Know which numbers can carry a decision.
The Trust Gate is Adgent's rule that weak evidence cannot carry a decision. Adgent checks a number before it can rank a decision or move money. Reliable evidence advances; weak signals become a named finding.
Pricing
How the gate works
Trust Gate
Trusted numbers can move money. Weak ones become named findings.
Every metric window is labelled trusted, degraded or untrusted before it is scored.

Q: What happens when a number can't be trusted?
A: It becomes a finding, not an action. With checkout-inflated ROAS, every ROAS- or CPA-ranked action in that run is held back.
Q: Does the gate fix my tracking?
A: No. It names the input that failed. The fix happens in your tag setup; later reads show when the signal becomes usable.
Q: What if pasted text contains instructions?
A: It is treated as data, not control. Security and data
Q: What gets logged when a change does go through?
A: The value it replaced, the new value, the time and who approved it, in the Change Ledger . Edits made directly in Meta or Google are recorded in the platform change log , with a date and the actor the platform reports.

# Change Ledger: what Adgent changed and what it replaced
URL: https://adgent.app/change-ledger

Every account move, its before-state and what happened next.
The Change Ledger is Adgent's record of every account move it applied, with the before-state and what happened next. Adgent keeps the owner, time, value replaced and execution status in one row. For supported reversible changes, it prepares the inverse from that history for your approval.

The ledger, plainly.
Q: Can I undo an edit made in Ads Manager?
A: No. Those are recorded in the platform change log , not undone. Adgent can prepare the old value as a new account move.
Q: Is putting a change back one click?
A: No. For supported reversible changes, the agent prepares the inverse from the recorded before-state. You approve it, and the put-back lands as its own row. Some action types cannot be reversed through Adgent.
Q: Can I put back something from last week?
A: For supported reversible changes, earlier rows retain their before-state so the agent can prepare the way back for approval. A recorded history does not make every action type reversible.
Q: Who can see the change history?
A: Everyone with access to that account's workspace sees the same rows, each with a date and a source. Per-person roles and seats aren't built yet. The history stays with that one company and never appears in another client's account.
Q: How much of this has run on live accounts?
A: 7 of 27 write action types end to end, as of 9 Sep 2026. Put-backs ran on one Meta and one Google Ads account.
See every account move and what it replaced.
Your first applied change lands here with its before-state, owner, time and execution status.

Q: Can Adgent undo an edit made in Ads Manager?

Q: Is this real time?

Q: Do I have to configure it?

Q: How does memory affect the next recommendation?
A: Confirmed facts, corrections and earlier decisions return as context in the next account read. The recommendation shows which remembered fact changed the advice, and earlier versions remain in history.
Q: Does one client's memory reach another account?
A: No. It is scoped to one brand, down to the ad, and each company's data is kept apart from every other's.
Q: What happens when someone new starts on the account?

Q: Does Adgent reconcile GA4 against my platform numbers?
A: No. It reads both side by side in chat; it doesn't produce a reconciled figure. Untrustworthy signals go through the Trust Gate .
Q: Do I have to connect my store?

Q: What revenue can't it see?

Questions about agents.
Q: What happens after I describe an agent?
A: Adgent turns the sentence into a schedule or condition, selects the sources and sends each run to Outputs. Open any run to see the evidence and next move.
Q: How do I build one?
A: Describe it in a sentence in chat, or fill in the settings yourself: name, sources, what wakes it, the instruction and where the output goes.
Q: Won't it become another stream of alerts?
A: It is built to speak when its condition changes, then cool down. Runs collect in Outputs, where you mark each one seen or dismiss it.
Q: What can an agent read?
A: Your Meta and Google Ads accounts, plus GA4, Search Console, Merchant Center and the Drive files you pick. What each source adds .

Questions about the ten.
Q: Do I have to set them up?
A: No. They are built in and start from the first run of a connected account. Their decisions land in Decisions .
Q: Where does a specialist finding go next?
A: It lands in Decisions with the evidence, current state and proposed move attached. Completed account moves continue into the Change Ledger with the value they replaced and their execution status.
Q: Are the monthly amounts a promise?
A: No. They are model estimates, not measured savings. The first nine cards come from one live account; the Budget-Pacing Cop card is a separate illustration.
Q: Can I add agents of my own?
A: Yes. Describe a check in a sentence and tie it to a condition, an event or a schedule. See Agents and workflows .

Q: What happens after the build is ready?
A: Inspect every field and its reason from the summary card. On Google Ads, a completed build is created paused, so switching it on remains a separate account move.
Q: Does it make the ads?
A: It writes the ad text and keeps the image slot open for your asset. Reading the creative you already run is Creative analysis .
Q: Which campaign types can it build?
A: Google Ads: Search, Display, Demand Gen and Performance Max. On Meta, a Leads build has reached a complete summary card on a live account; campaign creation has not yet been observed.
Q: What about campaigns already running?
A: Each edit starts from the live value and keeps the completed move in the Change Ledger with what it replaced.

Planning, answered plainly.
Q: Is media planning live?
A: Planning is in pilot. The plan on this page shows the shape of a plan, not a product capture or a forecast. The account-move cards, the 20% band check and the Change Ledger it hands off to are live today.
Q: What goes into a plan?
A: The budget, dates and goal you set. Adgent drafts the weekly split by line with the basis for each number, one test and its guardrails. Where the account's history is thin, it leaves expected CPA blank instead of guessing.
Q: Does the plan change the account by itself?
A: No. Going live is a change, so each budget step arrives as a card with its current and proposed value. Nothing moves until you approve it, and a completed move keeps the value it replaced.
Q: Can I share the plan?
A: Yes. The plan is a document you can save, reopen and share from the same account context, and open again at the client review.

Questions about reports.
Q: Does the client's link update itself?
A: No, on purpose. The link is a dated snapshot, frozen when you share it, so the numbers your client saw are the numbers you can stand behind. Inside Adgent the board stays live; share again for fresher numbers.
Q: Does my client need a login?
A: No. Anyone holding the link can open it, so send it to the people it is for and revoke it when the work is done.
Q: What can I export?
A: A PDF of any shared board or report, each page stamped Live or Static. Wide tables can break across PDF pages, so the link is the clean copy. Standing agents can file output as PDF, CSV, Excel or HTML. Agents and workflows
Q: What happens after a report finds a move?
A: The finding becomes a decision card with its evidence, current state and proposed state. Once completed, it enters the Change Ledger, so the next report can show what changed. Change Ledger

What changes when Adgent joins.
The team starts with the account in view. Questions get answered against evidence, decisions keep their reasoning and the agreed work keeps moving after the call.
In the room
Starts with the open question Retrieves the relevant brand context and checks the connected account before the review begins. What it reads
Brings back the brand memory Keeps confirmed goals, constraints and the reasoning behind earlier decisions in reach for the next discussion. Account memory
Tests the team's first answer Brings evidence, questions and alternatives into the conversation while the decision can still change.

After the room
Keeps the reasoning The goal, constraint and reason behind the decision are ready for the next analysis.

Returns the result What happened next becomes context for the following review. Change Ledger
Same expertise. Two ways to work together.

CTR +32.9%
Conversion rate −17.8%
Fix the form or page step first.
49% of a campaign's incremental sales come from the creative, in CPG studies. Targeting: 11%. NCSolutions (now Circana), Five Keys to Advertising Effectiveness, 2023.
Straight answers.
Q: Do I upload the creative?
A: No. It reads the ads already running on the Meta and Google accounts you connect.
Q: Does it make ads?
A: No. It reads them and briefs the next one. Making the ad stays with your team or agency.
Q: What does the dossier feed next?
A: The concept view, creative brief and report all use the same hook, angle, offer, persona and performance read, so the next piece of work starts from what the ad already proved.
Q: Can it read competitors' ads?
A: Not yet. Competitor creative from the ad library is on the roadmap. Today it reads your own connected accounts.
Q: Does it flag creative fatigue before CPA moves?
A: It reads the early signs. Fatigue is scored on every analysed ad, and each concept is tagged Scaling, Testing or Gen exhaustion. On one live account, 30 Sep 2026, it flagged a carousel whose click-through fell 19.8% while its messaging conversions rose 16.8%: the offer still worked, the hook had worn out. The data is daily, so it reads the trend, not the hour.
Pick the ad you can't explain. Let it read that one.
Adgent reads the creative already running beside its performance, identifies the pattern behind the winner or leak, and briefs the next move.

3 You get the findings Ranked by what each fix is worth.

The two readings illustrate how recommendations can vary between runs. Use the full window to judge the pattern.
Named is not recommended.
Every brand in every answer gets one of four levels. Only the top two count.
Absent Not in the answer.
Named only Mentioned, never offered as a choice.
Listed Counts as recommended One of the options, or its own card or listing.
Explicitly recommended Counts as recommended Singled out, or the only option.
Counts as recommended
List order is never weighted · a brand the answer warns against never counts as recommended · no 0 to 100 score

Agents and workflows For agencies: a new line in every client review
From an AI answer to a paid decision
What the answers show is weighed against the brand's goals and its ads before it becomes a plan. A gap is not by itself a reason to spend, and an ad doesn't change what the assistant answers on its own.

Straight answers.
Q: Will Adgent get ChatGPT to recommend us?
A: No vendor can promise that. Adgent measures where you are named and recommended, who wins instead, and on which sources. What to do stays your call.
Q: Which assistants and markets?
A: ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Mode and AI Overviews, the default logged-out answer, in one market today: Turkey, with questions asked in Turkish. Perplexity, Claude, Copilot, Meta AI and Grok are not covered, nor are brands that are themselves a marketplace or comparison site.
Q: Why is there no visibility score?
A: A score hides how many answers it rests on. Each reading is a count with its dates and a 95% range, marked early below 30 answers.
Q: Do we need ad accounts connected?
A: No. Without ads, setup starts from your brand name and a live search; gaps are then ranked by answers lost instead of spend.

Questions agencies ask first.
The longer read: what an AI media buyer does for an agency .
Q: How does the team know which client needs attention first?
A: The workspace shows every connected client as its own card, with health, spend and open items. Your team starts with the brand where the next decision is worth the most.
Q: How does each client keep its own context?
A: Each brand has its own memory, account history, goals and constraints. Open a client and the next read starts with that brand's working record.
Q: What leaves a client review?
A: The agreed report, board, follow-up or account move, with its evidence, owner and status attached.
Q: What can I share with the client?
A: A board link or PDF. The link opens a dated snapshot that you can update or revoke. Dashboards and reports
Q: Why not connect ChatGPT or Claude to our clients' accounts ourselves?
A: For a one-off question, that can work. Adgent stores each client's day-level account history outside the chat, syncs it nightly, reads the creative and gives its specialists the same confirmed brand context. The 28-day read, the 12-month audit and the next report stay on one working record.
Q: How would Adgent fit our agency?
A: Bring a client workflow you want to improve. We'll discuss who takes part, what needs to carry forward and where to start. Pricing

Running these accounts for clients? How Adgent works across a book of client accounts
Where the money leaks between the ad and the bank.
Three mechanics the platform report can't show you. The first one costs money every day it runs.
Ads keep spending after the shelf is empty.
A campaign selling well enough to clear your stock does not stop. It keeps buying clicks for a product nobody can buy, at the moment its history says scale it. Merchant Center connects read-only, so your catalogue, availability included, and item issues can be read for the account you pick. That read happens in chat; it isn't part of the daily analysis yet.
Returns can reorder the campaigns.
About 19.3% of online sales come back, after the month you reported has closed. Return rates are not even across campaigns: a discount-led winner can return hardest, so the ranking you budgeted against can change once refunds land. Unless you send the platform an adjustment, the original conversion stays counted.
Source: NRF, 2025 Retail Returns Landscape .
A test you can run without us.
Put the platforms' reported revenue next to your store's own figure for the same window. Do it again six weeks later. The first comparison shows how far apart they are; the second shows how much of what you reported was real, and that is the number to set budgets against.
What DTC teams ask before they connect anything.
Further reading
Why is my Meta ROAS dropping?
The Meta Ads audit: ten checks
Q: Why does the revenue in my ad account not match what my store banked?
A: Because the two count different things at different times. The platform credits a conversion when the pixel fires and keeps it unless you send an adjustment; your store nets out refunds, discounts and cancellations weeks later. Share your store's revenue in a Drive file and Adgent reads the platform's figure against it, with GA4 beside both as context. A direct store connection, Shopify first, is next. Ground truth
Q: Can it tell me which campaigns get restated by returns?
A: Share a refund export in Google Drive and it reads the returns next to your campaigns; where the export carries each order's source, it can say which campaigns the refunds came back from. Return rates and margins you confirm in chat are kept as account memory for later sessions.
Q: Does it know when I am paying to advertise something that is out of stock?
A: Partly. Merchant Center connects read-only, so the catalogue, availability included, and item issues for the account you pick can be read in chat. That feed isn't part of the daily analysis yet, so a sold-out product that is still being advertised is not flagged on its own. Ask, and it checks.
Q: Will it keep up during peak season?
A: Campaign data syncs every night, so the read is never more than a day old and a drift can be caught the next day rather than at month-end. The grain is day-level, current through yesterday; there is no hourly figure. In a season when the most expensive inventory of the year is bought in a few days, that is the difference that matters. Decisions
See which of your numbers January can rewrite.
Adgent keeps stock, returns and the store figures you share beside the ad account, so the next read starts from what the business kept, not what the platform claimed.

Running these accounts for clients? How Adgent works across a book of client accounts
In lead gen, the failure signal is a spike.
Every alert is built to watch for things falling. Junk leads do the opposite, and the season is too short to notice late.
The spike that looks like a win.
Spam and bot leads push the conversion count up and the cost per lead down, so the account trains itself on bots while every indicator reports success. Blocking the source afterwards stops new junk; it doesn't erase what the bidding already learned from it.
The form fill arrives late in the journey.
6sense's 2025 survey of nearly 4,000 B2B buyers puts first contact with a vendor at 61% of the way through the buying journey. The platform treats that one form fill as the conversion and optimises toward producing more of them.
Source: 6sense, 2025 Buyer Experience Report .
Hours, weeks, months.
Google can spend up to twice a campaign's average daily budget on a given day, capped at 30.4 times it over the month. After a change, a bid strategy can take up to three weeks to calibrate. Medicare's open enrolment runs 54 days, 15 October to 7 December. Whether the leads were any good arrives from the CRM weeks or months later, often after the season it belonged to.
Sources: Google Ads Help, spending limits and learning period ; Medicare.gov, Open Enrollment .
The questions lead-gen teams ask first.
Q: How do I know whether my cheap leads are any good?
A: Usually you can't tell from the ad account alone. Your lowest cost per lead is often your highest cost per customer, and a dashboard sorted by cost per lead will never show it. Measurement Integrity checks what the tracking is counting before any lead is counted, and a CRM export in Google Drive can be read in chat next to your campaigns.
Q: What if my campaigns are optimising toward the wrong conversion?
A: That gets checked first. Primary and secondary conversion events are classified separately, so the event actually driving the bidding is visible rather than assumed. A metric window the Trust Gate can't trust may raise a finding, never an action. Trust Gate
Q: Can it judge a channel on closed deals instead of form fills?
A: Not from the CRM directly; Adgent doesn't connect to one. A CRM export dropped into Google Drive is read in chat beside the campaigns, but it doesn't feed the daily analysis or send offline conversions back to the platforms. Worth knowing why nobody closes this cleanly: Google keeps a click identifier for 90 days, and B2B payback runs around 16 months. Ground truth
Q: What happens if my tracking breaks and nobody notices?
A: Broken tracking is treated as a finding, not a blank space. Conversion tracking health is monitored, on Meta including the Conversions API feed, and each day's data is checked against the account's own history, so a collection that stops or a count that jumps overnight shows up the next day instead of at month-end.

Running these accounts for clients? How Adgent works across a book of client accounts
The report keeps restating itself for months.
Three things a revenue manager already knows that the ad account doesn't.
A documented case, wrong in both directions.
One hotel group's Google Ads reported $139,500 in revenue at 6.98× ROAS over a 45-day window. Fourteen of those bookings, worth $21,000, were later cancelled and stayed in the report, while 43 real bookings were never tracked at all: 68.4% coverage. The figure was too high and too low at once, which is why it looked plausible.
Source: Stape, hotel group case study, June 2026 .
Click date against arrival date.
Dashboards add spend up by the day of the click; you decide by the night of the stay. On a compression night the spend is waste, because those rooms were selling anyway. On a need period thirty to sixty days out it can be the best money in the account. Revenue management reads pickup against the same time last year in the pace report; ad spend has no equivalent.
Brand defence is the quiet leak.
Paying to win back guests who were already coming to you is the most profitable-looking spend in the account and the hardest to defend on incrementality. Branded search and retargeting often report the highest return because they intercept demand you already owned.
The questions revenue managers ask first.
Q: Our booking window is weeks long. Does a daily read help at all?
A: Yes, because it isn't trying to close the booking window. The outcome arrives about 79 days after the click, a 40-day booking window plus a cancellation landing 39 days before arrival, so no attribution window will hold it. What changes is that a drift is caught in week one instead of in a month-end figure that keeps restating itself. Decisions
Q: Plenty of our bookings land by phone or through an OTA. What then?
A: Then the ad account is scoring the wrong event, and Adgent says so rather than modelling around it. Stayed revenue and cancellations by channel live in your booking engine or property system, which Adgent doesn't read. Bring them as a Drive file and the agent reads it in chat. Ground truth
Q: Can it tell a compression night from a need period?
A: Not from ad data alone: occupancy and pickup live in revenue management, which Adgent doesn't read. You can tell it. Facts you confirm in chat are kept as account memory and loaded into later sessions, so “these dates sell themselves, stop buying them” is something it carries rather than something you repeat. You can override it at any time. Account memory
Q: The platform's revenue and my analytics disagree. Which do I believe?
A: Neither one is stayed revenue. Adgent reads GA4 and Search Console beside the ad platforms as context, read-only; it doesn't reconcile them or pick a winner. Before a number can move money, the Trust Gate checks the window behind it, and a window it can't trust raises a finding, never an action. Trust Gate
See which channels book, and which ones cancel.
Adgent keeps booking and cancellation context beside the ad account, so the next report ranks channels by what stayed booked.

Your take rate, unless you tell it.
The number that decides everything is the one the ad platform never holds.

Running these accounts for clients? How Adgent works across a book of client accounts
Two sides to buy, and one number the pixel never holds.
Why a marketplace ad account misprices itself by default, and what the research says about where it leaks.
You have two costs of acquisition.
Take an $85 order at a 13% take rate: you keep about $11, so that is roughly what a buyer's first order is worth to you. An active seller keeps producing orders for years and can be worth many times that. One ad account, two very different values per click, and the platform reports both the same way.
Liquidity is local; budgets are not.
Below a threshold of live listings in a city, buying demand is waste however cheap the click, because the request can't be filled. The same campaign can be right in one city and wrong in the next, and averaged into one account figure both disappear. Geography breakdowns are part of what Adgent reads.
Trust can move the transaction off the platform.
A randomised trial on an online freelance marketplace found that once trust between the two sides was high enough, more of them took the work off the platform, offsetting the revenue gained from better matches. A match your ads paid for is not always a transaction you bill.
Source: Gu & Zhu, “Trust and Disintermediation”, Management Science, 2021 .
Bidding against your own supply.
When eBay switched off brand-keyword search ads in a controlled test, the traffic came back through its own organic results; the paid clicks had bought little it wasn't already getting. Marketplaces routinely buy branded and category terms their own listings already win.
Source: Blake, Nosko & Tadelis, Econometrica, 2015 .
The questions marketplace teams ask first.
Q: Why does our ROAS look strong when the business barely breaks even?
A: Check what your conversion value is passing first. Most marketplace accounts send gross transaction value, so the reported return is the real one divided by your take rate. At 13%, a reported 6× is roughly 0.8× on the revenue you keep. Changing the field takes a minute; the bidding then needs time to unlearn what it was bidding against. Ground truth
Q: Can it show me which listings sell, or only campaign totals?
A: Lower than campaign totals. Each account is read bottom-up, ad, ad set, campaign, account, with breakdowns by geography, placement, device and demographic, so a campaign that is fine on average but failing in half its cities shows up. Where you run Shopping, the Merchant Center catalogue and item issues can be read too, read-only. Listing-level margin still lives in your own systems.
Q: How do I stop budget flowing to what only looks profitable?
A: Fix what the account counts before you move money. The Trust Gate labels each metric window before it is scored, and a window it cannot trust can raise a finding, never an action. Each account move then keeps its evidence, before-state and later result in the Change Ledger. Trust Gate
Q: What can't it see about my marketplace today?
A: Your take rate, unless you tell it. Net revenue, take rate by category and acquisition cost per side sit in your backend or warehouse, and Adgent doesn't read them. Seller-account connections for marketplaces such as Trendyol and Hepsiburada are a low-priority roadmap item, pulled forward only by demand. Today it reads Meta and Google Ads, with GA4, Search Console and Merchant Center.
Find out whether you are bidding on gross volume.

Settings that teach the bidding the wrong thing.
Each one gets worse with time rather than staying flat, because each one trains the algorithm.
Call length as the conversion.
Count any call over thirty seconds as a conversion and the bidding learns to buy long calls: wrong numbers, reschedules, vendors, job applicants. It does exactly what it was told. Across more than 60 million calls, only 61% of callers to businesses spoke with a person at all.
Source: Invoca, Call Conversion Industry Benchmarks Report, June 2025 .
Locations bidding against each other.
Campaigns built by service rather than by location can put several of your own offices into the same auction. You pay a premium to compete with yourself, and the account report shows nothing unusual because in aggregate it is fine. Account Architect looks for campaigns chasing the same objective inside an account; comparing one location's account with another's is roadmap.
Presence or interest, on by default.
Google's default location option reaches people in your area and people who have only shown interest in it. For a clinic with a ten-mile catchment, an out-of-area click is rarely a patient, and it is the setting nobody checks.
Source: Google Ads Help, advanced location options .
Nobody in this vertical says ROAS.
Operators say cost per new patient, cost per booked appointment, show rate, chair utilisation. Near full capacity, more budget tends to buy leads booked into distant slots, and distant slots no-show more. That number lives in your booking system, not the ad account.
What multi-location operators ask first.
Q: We have twelve locations. Does it read all of them or just the biggest?
A: All of them, one at a time. Every connected account is read daily, including the ones nobody opened this week, each against its own history, so a healthy group average can't hide three sites losing money. It doesn't rank one location against another; that needs cross-account reading, which is roadmap. Decisions
Q: Can it move budget from a weak location to a strong one?
A: Not across accounts. Adgent opens one company's data per session, so there is no blended judgment across the group. Within a location it prepares budget and bid moves from that account's own numbers, while the workspace shows which account needs attention first.
Q: Google says we got store visits. Should I trust that number?
A: Treat it as a model, not a count. Google estimates store visits from a panel, with thresholds it doesn't publish, and since September 2025 they count as conversions by default at a value Google sets. Adgent shows which conversion actions are primary and actually driving your bidding, and a metric window the Trust Gate can't trust never raises an action. Trust Gate
Q: What about show rate and the calls nobody answers?
A: Adgent can't see either: show rate and revenue per patient live in your booking or practice-management system, and there's no connection to it. What it can see is what your bidding is trained on: a short call counted as a conversion, a radius running past your catchment, placement and demographic waste. Fixing what the account counts comes first. Ground truth

Measurement here is an adoption problem as much as a technical one.
What iOS attribution gives back, what most teams leave on the table, and why early returns mislead.
Most users say yes. Almost nobody asks.
Only about 8% of the apps Kochava sees show Apple's tracking prompt, yet close to 70% of people who see it now accept. Only 11% of advertisers have fully implemented SKAdNetwork and are actively optimising it; roughly a third haven't implemented it at all.
Source: Kochava Foundry interview, Adikteev, July 2026 .
A blended day-7 return describes no campaign.
By day 7, ad revenue has reached 89% of its day-60 total, in-app purchases 60% and subscriptions 52%. Average them into one early figure and a subscription campaign looks worse than it is.
Source: AppsFlyer, State of App Monetization, 2026 .
Nulls are not zeros.
Below Apple's anonymity threshold you get no value back, not a zero. Read the blanks as zeros and you understate exactly the new and small campaigns you are trying to judge.
Creative volume has outrun the monthly review.
The top user-acquisition spenders produced around 2,400 to 2,600 creatives per app per quarter in 2025, up 25 to 30% on the year. At a five-to-fourteen-day creative life, a monthly review is reading work that has already been retired.
Source: AppsFlyer, State of Gaming for Marketers, 2026 .
What user-acquisition teams ask first.
Q: Can it tell me whether the installs I'm buying are any good?
A: Not on its own, and it says so. Install quality lives in your attribution provider, mediation platform and warehouse, and Adgent reads none of them. It reads Meta and Google Ads and the creative running on them, the half of this problem that moves fastest.
Q: How do I judge iOS campaigns when attribution is noisy on purpose?
A: As an estimate, never a count, and never with blanks read as zeros. Adgent reads each connected account daily, current through the previous full day, and the Trust Gate labels a metric window before it is scored: one it can't trust can raise a finding, never an action. Trust Gate
Q: How early can I tell a creative is wearing out?
A: Before the cost confirms it. Each running ad is read for hook, format, persona, angle, offer, visuals and audio, with the hold curve showing where viewers leave, and each concept gets a call: still scaling, or wearing out and needing a new angle rather than another variant. It reads the ads already running, with no upload step. Creative analysis
Q: What does ground truth mean when the conversion happens in the app?
A: A number the ad platform doesn't control. For in-app revenue that sits in your attribution provider, mediation platform or warehouse, and Adgent doesn't read those. On the web side it reads GA4 and Search Console beside the platforms, as context. If install-level truth is all you need, we're not the right tool this quarter. Ground truth

The free tools, answered.
Q: Do I need an Adgent account to use these?
A: No. There is no signup, no email wall and no ad-account connection. Both tools compute in your browser, and neither page makes a network request while you use it, so we never see the numbers you type.
Q: Why is the arithmetic printed on the page?
A: Because a number you cannot check is not much use. Each tool states the formula it runs, the assumptions behind it, and the source of any figure it quotes, so you can reproduce the result on paper without trusting us.
Q: What do these tools not do?
A: They do not read your ad accounts. Nothing here can tell you whether your conversion tracking is intact, which campaign is leaking budget, or what changed overnight. That needs read access to the accounts.
Q: What gets added next?
A: Checks we can compute from numbers you already have. Anything that needs account data belongs in the product, not in a browser calculator. We would rather ship two tools with inspectable arithmetic than a wall of generators.

# Break-even ROAS calculator with returns and fees · Adgent
URL: https://adgent.app/break-even-roas-calculator

Free tools Break-even ROAS
The ROAS you have to beat, after everything comes out.
The platform reports the revenue its pixel saw. It never subtracts cost of goods, shipping, payment fees or the orders that come back. Put those in for the number a campaign has to clear.
No signup · nothing leaves your browser
Your numbers, per order
Average order value revenue the platform reports
Cost of goods % of order
Payment & platform fees %
Shipping & fulfilment per order
Return rate %
Profit you want to keep % of order value
Reset to the example
Computed in your browser. Nothing is sent.
Break-even ROAS
2.49×
On the revenue the platform reports. Below this, the campaign buys orders that cost more than they leave behind.
Contribution per order, before ad spend 321.28
Contribution margin 40.2%
Orders you keep per 100 the platform reported 88
Target ROAS to keep that profit 3.32×
There is room here: at a 10% profit target you need 3.32× on reported revenue, against a break-even of 2.49× .
Break-even ROAS 2.49×
The calculator needs JavaScript. The formula and the reference table below work on paper.
contribution = (1 − return rate) × (order value × (1 − cost of goods % − fees %) − shipping) − return rate × 2 × shipping
break-even ROAS = order value ÷ contribution
What it assumes. A returned order refunds the revenue, recovers the goods and refunds the fees, but you pay shipping twice, out and back. If returns can't be resold, raise cost of goods instead of the return rate. Everything is per order, in whatever currency you run.
The platform grades itself before four deductions.
Ad spend comes off last. Cost of goods, payment fees, shipping and returns come out first, and the system bidding for you sees none of them. That is how a campaign hits its target on the platform's own dashboard and still loses money on every order it wins: the target was set against gross revenue.
Returns make it concrete. About 19.3% of online sales come back , usually after the month you already reported, and the platform does not retract a conversion it has counted (more on the ecommerce page ). Marketplaces have it worse when conversion value passes gross transaction value: a reported 6× at a 13% take rate is 0.8× on the revenue you bank ( the marketplaces page ).
Return rate: NRF, 2025 Retail Returns Landscape, 15 October 2025.
Break-even ROAS by margin and return rate.
Shipping excluded, so this is the clean version: break-even ROAS = 1 ÷ (contribution margin × (1 − return rate)). Read down your margin, across your return rate.
Contribution margin 0% returns 10% 20% 30%
20% 5.00× 5.56× 6.25× 7.14×
30% 3.33× 3.70× 4.17× 4.76×
40% 2.50× 2.78× 3.13× 3.57×
50% 2.00× 2.22× 2.50× 2.86×
60% 1.67× 1.85× 2.08× 2.38×
The 20% column is shaded because it sits close to the online average, not because it is a recommendation. Use your own return rate, per cohort: a discount-led campaign and a full-price one rarely return at the same rate.
Three ways this number gets read wrong.
Against the wrong revenue figure. Break-even here is stated against the revenue the platform reports, because that is what the bid strategy optimises toward. Compare it against net revenue and you count the returns twice.
With one return rate for the whole account. The campaigns that return hardest are often the ones with the best reported ROAS: discount-led volume comes back more often than full-price demand. One blended rate hides exactly the campaign this calculation exists to find.
Across platforms, as if the inputs matched. Meta and Google count a conversion over different windows with different models, so the same break-even means two different things on the two dashboards. Why the two ROAS figures are not comparable .
The limit of this page: it is arithmetic on numbers you type. It can't tell whether your tracking is intact, whether the account has enough conversions to optimise on (the conversion signal check answers that in a minute), or whether yesterday's ROAS has finished maturing. On a live account, Adgent's Trust Gate keeps a metric window it can't trust from turning into an action, and its agents read Meta and Google next to GA4 and Merchant Center ( ground truth ).
Break-even ROAS, answered.
Q: What is break-even ROAS?
A: Break-even ROAS is the return on ad spend at which a campaign makes you exactly nothing. It is your reported revenue divided by the contribution each order leaves after cost of goods, shipping, payment fees and returns. Above it you are buying profit; below it you are buying volume at a loss.
Q: How do returns change break-even ROAS?
A: A return removes the revenue but not all of the cost, so the orders you keep have to carry the ones that came back. With a 40% contribution margin and no returns you break even at 2.5×. At a 20% return rate the same account breaks even at 3.13×. The platform never sees the difference, because it does not retract a conversion it already counted.
Q: Is break-even ROAS the same as target ROAS?
A: No. Break-even ROAS is where profit is zero. Target ROAS is the number you set in the platform to leave yourself a margin. It is higher when you want to keep a positive profit, and equal to break-even when the profit target is zero. This calculator gives you both.
Q: Why is my platform ROAS higher than the ROAS in here?
A: Because they measure different things. The platform reports revenue at the moment its pixel fires, before refunds, discounts, marketplace commission or cost of goods. This calculator works on the money you keep. A marketplace passing gross transaction value at a 13% take rate reports 6× on revenue it banks 0.8× of.
Method. The calculator applies the two formulas printed above and nothing else: no benchmark data, no model, no stored inputs. Every figure is computed in your browser; the page makes no network request while you use it, and we never see what you type. Source for the one figure this page cites: return rate from the NRF 2025 Retail Returns Landscape , published 15 October 2025. Written by the Adgent team. Published 7 September 2026 . If a formula here is wrong, tell us and we will correct it on the page.
Now judge the real account against it.

# Conversion signal check for Meta and Google Ads · Adgent
URL: https://adgent.app/conversion-signal-check

Free tools Conversion signal check
Is there enough signal in the account to optimize on?
Both platforms publish a minimum conversion volume, and both keep spending below it. Put in what the account produced and see how far it is from the floor, before you read anything into the cost per result.
No signup · nothing leaves your browser
What the account produced
Platform
Meta · per ad set, last 7 days
Google · per campaign, last 30 days
Bid strategy
Target CPA
Target ROAS
Maximize conversions
Conversions in the last 7 days
Ad sets sharing that volume optimizing the same event
Count only the ad sets or campaigns optimizing toward the event you care about. Volume on a different event does not help the one being learned.
Reset to the example
Computed in your browser. Nothing is sent.
Share of the published floor
23%
Floor
Per unit, per window 11.3
Published floor 50
Shortfall per unit 38.7
Units that would clear it if consolidated 0
11.3 conversions per ad set per 7 days, against Meta’s stated minimum of 50.
Below the floor. Consolidating will not reach it at this volume, so optimize toward an event higher in the funnel that clears 50, and treat the current cost per result as unstable rather than as a verdict.
Share of the floor 23%
The check needs JavaScript. The published thresholds it compares against are in the table below, which does not.
Both platforms wrote the number down. Neither enforces it.
Every figure is quoted from the platform’s own documentation, linked in the last column. Nothing in this table is our estimate.
Platform & strategy Published minimum Level it applies to Source
Meta · any optimization event 50 events / 7 days per ad set Meta for Developers
Google Search & Shopping · Target ROAS 15 / 30 days conversion-tracking level Google Ads Help
Google Display · Target ROAS 15 / 30 days across all campaigns Google Ads Help
Google Demand Gen · Target ROAS 50 / 35 days per campaign, 10 in the last 7 Google Ads Help
Google Video Action · Target ROAS 30 / 30 days per campaign Google Ads Help
Google · any Smart Bidding, for reading results 30 conversions (50 for Target ROAS) over the period you evaluate, “a month or longer” Google Ads Help
Read the last row carefully: Google frames 30 (and 50 for Target ROAS) as the volume you need to evaluate performance, not as an eligibility gate. The campaign will run below it, and the number it reports back will move for reasons that have nothing to do with your changes.
Tidy structure is how accounts fall under the floor.
Nothing warns you. A campaign below the threshold spends exactly like one above it: delivery stays exploratory, the cost per result swings on small numbers, and every weekly report reads as a performance story when it is a sample-size story. Split one campaign carrying 90 conversions a month into six tidy product campaigns and you get six units of 15, all under Google’s evaluation floor ( Google Ads account structure in 2026 ).
On Meta the same thing happens through scaling: a large budget change re-opens the learning phase, and the ad set needs its 50 events again from a standing start ( how to scale a winner without breaking it ). When the volume is not there, change the event, not the target. On one live account in August 2026, Adgent’s agent checked the pixel before drafting a sales campaign and found 4 purchases in 30 days: about one a week, against a floor of fifty in seven. That check is part of the Trust Gate .
Volume is not correctness. Clearing the floor says the optimizer has enough examples to learn from. It says nothing about whether the conversions are counted once, valued correctly, or attributed to the right click.
Day-one numbers are not final. Meta’s 7-day click window keeps rewriting yesterday, so a thin account looks worse in the morning than it will by Thursday. Why day-one data reads pessimistic by construction .
The floor is per event. Optimizing three ad sets toward three different events splits the signal three ways even when the account total looks healthy. Pick the deepest event that clears the floor, and judge the rest on the business outcome.
Conversion volume, answered.
Q: How many conversions does Meta need to exit the learning phase?
A: Meta’s own developer documentation says to structure ad sets for a minimum of 50 events over a 7-day period, and that not meeting the minimum events threshold can increase your costs per result. The threshold is per ad set, per week, on the event you optimize for: not per campaign and not per account.
Q: How many conversions does Google Smart Bidding need?
A: It depends on the strategy and the campaign type. Google states 15 conversions in the past 30 days at the conversion-tracking level as a Target ROAS requirement for Search and Shopping, 50 in the past 35 days for Demand Gen, and 30 in the past 30 days for Video Action campaigns. Separately, Google recommends evaluating performance over a period with at least 30 conversions, and 50 for Target ROAS.
Q: What should I do if the account is below the floor?
A: Consolidate rather than split: three ad sets at 12 conversions a week each are all below the threshold, while one at 36 is closer to clearing it. The other two moves are optimizing toward an event higher in the funnel that does clear the floor, knowing it carries less value, and fixing whatever is dropping conversions before adding budget.
Q: Does clearing the floor mean the numbers can be trusted?
A: No. Volume and correctness are different problems. An account can clear every published threshold and still report a ROAS that is wrong because the conversion value is set to gross revenue, the pixel is double-counting, or yesterday’s figure has not finished maturing inside the attribution window. This check answers the volume question only.
Method. The check divides the conversions you enter by the number of ad sets or campaigns sharing them and compares the result against the published figure for that platform and strategy; the table above is the whole model. No benchmark data, no estimate, nothing stored: it computes in your browser and the page makes no network request while you use it. Every threshold was re-read at source on 7 September 2026 and is quoted, not paraphrased. Written by the Adgent team. If a platform changes a number, tell us and we will date the correction on this page.
See which of your ad sets are under the floor.
This page works on one number you type. Talk to us about reviewing conversion signals across your Meta and Google accounts.

# About Adgent: what we believe about growth work
URL: https://adgent.app/about

Growth doesn't lack data. It lacks judgment at the moment of decision.
Adgent is an AI marketing employee that learns your business and helps your team make better decisions, from the meeting to the execution plan and completed work. The scarce thing in growth work is the expert who can weigh many signals against what a brand is trying to do, and say what to do next. Adgent builds that expertise into agents a team can question, argue with and hand work to.

Reasoning is the value
A chart is not a decision. The work is weighing the account, the creative and the measurement against the brand's goals, and saying what to do.
Memory keeps it continuous
What a team decided last month should shape this month's advice without being explained again.
Working together is how it's used

# Security: how Adgent protects your ad data
URL: https://adgent.app/security

Home / Security
Security
Last updated 7 September 2026
Contents
Our approach
Encryption
Access tokens & secrets
Access controls
Read-only by default
Change Ledger & revert
Infrastructure
Monitoring & logging
Incident response
Service providers
Retention & deletion
Report a vulnerability
Compliance
Contact us
Legal
Privacy Policy
Terms of Service
Data use
Data deletion
Business information
Security
Adgent connects to your advertising and analytics accounts, so protecting that access is core to the product, not an afterthought. This page explains the measures Adgent takes to keep your data and your connected accounts safe. For how we collect and use data, see our Privacy Policy ; for what data we access and why, see Data Use .
01 Our approach
We design Adgent around a few simple principles: collect only the access we need, protect it in transit and at rest, keep humans out of your data by default, and make every change to your accounts something you approve. Security is a continuous practice — the measures below describe our current safeguards, which we review and improve over time. The model has seven layers: per-company file isolation, credential separation, the API and MCP boundary, prompt-injection mitigation, capability restriction, output validation with human approval, and audit logs.
02 Encryption
In transit — all traffic to and from Adgent, and all calls to platform APIs, are encrypted using TLS (HTTPS).
At rest — data we store, including connection tokens and cached reporting data, is encrypted at rest.
03 Access tokens & secrets
When you connect a platform, we store the authorization tokens that let Adgent act on your behalf. We never ask for or store your platform passwords.
Tokens are encrypted at rest and treated as secrets. They are used only to authenticate requests to the platform you connected, are never exposed to other customers, and are never included in AI prompts or sent to AI model providers.
We request the minimum scopes needed for the features you use.
You can revoke Adgent's access at any time from your Adgent settings or from the platform's own permission settings, which immediately stops new scheduled access.
Application secrets and API credentials are kept confidential and rotated when appropriate.
04 Access controls
Access to systems and data is governed by least-privilege principles. Internal access is limited to personnel who need it to operate the service, is authenticated, and is logged. We do not allow humans to read your connected data except in narrow circumstances: with your affirmative consent (for example, support you request), where necessary for security or to investigate abuse, where required by law, or where the data has been aggregated or de-identified for internal operations.
05 Read-only by default
Adgent operates in read-only mode unless you grant execution access. Even with execution access, no change is applied to your accounts until you explicitly approve it . This approval gate is a security control as much as a product choice — it keeps automated changes from ever reaching your spend without your say-so.
06 Change Ledger & revert
Every change is stored with the value it replaced, so putting it back is a restore, not a reconstruction. A ledger entry can be reverted from the ledger itself; the revert goes back through the same approval gate and lands as its own entry. Each action type carries an honest reversibility label — reversible , best_effort or irreversible — and anything not mapped defaults to irreversible .
The ledger covers the changes Adgent made. Changes made directly on the platform are recorded so we can explain what moved, but they cannot be undone from Adgent.
07 Infrastructure
Adgent runs on reputable cloud infrastructure providers that maintain industry-standard physical and network security and recognized certifications. Environments are isolated, and each company's analytics data is stored in its own separate database file , which the agent mounts read-only for the length of a single company's session. The separation is physical, not a filter over a shared table, so one customer cannot reach another's data.
08 Monitoring & logging
We log access to systems and key actions to support security, debugging, and abuse detection, and we monitor for anomalous activity. Logs are protected and retained for a limited period consistent with security and legal needs.
09 Incident response
If we become aware of a security incident that compromises user data, we begin remediation immediately, investigate the cause, and notify affected users and the relevant platforms and authorities as required by applicable law and platform policies. We also report incidents to platforms where their terms require it.
10 Service providers
We use a small set of trusted service providers (sub-processors) to host, operate, secure, and support Adgent, including cloud infrastructure and the AI model provider that processes data to generate your results. We require them to protect data, to use it only to provide their service to us, and to delete it when it is no longer needed. We do not sell your data, and we do not transfer it for advertising.
11 Retention & deletion
We keep data only as long as needed to provide the service and for legitimate legal and security purposes. Disconnecting a platform stops new scheduled access but does not, by itself, delete data already stored by Adgent. A verified platform-data deletion request begins without undue delay. Deleting a company closes access immediately and schedules permanent deletion of its data from active systems within 30 days, subject to limited retention required by law. See Your rights & data deletion .
12 Report a vulnerability
Found a security issue? We want to hear from you. Email osman@adgent.app with the details and we will acknowledge your report and work to address it promptly. Please give us a reasonable chance to fix an issue before disclosing it publicly.
13 Compliance
We build Adgent to align with applicable data-protection laws, including the GDPR and CCPA, and with the developer and data-protection requirements of the platforms we integrate with, including Meta and Google. As we grow, we continue to mature our security program and pursue recognized certifications and assessments.
Contact us
Security questions or reports? Email osman@adgent.app .
Adgent is operated by Osman Tıkna, a sole proprietorship established in Türkiye.

# Data use: what Adgent reads, and what it never does
URL: https://adgent.app/data-use

Home / Data use
Data Use
Last updated 14 September 2026
Contents
What we connect to
Why we access it
How we use it
What we never do
Google Limited Use
Your control
Per-platform notes
Contact us
Legal
Privacy Policy
Terms of Service
Data use
Data deletion
Business information
Security
This is the plain-language version of how Adgent handles the data in your connected accounts. It is a companion to our full Privacy Policy — where the two cover the same ground, the Privacy Policy governs. The short version: we read what you connect to do the analysis you asked for, we keep you in control of every change, and we never sell your data, use it for ads, or train AI models on it.
01 What we connect to
With your authorization, Adgent reads data from the platforms you connect. We request only the access the features you use require. Depending on what you connect, that includes:
Meta & Google Ads (advertising) — account, campaign, ad set, and ad structure; budgets, bids, and settings; and performance metrics such as spend, impressions, clicks, conversions, ROAS, CPA, CPM, placements, and audiences. Where you grant execution access, we can apply changes you approve.
Google Analytics 4 — aggregated traffic, engagement, and conversion reporting, to give your ad data on-site context.
Google Search Console — search performance reporting such as queries, clicks, and impressions.
Google Merchant Center — product catalogue, item issues, account status, and Shopping performance for the account you select, to diagnose Shopping campaigns against your feed. Read only; Adgent never changes anything in Merchant Center.
Google Drive and Google Sheets — the content and metadata of files you select or create for use with Adgent, to import or export reports and provide business context. This permission does not let Adgent browse or access other files in your Drive.
02 Why we access it
Every connection exists to power a feature you can see. We use the data to produce the decisions and health score you see in the product, detect anomalies, answer the questions you ask, generate the reports and audits you request, and prepare recommended changes. We do not request access to data we do not need, and we do not request access for features that do not yet exist.
03 How we use it
Your connected data is used solely to provide the service back to you. It is processed — including by the AI that powers Adgent's analysis — to generate your briefs, answers, and reports, and, on your approval, to carry out changes you ask for. At the model provider that processing is transient and nothing is retained after the request; on our own infrastructure we keep a session record of the question, the answer, and the tool calls for up to 30 days to diagnose faults. We do not use one customer's data to benefit another. OAuth tokens authenticate requests to the platform you connected; they are never included in AI prompts or sent to AI model providers.
04 What we never do
We never sell your data or transfer it to data brokers or resellers.
We never use your data for advertising , including retargeting or interest-based ads.
We never use your data to train generalized or non-personalized AI/ML models .
We never send your data to an AI endpoint that trains on it — we route only to inference endpoints that publish a no-training and zero-data-retention commitment, training-permitted endpoints are excluded at the account level, prompt logging is off on our account, and every request carries an explicit no-training flag.
We never let humans read your data except with your consent, for security, to investigate abuse, where required by law, or in aggregated/de-identified form for internal operations.
We never use your data to determine credit-worthiness or for lending.
05 Google Limited Use
Adgent's use and transfer of information received from Google APIs to any other app will adhere to the Google API Services User Data Policy , including the Limited Use requirements.
06 Your control
Read-only by default — Google Analytics and Search Console permissions are read-only, and Google Drive is limited to files you select. Google Ads and Merchant Center each come as one OAuth scope covering read and write, with no read-only alternative: Adgent gates every Ads write behind your approval and never writes to Merchant Center.
You approve every change — nothing is applied to your accounts until you say go.
Disconnect anytime — disconnect in Adgent to stop new scheduled access through that connection. To revoke the OAuth grant itself, remove Adgent from the platform's app or permission settings. Neither action deletes data already stored by Adgent.
Delete anytime — the in-product company-deletion control closes access immediately and disconnects its platform connections. Deletion of the stored data is automated from there: verified deletion requests are picked up and processed every hour , with no manual step. You can also request removal of stored company data or your Adgent login account through our data-deletion instructions .
07 Per-platform notes
Google
Adgent requests only these Google OAuth scopes:
Google Ads — https://www.googleapis.com/auth/adwords for account, campaign, settings, and performance data. Because Google provides one scope for both read and write access, Adgent separately gates every write action behind your explicit approval.
Google Analytics — https://www.googleapis.com/auth/analytics.readonly for aggregated reporting.
Google Drive — https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.file for files you select or create for use with Adgent.
Google Search Console — https://www.googleapis.com/auth/webmasters.readonly for authorized site-performance reporting.
Google Merchant Center — https://www.googleapis.com/auth/content for your product catalogue, item issues, and Shopping performance. Google publishes no read-only variant of this scope; Adgent only ever reads.
Sign-in — openid and https://www.googleapis.com/auth/userinfo.email , used only to identify which Google account granted a connection and associate it with the correct Adgent user. We do not store the email address they return.
Our use of information from Google APIs adheres to the Google API Services User Data Policy, including the Limited Use requirements. We do not use Google user data for ads, do not sell it, and do not use it to train generalized AI/ML models.
Meta
Data accessed via Meta's APIs is processed only as described here and in our Privacy Policy, and in line with applicable Meta terms and developer policies. You can revoke access in Meta and follow our data-deletion instructions at any time.
Contact us
Questions about how we use your data? Email osman@adgent.app .
Adgent is operated by Osman Tıkna, a sole proprietorship established in Türkiye. Read the full Privacy Policy .

# Data deletion: remove your Adgent and platform data
URL: https://adgent.app/data-deletion

Home / Data deletion
Data Deletion
Last updated 14 September 2026
Contents
Disconnect a platform
Delete company data or your account
Meta data deletion
What deletion covers
Verification and timing
Contact us
Legal
Privacy Policy
Terms of Service
Data use
Data deletion
Business information
Security
You can disconnect a platform, delete a company and its connected-platform data, request deletion of your Adgent login account, or send us a platform-data deletion request at any time. These instructions apply to data accessed from Meta and Google as well as the account information you provide directly to Adgent.
01 Disconnect a platform
Open Settings → Connections in Adgent and disconnect the relevant platform. This immediately stops Adgent from using that connection or starting new scheduled collection. To revoke the underlying OAuth grant as well, remove Adgent from the platform's app or permission settings; for Google, use Google Account → Third-party connections .
Disconnecting a platform does not delete data already stored by Adgent or your login account. To delete stored data, follow the company-data or email-request steps below.
02 Delete company data or your account
Sign in to Adgent and open Settings .
Use the company deletion control to close access to that company, disconnect its platform connections, and remove it from active use.
To permanently delete stored company data or your Adgent login account, email osman@adgent.app from the address associated with your account. Include your account email and company or workspace name. Do not send platform passwords, access tokens, or other credentials.
03 Meta data deletion
To revoke Adgent's Meta access, open Facebook Settings & privacy → Settings → Apps and Websites , select Adgent, and choose Remove . Then delete the relevant company data as described above or email osman@adgent.app to request deletion of data previously accessed through Meta.
For an email request, include the email address used with Adgent and the affected business or ad-account name. We will send status and completion confirmation to the verified email address.
04 What deletion covers
Deletion covers the requested Adgent account or workspace, including stored profile information, authorization tokens, Connected Platform Data, and reports associated with it. It does not delete information held independently by Meta, Google, or another platform; use that platform's own deletion controls for its copy.
Limited records may be retained where required by law, for security and fraud prevention, or in encrypted backups until those backups are overwritten. Any retained data remains protected and is not used for other purposes.
05 Verification and timing
We may ask for reasonable information to verify your identity and authority over the affected account. Disconnecting in Adgent closes access immediately and prevents new scheduled collection; revoking the platform grant separately invalidates the platform authorization. Verified requests to remove stored data are processed automatically — a scheduled job picks them up every hour — and you receive confirmation when deletion from active systems is complete. Limited records may remain where required by law or in encrypted backups until overwrite. We never ask for your Meta or Google password or OAuth token.
Contact us
Send deletion requests or questions to osman@adgent.app .
Adgent is operated by Osman Tıkna, a sole proprietorship established in Türkiye. See our Privacy Policy and Data Use summary.

A sole proprietorship in Türkiye is registered under the name of the person who owns it, so the legal business name and the owner's name are the same string. There is no separate company name, trade title or registration number behind the Adgent brand today.
The registered address is not published on this page. A sole proprietorship registers at its owner's address, so it is a private address rather than an office; it is supplied in full inside platform verification flows and to counterparties on request at the email or phone number above.

Brand / service name Adgent
Website https://adgent.app
Operated by Osman Tıkna, sole proprietorship, Türkiye
Adgent connects to advertising accounts the customer already owns on Meta and Google Ads, reads them, and proposes changes. It is read-only by default: nothing is written to an advertising account until a person approves that specific change, and every applied change is recorded with the value it replaced. The advertising-platform applications, API access and business accounts used to deliver the service are held by the business named above.
03 Data controller and applicable law
The data controller for the service is Osman Tıkna , the sole proprietorship named above, established in Türkiye. Turkish data-protection law (KVKK) applies, and the GDPR applies where its territorial scope is triggered.

# Privacy Policy: how Adgent handles your data
