This Privacy Policy explains how Adgent , a service operated by Osman Tıkna (a sole proprietorship established in Türkiye, the data controller) ("Adgent", "we", "us", or "our"), collects, uses, stores, shares, and protects information when you use our website and our marketing-intelligence service. A core part of Adgent is connecting, with your authorization, to your advertising and analytics platforms — including Meta , Google Ads , Google Analytics 4 , Google Merchant Center , Google Search Console , and the Google Drive and Google Sheets files you select — to read reporting data and, only on your explicit approval, carry out changes you ask us to make.
01 Who we are and scope
Adgent is an AI marketing-intelligence service for performance marketers. It reads the advertising and analytics accounts you connect, tells you what is working and what is not, answers your questions, and — when you approve it — applies changes back to those accounts.
This policy covers the Adgent website and the Adgent application. It applies to two broad groups of information: (1) information about you as a user or prospective user of Adgent, and (2) the data we access from the platforms you connect on your behalf. It does not govern the platforms themselves — your use of Meta, Google and related services remains subject to their own terms and privacy policies.
02 Information we collect
Information you give us
Account & contact details — your name, work email, company, role, and similar details you provide when you request a demo, sign up, or contact us.
Communications — messages you send us, including support requests and the questions you ask the Adgent assistant.
Billing details — where you hold a paid plan, billing contact information and payment status (card processing is handled by our payment provider; we do not store full card numbers).
Information we collect automatically
Usage & device data — log data such as IP address, browser type, pages viewed, and actions taken, used to operate, secure, and improve the service.
Cookies & similar technologies — necessary cookies support sign-in, security, and remembering your cookie choice. On our website, Google Analytics and Google Tag Manager stay off unless you enable the optional analytics or advertising categories. If you enable the advertising category, Google Tag Manager also loads Microsoft Clarity , which records how our website pages are used (clicks, scrolling, heatmaps and session recordings) so we can improve the website. You can change or withdraw your consent at any time through Cookie settings in the footer.
Connection credentials
When you connect a platform, we receive and store authorization tokens (for example, OAuth access and refresh tokens) that let Adgent access that account on your behalf. We never ask for, collect, or store your platform passwords.
03 Connected platform data
With your authorization, Adgent accesses data from the platforms you connect. The data we read depends on which platforms you connect and the permissions you grant, and may include:
Advertising platforms (Meta, Google) — account, campaign, ad set, and ad structure; budgets, bids, and settings; performance and delivery metrics (such as spend, impressions, clicks, conversions, ROAS, CPA, CPM, placements, and audiences). Where you grant execution access, we can apply changes you approve, such as adjusting budgets, pausing or editing campaigns, or building new campaigns.
Google Analytics 4 — aggregated traffic, engagement, and conversion reporting, used to give your advertising data on-site context.
Google Search Console — search performance reporting such as queries, clicks, and impressions for properties you authorize.
Google Merchant Center — product catalogue entries, item issues, account status, and Shopping performance for the account you select, used to diagnose Shopping campaigns against your product feed. Adgent only reads this account; it never creates, changes, or deletes anything in it.
Google Drive and Google Sheets — the content and metadata of files that you select or create for use with Adgent, used to import or export reports and provide business context. Adgent cannot browse or access other files in your Drive through this permission.
We request only the access needed to provide the features you use. We do not request access to data we do not need, and we do not "future-proof" by requesting access to data for features that do not yet exist.
Read-only by default. Google Analytics and Search Console permissions are read-only, and Google Drive access is limited to files you select. Google Ads and Google Merchant Center are each published by Google as a single OAuth scope covering both reading and writing, with no read-only alternative. Adgent gates every Google Ads write behind your explicit approval, and never calls a write method on Merchant Center at all. You remain in control of every change.
04 How we use information
We use information solely to provide, secure, and improve the user-facing features of Adgent. Specifically, we use it to:
Analyze your connected accounts and produce briefs, health scores, anomaly alerts, and reports;
Answer your questions about your accounts and generate the reports and audits you request;
Prepare recommended changes and, on your explicit approval, apply them to your connected accounts;
Provide support, communicate with you about the service, and manage billing;
Maintain the security, integrity, and reliability of the service, and detect and prevent fraud or abuse;
Comply with legal obligations.
Our use of data accessed through platform APIs is limited to the practices described in this policy. Before accessing a type of Google user data not previously disclosed, or using Connected Platform Data for a new or different purpose, we will update this policy, notify affected users, and obtain consent where the connected-platform rules or applicable law require it.
05 Limited use & AI commitments
We hold ourselves to strict limits on what we do with the data we access on your behalf. We do not :
Sell or transfer your data to third parties such as advertising platforms, data brokers, or information resellers;
Use your data for serving advertising, including retargeting, personalized, or interest-based advertising;
Use your data to determine credit-worthiness or for lending purposes;
Allow humans to read your data, except with your affirmative consent (for example, for support you request), where necessary for security or to investigate abuse, to comply with law, or where the data has been aggregated/de-identified and is used for internal operations;
Use your Connected Platform Data to train generalized or non-personalized artificial-intelligence or machine-learning models.
Adgent uses AI to analyze and reason over your data in order to deliver the service back to you . At the model provider, your data is processed transiently : it is used to generate your briefs, answers, and reports and is not retained once the request completes. On our own infrastructure we keep a session record — the question asked, the answer returned, and the tool calls behind it — for up to 30 days , so that we can diagnose faults and investigate abuse. That record is deleted on that schedule, or sooner if you submit a verified deletion request. Your data is not used to train foundation models or models for the benefit of any other customer.
The AI provider that processes your data is configured not to train on it: we route only to inference endpoints that publish a no-training and zero-data-retention commitment, prompt logging is disabled on our account, training-permitted endpoints are excluded at the account level, and every request carries an explicit no-training flag. Your data is never used to create, train, or improve any generalized or foundational AI/ML model — by us or by our providers.
OAuth access and refresh tokens are never included in AI prompts or sent to AI model providers. Each customer's Connected Platform Data is maintained separately and is not used to provide or improve the service for another customer or advertiser.
Adgent's use and transfer of information received from Google APIs to any other app will adhere to the Google API Services User Data Policy , including the Limited Use requirements.
06 Legal bases
Where the GDPR or similar laws apply, we process personal data on the following bases: performance of a contract (to provide the service you sign up for); legitimate interests (to secure, maintain, and improve the service, where not overridden by your rights); consent (for example, when you authorize a platform connection or opt in to non-essential cookies); and legal obligation (to comply with applicable law). You may withdraw consent at any time.
07 How we share information
We do not sell your data. We share it only as needed to run the service:
Service providers (sub-processors) — trusted vendors that help us host, operate, secure, and support Adgent, including cloud infrastructure providers and the AI model provider that processes data to generate your results. They may only process data on our instructions and to provide their service to us, and are contractually required to protect it and delete it when no longer needed.
The platforms you connect — when you approve a change, we send the corresponding instruction to that platform's API to carry it out.
Legal & safety — where required by law, regulation, legal process, or governmental request, or to protect the rights, property, or safety of Adgent, our users, or the public.
Business transfers — in connection with a merger, acquisition, financing, or sale of assets, subject to the protections of this policy and with notice to affected users. Data received from Google APIs will not be transferred as part of a business transfer without your explicit prior consent.
08 Data retention
We keep information only as long as needed to provide the service and for legitimate legal, security, and operational purposes. Disconnecting or revoking a platform connection stops new access but does not, by itself, delete data already stored by Adgent. Connected Platform Data is deleted when it is no longer necessary to provide the service, when you submit a verified deletion request, or when permanent account deletion completes — subject to limited retention required by law. AI session records kept for fault diagnosis and abuse investigation are deleted within 30 days . You can request deletion at any time as described below.
09 Your rights & data deletion
Depending on where you live, you may have rights to access, correct, delete, restrict, or object to the processing of your personal data, to data portability, and to withdraw consent. We give every user an easily accessible way to exercise these rights:
Disconnect at any time — disconnecting a platform in Adgent stops further use of that connection and new scheduled collection. To revoke the OAuth grant itself, remove Adgent from the platform's app or permission settings.
Request correction or deletion — follow our data-deletion instructions or email osman@adgent.app , and we will action your request without undue delay.
Delete company data or your account — the in-product company-deletion control closes access to that company immediately and marks its connections disconnected. Deletion of the stored data is then automated : a scheduled job picks up verified deletion requests every hour and removes them from our active systems, with no manual step. You can also request removal of stored company data or your Adgent login account through our data-deletion instructions . Limited records may be retained where required by law.
We will not charge you to exercise these rights, and we will not discriminate against you for doing so. If you are in the EEA or UK and have an unresolved concern, you may contact your local data protection authority.
10 Security
We take reasonable and appropriate measures to protect data against unauthorized access, use, alteration, loss, or disclosure. These include encryption of data in transit and at rest, access controls and least-privilege practices, protection of access tokens and application secrets, and monitoring. We provide a clearly marked way to report security concerns, and we begin remediation and notify affected parties as required by law if an incident occurs. No method of transmission or storage is completely secure, but we work to protect your data and continually improve our safeguards.
11 International transfers

12 Children
Adgent is a business tool intended for use by adults aged 18 and over. It is not directed to children, and we do not knowingly collect personal information from children. If you believe a child has provided us with personal information, contact us and we will delete it.

The Analytics and Search Console scopes are read-only. The Drive scope limits access to files you select or create for use with Adgent. The sign-in scopes are used only to read the stable account identifier that tells us which Google account granted a connection, so it can be matched and revoked cleanly; we do not store the email address they return.

# 11.11 vs Black Friday in Türkiye: What the Data Shows · Adgent
URL: https://adgent.app/11-11-vs-black-friday-turkey

Blog Research
When does November really peak? 11.11 and Black Friday in Türkiye
Product searches, marketplace transactions and advertiser activity show how November's peaks change with the product, the query and the measurement window.
Adgent Research · Original data analysis
Type
Research
Topic
November ecommerce in Türkiye
Reading time
13 min
Published
11 November 2026
On this page
Product comparison
Day versus week
Related searches
Marketplace transactions
Meta advertiser panel
Account review questions
Methodology
About Adgent
Sources
All articles
What this research covers Search data: 2023–2025. Marketplace transactions: 2024–2025. Meta observations: 3–8 November 2026.
Research cutoff: 10 November 2026. Publication date: 11 November 2026.
Across 2023, 2024 and 2025, the electronics and home terms we tracked drew more search interest around 11.11 than around Black Friday. Our winter-heavy fashion terms leaned toward Black Friday in every year.
Even within one product group, the answer could change with the window. In 2023, all five small-appliance terms were higher on 11 November than on Black Friday itself. Across the surrounding seven days, the Black Friday window was slightly higher.
We compared selected product searches across three years with official marketplace transaction data and a separate panel of 30 advertiser pages. The research covers Türkiye (Turkey); it compares the 11 November shopping event, often called 11.11 or Singles' Day, with Black Friday.
11.11 or Black Friday: does the product change the answer?
Electronics and home leaned toward 11.11 in all three years. Winter-heavy fashion leaned toward Black Friday throughout. Small appliances changed direction after 2023, while sports and outdoors was close to parity in 2024 and 2025.
We compared 8–14 November with a seven-day window centred on Black Friday in each year. Each window includes all seven weekdays. The table shows how much higher or lower combined normalized search interest was around 11.11, relative to the Black Friday window.
Selected query basket

+8.0%
+6.0%

Positive values mean higher interest around 11.11; negative values mean higher interest around Black Friday. Five selected terms per basket, except beauty, which uses three complete series. Source: Adgent analysis of Google Trends, Türkiye.
The electronics gap was narrow in 2023, while the fashion gap was much larger. Neither establishes a dependable future advantage; term selection and the comparison window still matter.
The fashion selection also has a seasonal bias: three of its five terms are “mont”, “bot” and “kazak”, meaning coats, boots and sweaters. Its later-November pattern cannot be attributed to Black Friday alone. “Bot” also has a software meaning, addressed in the sensitivity checks below.
For a marketing team, the useful next step is to examine the products that drive its own sales. A category label gives a starting point; the actual range determines whether this comparison is relevant.
Can a stronger shopping day sit inside a weaker week?
In the 2023 small-appliance basket, all five tracked terms had higher relative search interest on 11 November than on Black Friday, 24 November. The combined basket also reached a higher daily level against its own October baseline. Yet the seven-day Black Friday window was 3.0% higher than the 11.11 window.
Daily Trailing 7-day average Comparison windows
Small-appliance search interest in Türkiye, 15 October–15 December 2023. October 15–31 daily mean = 100. Thin line: daily values; thick line: current day plus six prior days. Shaded windows: 8–14 and 21–27 November. Source: Adgent analysis of Google Trends. Scroll the chart horizontally on smaller screens.
Small-appliance basket in 2023
Relative to the 15–31 October daily mean
11 November
1.64×
Black Friday, 24 November
1.42×
The weekly result is the same comparison as the −2.9% in the first table, expressed in the opposite direction: each percentage uses a different denominator. The daily result describes two dates; the weekly result includes interest around each event. Neither calculation tells us which period delivered more sales.
This single-year example checks a planning assumption: does an apparent advantage survive when the comparison expands from the event day to the surrounding week? It does not establish a recurring advantage for either period.
Stable product queries can hide changes in related searches
In October and November 2025, “laptop”, “kulaklık” and “süpürge” stayed in the same reported search-volume range. Some related discount and comparison queries increased, while “laptop kampanya” decreased.

“İndirim” means discount, “kampanya” refers to a campaign or promotion, and “karşılaştırma” means comparison. “Kulaklık” and “süpürge” mean headphones and vacuum cleaner. Source: Google Keyword Planner monthly estimates for Türkiye, retrieved via DataForSEO.
Looking only at general product names would miss these differences. Grouping every promotional phrase together would also conceal the opposite movements in “laptop indirim” and “laptop kampanya”.
Some query contrasts also appeared in 2024. “Laptop” stayed at a reported 246,000 while “laptop indirim” rose from 880 to 1,300. “Süpürge” stayed at 40,500 while “süpürge karşılaştırma” rose from 720 to 1,000. But “laptop kampanya” increased from 1,600 to 1,900 that year, unlike its decline in 2025.
Across the broader set of 30 general product terms, seven increased from October to November 2025, 15 stayed in the same reported range and eight decreased. The selected terms did not move uniformly.
These are rounded estimates, not exact counts or tracked user journeys. Specific queries are much smaller than the general terms, so read their percentage movements alongside their absolute volumes. For an account review, keep product, discount, campaign and comparison queries separate, then use your own search-term and conversion reports to assess their value.
Was 11.11 bigger than Black Friday for marketplace transactions?
11 November had the highest marketplace transaction count in both 2024 and 2025, according to the Ministry of Trade's ETBİS reports ( 2024, Table 2 ; 2025, Table 1 ). In 2025, 27 November ranked second, ahead of Black Friday on 28 November.
11 November accounted for 0.79% of annual marketplace transactions in 2025. That is approximately 2.9 times the year's daily average, calculated from the published share. The same table gives 28 November a 0.53% share. Comparing the two rounded shares implies about 49% more transactions on 11 November than on Black Friday itself.
These are different comparisons: 2.9× uses the annual daily average; approximately 49% uses Black Friday's transaction count. Both concern individual days and marketplace transaction counts, not full campaign revenue, profit or advertising returns. The product-search comparisons add detail about selected queries; they do not explain the causes of the aggregate transaction pattern.
How did Meta advertiser activity change in November 2026?
Across the same 30 tracked pages, reported active ads rose from 5,548 on 3 November to 6,468 on 8 November 2026, an increase of 920, or 16.6%. The change varied considerably across the selected groups.

Source: Adgent observations of Meta Ad Library, matched pages on 3 and 8 November 2026. Counts are platform/provider-reported active-ad totals, not the number of ads whose text was read.
Electronics had the largest absolute increase and the highest percentage change in this panel. MediaMarkt added 129 reported active ads and Samsung added 96. Together, they accounted for 225 of the group's 241 additional active ads, about 93%.
Across the full panel, 26 pages increased, two were unchanged and two declined. Growth was widespread among the selected pages, while the size of the increase remained concentrated in particular accounts.
Absolute and percentage changes answer different questions. Sports and outdoors grew by 29.6%, adding 40 active ads from a smaller starting point. Small appliances grew by 25.4%, adding 204. Reporting both avoids confusing a high growth rate with a large contribution to the total change.
The panel is not representative of Türkiye's market. Active-ad counts do not directly measure spend, reach, auction pressure or performance. They cover a different period from the historical search series, so these observations cannot show that advertisers responded to those search patterns.
Questions for your November account review
Which timing pattern fits your product queries? Compare the products you actually sell across both event windows. Check whether one large term drives the basket result and whether the direction remains when you look at individual days and full weeks.
Which query phrases are changing? Keep general product searches, discount phrases and comparison queries distinct long enough to see their differences. Then use your search-term and conversion reports to assess which changes matter to your business.
Do your searches and transactions tell the same story? Compare external search patterns with your own orders and campaign results over matching periods. Stock, offer dates and measurement changes can help explain differences. Use a consistent attribution window when reviewing campaign results.
How does advertiser activity compare with your results? Examine the particular advertisers behind a panel change. Assess your own delivery, costs and returns before using active-ad counts to inform a campaign decision. Our Meta Ads account audit checklist provides a separate account-level review process.
Methodology and original queries
Scope and data
The historical study starts with six selected product baskets of five Turkish terms each. The weekly beauty comparison uses three complete series; two sparse terms are excluded. The 2026 Meta panel tracks 30 selected advertiser pages. Neither selection represents an entire industry.
Google Trends web search data was retrieved via DataForSEO on 2 November 2026. Each basket and year was requested separately, with all five terms together on a shared 0–100 scale, covering 15 October to 15 December.
Google Keyword Planner history for 159 selected queries was retrieved via DataForSEO on 3 November 2026, using Türkiye, Turkish language and search partners disabled. Monthly history was returned for 130 queries. The examples compare October and November within the same year. The history ended in September 2026, so no October-to-November 2026 search-volume comparison is included.
Product basket
Original Turkish search terms
Electronics
televizyon, laptop, cep telefonu, kulaklık, tablet
Small appliances
airfryer, süpürge, kahve makinesi, blender, ütü
Beauty
parfüm, ruj, cilt bakım, şampuan, makyaj seti; the weekly comparison excludes cilt bakım and makyaj seti
Winter-heavy fashion
mont, çanta, bot, kazak, elbise
Home and living
nevresim takımı, halı, yemek takımı, perde, koltuk takımı
Sports and outdoors
spor ayakkabı, eşofman, koşu bandı, dambıl, termos
Comparison windows and calculations
The 11.11 window is 8 to 14 November in every year. The Black Friday windows are 21 to 27 November 2023, 26 November to 2 December 2024, and 25 November to 1 December 2025. The latter two include early December to preserve the same seven-day comparison.
Within each basket-year request, daily indices are summed for the included terms and averaged across each seven-day window. Five terms are included except for beauty, which uses three complete series. The table reports:
(11.11 window average ÷ Black Friday window average − 1) × 100
For the daily small-appliance comparison, the basket's event-day index is divided by its own mean daily index over 15–31 October. The chart sets that baseline to 100. The trailing seven-day average includes the current day and the six preceding days; it is distinct from the fixed event-window comparison.
The 2023 small-appliance window sums are 1,468 for 11.11 and 1,512 for Black Friday. Thus (1,468 ÷ 1,512 − 1) × 100 = −2.9%, while (1,512 ÷ 1,468 − 1) × 100 = +3.0%, after rounding.
For 2025 marketplace transactions, the annual-average ratio is 0.0079 × 365 = 2.8835, rounded to 2.9×. The direct comparison with Black Friday is (0.79 ÷ 0.53 − 1) × 100 ≈ 49.1%. Both use published rounded shares, so the ratios are approximate.
Meta panel and coverage

The collection requested active ads delivered in Türkiye and retained reported totals separately from sampled ad text. Both comparison dates cover all 30 pages. Percentage change is (8 November total ÷ 3 November total − 1) × 100; group rates use group totals.
The 7 November collection covered 25 pages and the 9 November collection covered 14. Their raw totals are not compared with the complete 30-page panel. Ad-text samples and automated message tags are not used to estimate message prevalence in this article.
Interpretation limits
Google Trends uses sampled, normalized search data. Its index measures relative interest rather than absolute search counts. Independent basket-year scales cannot be compared as category market sizes or as absolute growth across years. Within a request, larger-index terms contribute more to the combined basket; this is not an equal-weight average of each term's percentage change.
The weekly beauty results exclude the sparse “cilt bakım” and “makyaj seti” terms. A missing observation or low index is not proof of no demand. Monthly search volumes are rounded and related variants may overlap; we do not sum them into market size or intent shares.
“Bot” can refer to boots or software bots. A recorded sensitivity check retained the fashion direction when “bot” was removed; removing “bot”, “mont” and “kazak” together brought the two periods close to parity.
The results are descriptive. The study does not estimate advertising returns, causal effects or an optimal budget split.

The first multiplayer AI in the marketing vertical.
An AI marketing employee that learns your business and helps your team make better decisions. It joins your meetings with account intelligence, then carries that understanding into execution plans and completed work.

# AI media buyer for agencies: a senior read · Adgent
URL: https://adgent.app/ai-media-buyer-for-agencies

Blog Field note
You can't put a senior on every account. You can put a senior read on every account.
Twelve clients means twelve separate reads every day, each on its own data, each ranked by
what that account is costing you. The same standard on the twelfth as on the first, with the reasoning
ready for the team to inspect and carry forward.
Adgent · Notes from building the analyst
Type
Field note
Reading time
8 min
Published
22 July 2026
On this page
The agency problem
One tool, every account
Junior teams, senior output
Win the pitch, keep the client
Keep every decision legible
What it adds up to
Questions
All articles
Agencies live and die on a staffing ratio. Every client wants a senior buyer's attention; the P&L
only supports one senior for every handful of accounts. So the senior gets spread thin, the juniors
carry accounts they are not quite ready for, and the accounts that are quietly leaking never reach
the top of anyone's morning. This is the problem an AI media
buyer is for: not to replace the buyer, but to put the same careful read on every account you
run.
Short answer
An AI media buyer lets an agency apply senior-level judgment to every client account
it runs: the same daily read, the same ranked decisions and the same account-specific context, worked
out separately for each client. Junior teams operate at senior output, seniors spend their time on
strategy, and reporting stops being a weekly scramble.
The agency problem: you can't staff a senior per account
The best agency work happens when a senior buyer opens an account, reads it in context, and knows
within a minute what actually matters today. That read is the product. The trouble is that it does not
scale. A senior can hold maybe six or eight accounts in their head at that depth, and the moment you
win the ninth client, something gives.
So agencies do what every agency does: push accounts down to juniors and hope the training holds. It
mostly does, until a Tuesday when three accounts move at once and the one person who would have caught
the placement leak is heads-down on a pitch. The cost is not a blown quarter. It is the slow erosion of
the accounts nobody had time to look at closely.
Capacity is one problem. Consistency is the other. Two juniors looking at the same symptom will reach
different conclusions, because judgment lives in people, not in the agency. When your senior is out,
the standard walks out with them. Clients notice the wobble even when they cannot name it: the report
that used to lead with a clear call now leads with a caveat, and renewal conversations get harder.
You do not need a senior on every account. You need every account read the way a senior would
read it.
That reframing is the whole point. The scarce thing was never the click or the report. It was the
judgment : knowing which number matters today, why it moved, and whether the obvious fix
is the right one. If that read can be automated and applied to each client to the same standard, the
staffing ratio stops being a ceiling.
One tool, every account
An AI media buyer built for agencies reads every client you connect, Meta and Google, every day, and
treats each account as its own world. Same engine, same standard, but each client gets its own
baselines, decisions, history and next moves. One client's spike never colours another client's read,
because each analysis starts from that account's evidence and brand context.
In the morning you do not open twelve dashboards. You open twelve verdicts, each one position first:
what changed on that account, why, and what to do about it. The workspace shows a card per client with
that account's health, spend and open items, so you can see which one needs you first and switch to it.
The ordering is a sort over separate results, not a comparison between clients. The junior running six
accounts starts the day already knowing which two to open first.
Each account, its own verdict. Baselines and anomalies are worked out per client, so a
verdict on one account is never diluted by the average of the book, and never benchmarked against
another client's numbers either.
Both platforms, per client. Meta and Google are read side by side for each client,
with GA4, Search Console and Merchant Center alongside for context.
Changes stay with their client. Each client's proposed changes belong to that client's
account, and the workspace shows which accounts have open items, so you know where to go without
opening every tab.
Junior teams, senior output
Here is what actually changes on the floor. A junior buyer's weakness is not effort; it is pattern
library. They have not seen a thousand accounts, so they do not yet recognise the placement drift
hiding inside a healthy blended ROAS, or the day-one number that is still inside the attribution
window and should not be trusted. A senior recognises those at a glance.
An AI media buyer carries that pattern library into every account. Adgent works through ten
specialists, each reading the account through one lever. When Budget Allocator finds money split by
history rather than by result, when Placement & Network Optimizer finds a cheaper placement starved
of budget, or when Account Architect finds four campaigns competing for the same goal (all three came
up in one live account's first run, September 2026), the junior is not guessing. They are reviewing a
senior-quality read and making the call. That is how a team of juniors ships senior output: the
judgment is supplied, and the person still owns the decision. For the Google-side version of the same
checklist, see what a Google Ads audit should
surface .
Juniors who spend six months reviewing position-first decisions learn the patterns faster than
juniors who spend six months pulling numbers into spreadsheets. Every decision is a worked example
(cause, evidence, proposed change), so training happens on every account instead of waiting for a senior
to find a spare hour.
It also standardises what “good” looks like. Because the same engine reads every account to the same
standard, a client on a junior's book gets the same quality of read as a client on the senior's book.
The agency's judgment stops being a property of whoever happens to be assigned and becomes a property
of the agency itself, which is exactly what you want when you are growing headcount without diluting
the work.
Win the pitch, keep the client
Agencies win two ways: landing the account and not losing it. An AI media buyer helps with both, and
the mechanism is the same. You walk in with a real read instead of a promise.
Win the pitch with a live read
Connect a prospect's account and you can walk into the pitch with an actual account audit
(the placement leak, the wasted brand spend, the conversion setup nobody has questioned) instead of a
generic capabilities deck. Nothing lands a new client like showing them a problem on their own account
that their current agency missed.
Keep the client with reports that lead with the verdict
Reporting is where agencies quietly bleed hours and, eventually, clients. Describe the report you want
in one sentence and it comes back built, leading with what changed, why, and what you did about
it , with the charts underneath for anyone who wants them. Send the client a link they open
without logging in, a dated snapshot you can re-share or revoke, or download it as a PDF. The client
stops feeling like they are paying for a dashboard export and starts feeling like they have a senior on
the account.
Keep every client decision legible
Agency scale breaks when nobody can reconstruct why an account move happened. Adgent keeps the
proposed state, the value it replaced, the owner and execution status together. The team can move from a
verdict to account work without losing the reasoning that made the change worth doing.
The Change Ledger turns that history into working context. Open a row to see the before-state and
applied state. For supported reversible changes, Adgent prepares the inverse from the same row
for approval rather than asking the team to rebuild it from memory.

A separate platform change log records edits made directly in Ads Manager or Google Ads. If a client

What it adds up to for an agency
Put it together and the agency math changes. You stop pricing on how many senior hours you can spare
per account and start pricing on the standard you can hold on each of them. Juniors run bigger books at
a higher standard. Seniors move from pulling numbers to setting strategy and reviewing the calls that
matter. Reporting stops being a Friday fire drill. And every account, including the quiet ones that
used to leak unnoticed, gets read the way a senior would read it, every day.
That is the bar we build Adgent to. It is a team of AI agents working toward each client's marketing
goals: it remembers what you confirm about each brand, takes the initiative on what it finds, and
carries each decision into the next report, account move and measured result. Each account keeps its
own baselines, memory and work history.
If you would rather see it than read about it, start with the client account you are least sure about.
Adgent reads it, ranks the leaks by monthly impact and returns the verdict with that account's evidence
underneath.
Frequently asked
Q: What's the best AI tool for a media buying agency?
A: One that reads each client account across Meta and Google as its own world, gives each a position-first verdict, and carries the decision into reports and account work. For an agency, the differentiator is not cleverness on one account; it is the same senior-level judgment applied to the fortieth client as to the first.
Q: Can AI manage multiple client accounts?
A: Yes. A good AI media buyer gives each client its own baselines, brand memory, decisions and work history. It reads every connected account and ranks which ones need attention first, so a small team can cover more clients without dropping the quiet leaks.
Q: How does each client's context stay separate?
A: Each analysis starts from one client's connected sources, confirmed brand context and past decisions. The workspace can order separate verdicts by urgency, but one client's performance does not become another client's benchmark or recommendation.
Q: How does an AI media buyer help agencies scale?
A: It takes on the reasoning layer: the daily account read, anomaly detection and report building. Junior teams start from a worked recommendation instead of a blank dashboard, while senior buyers spend their time on strategy and the calls that matter.
Q: Can AI generate client reports?
A: Yes. Describe the report in a sentence and it comes back built, leading with what changed, why and what the team did about it. Share a dated no-login link, reopen the document in Adgent or export it as a PDF.
Q: Does it work across Meta and Google?
A: Yes. Meta and Google are read side by side for each client, with GA4, Search Console and Merchant Center alongside for context. The verdict rests on the client's whole working record instead of one platform's view.

# AI media buyer vs Performance Max vs dashboard · Adgent
URL: https://adgent.app/ai-media-buyer-vs-performance-max-vs-dashboard

Blog Comparison
AI media buyer vs Performance Max vs dashboard: which do you need?
They get compared as if they were the same purchase, but they are not even the same
category. One reports what happened, one optimizes the auction for you, one reasons about your account
for you. Here is how to tell which one you actually need.
Adgent · Notes from building the analyst
Type
Comparison
Reading time
8 min
Published
21 July 2026
On this page
The three, side by side
When a dashboard is enough
When Performance Max fits
When you need an AI media buyer
How to choose
Where Adgent sits
Frequently asked
All articles
Ask an AI engine “AI media buyer vs Performance Max vs dashboard” and it will try to rank them like
competing products. That framing is the mistake. These three are compared constantly, but they aren't
rival tools fighting for the same slot. They are three different layers of the same job, and the honest
answer to “which do you need” is usually “it depends what you are trying to do, and probably more than
one”.
Short answer
Pick by the job. A dashboard if you just need to see the numbers and read them yourself.
Performance Max if you want Google's AI to optimize bids and placements inside its own
auction. An AI media buyer if you want judgment on your side: reasoning across Meta and
Google that continues into the next piece of growth work. Most serious advertisers run all three.
So let's separate them cleanly. A dashboard reports. Performance Max
optimizes the auction. An AI media buyer reasons for you. Get that distinction
right and the choice makes itself.
The short version
One shows you the score. One plays the game. One tells you whether you are playing the right game at
all.
The three, side by side
Compare them against the capabilities that decide the outcome. Performance Max is genuinely good at
auction optimization, and the table gives it credit for that.
Capability Dashboard Performance Max (platform AI) AI media buyer
Whose side it's on Yours (reporting) The auction Yours
Reasons about why a metric moved No No Yes
Reads Meta and Google together Partly Google only Yes
Reacts to auction signals in real time No Yes No
Carries the decision into work No Inside Google Yes
Keeps reasoning, move and result linked No No Yes
Holds advice back when the signal underneath is unreliable No No Yes
Best for Seeing the data Auction-side scale Judgment and execution
The table doesn't strawman Performance Max: it executes, it scales, and inside Google's auction
it is faster than anything else here. The gaps are structural: it works for the auction, on one
platform, and it can't tell you why.
When a dashboard is enough
A dashboard (Looker Studio, a GA4 view, whatever your agency built in a spreadsheet) does one thing
well: it renders your data so you can read it. For a real set of situations, that is genuinely all you
need.
If you run a single channel, check it yourself every day, and already know what each metric means and
what you would do about it, a clean dashboard is the right tool. You don't need software to reason for you
if you are doing the reasoning fine on your own. The dashboard's honesty is its limit: it hands you the
numbers and stops. The analysis, the “why” and the decision are all still yours.
Where a dashboard runs out of road is the moment you have more accounts than mornings. Two platforms,
five clients, a ROAS that dropped and you don't know why: a dashboard shows you that it dropped
and leaves you to work out the rest. That isn't a flaw; it is just where its job ends.
When Performance Max is the right tool
Performance
Max is Google's goal-based campaign type: you give it a target and creative assets, and its AI decides
bids, placements and audiences across Search, Display, YouTube, Gmail and Maps to hit that target. Meta's
equivalent is Advantage+. And here is the honest part: they are good at what they
do.
Fed clean conversion data and a real optimization goal, Performance Max is a strong auction-side engine.
It reacts to bid signals faster than any human, tests placement combinations at a scale you couldn't
manage by hand, and genuinely finds pockets of cheap conversion volume. If your job is “get me more of
this conversion at roughly this cost inside Google”, Performance Max often does it well.
Its limits are structural, not about quality. It optimizes toward Google's auction, not your
margin, so it is happy to spend into view-through credit or count conversions your store never saw. It is
Google-only, so it can't reason about how Meta interacts with it. And it hides account structure, so when
it drifts you often can't see why. Performance Max is a superb executor. It was never designed to be the
judgment on your side of the table.
When you need an AI media buyer
An AI media buyer is the layer none of the others cover: the
reasoning part of a media buyer's job. It reads accounts across Meta and Google, reasons about how they
are built and why a number moved, commits to a conclusion, then carries that conclusion into the next
report, plan, campaign build or account move.
You need one when the question you keep asking is “why”, not “what”. Why did ROAS drop yesterday? Is
this Performance Max campaign earning, or taking credit for brand demand you already own? Which of my
accounts needs me first today? Those are judgment questions, and neither a dashboard nor Performance Max
is built to answer them.
The distinguishing traits are the ones platform AI does not cover. It works for the advertiser, not
the auction. It reads Meta and Google together, with your analytics alongside. When the measurement
under a number cannot be trusted, it changes the basis of the recommendation. The decision, next move
and later result remain in one account history.
How to choose
Strip it to an if/then and the decision is quick:
If you just need to see the numbers and you are comfortable reading them yourself, a
dashboard is enough. Don't over-buy.
If you want the platform to optimize within its own auction (bids, placements,
volume at a target CPA or ROAS inside Google or Meta), reach for Performance Max or
Advantage+. Feed it clean data and it earns its keep.
If you want judgment on your side of the table (reasoning across platforms,
careful with numbers it cannot trust, with the next piece of work already attached), choose an
AI media buyer . It asks whether the auction-side tools are doing the right thing.
These aren't mutually exclusive. The common, correct answer for a serious advertiser is: run
Performance Max where it earns, keep a dashboard for a quick glance, and put an AI media buyer over the
top to supervise both, to catch the Performance Max campaign that is winning on paper and taking credit it
didn't earn.
Where Adgent sits
Adgent reads every connected Meta and Google Ads account each day, with GA4, Search Console and
Merchant Center alongside, and leads with the verdict: decisions ranked by what they cost, each with an
estimated monthly amount. Ask “why did Meta ROAS drop?” and you get an answer with the evidence from
your own account. The same decision can continue into a report, media plan, campaign build, recurring
agent or account move, with the result available to the next read.
What that looks like on one live account (a hotel group, August 2026): asked for a ₺250 ($5.16) cost
per conversion where a booking cost about ₺4,028 ($83), it declined and showed the arithmetic. That is
the check Performance Max's own reporting can't give you.
For the longer definition, read what an AI media buyer actually
is , or see the reasoning applied in how to audit a
Google Ads account .
Frequently asked
Q: Is Performance Max an AI media buyer?
A: No. Performance Max is Google's own AI, optimizing bids and placements toward Google's
auction. An AI media buyer sits on the advertiser's side, reasons across Meta and Google together,
and carries the decision into the next piece of account work. Performance Max is a campaign type;
an AI media buyer is a decision layer that works for you.
Q: Can an AI media buyer replace Performance Max?
A: No, and it isn't meant to. Performance Max runs the auction-side bidding inside Google
Ads; an AI media buyer sits a layer above and decides whether Performance Max is the right campaign to
run, how much budget it should get, and whether its reported ROAS is taking credit for demand you
already own. They operate at different layers, so the AI media buyer manages Performance Max rather
than replacing it.
Q: Do I need both Performance Max and an AI media buyer?
A: Often, yes. Performance Max is a strong auction-side tool when you feed it good signals
and real conversion data. An AI media buyer decides whether those signals are right, whether the
campaign is actually earning, and what to change when it drifts. One executes bids; the other holds
the judgment.
Q: Is a dashboard enough for a small account?
A: Sometimes. If you run a single channel, check it daily yourself, and already know what
each metric means, a dashboard that renders your data cleanly can be enough. Once you are across two
or more platforms or need the cause behind a movement, a dashboard stops answering the question you
actually have.
Q: Which is best for an agency?
A: An AI media buyer, in most cases. Agencies run many accounts across Meta and Google and
cannot read every one deeply every day. One that reads both platforms on each account, flags
numbers it cannot trust and carries the verdict into reports and account work gives every client
the same senior standard. Performance Max still runs inside the Google accounts; the AI media buyer
supervises it.
Q: Does an AI media buyer work with Performance Max campaigns?
A: Yes. It reads Performance Max campaigns like any other, questions a reported ROAS
that looks too good, flags when the numbers underneath cannot be trusted and turns the finding into
a budget or structure decision. It works with Performance Max, not against it.
Q: What's the difference between platform AI and an AI media buyer?
A: Platform AI, such as Performance Max or Meta Advantage+, optimizes toward the
platform's own auction and hides account structure from the buyer. An AI media buyer works on the
advertiser's side, reasons across Meta and Google, explains why a metric moved and carries the
decision into work. Same word, AI, on opposite sides of the table.

# Attribution window: why day-one numbers lie · Adgent
URL: https://adgent.app/attribution-window-day-one-data

Blog Field note
The 7-day window is lying to you before noon
Meta's attribution window quietly rewrites yesterday's numbers for a week. Pausing a
campaign on day-one data is the most expensive reflex in performance marketing. Here is how to read a
metric that is not done yet.
Adgent · Notes from building the analyst
Type
Field note
Topic
Attribution
Reading time
8 min
Published
14 April 2026
On this page
Why the morning read is worst
Reading a number that isn't done
The exception that costs money
What the window does
Fast metrics, slow metrics
Deciding before it closes
Questions
All articles
Open Ads Manager at 9am and a campaign you launched yesterday shows a ROAS of 1.9×. The instinct is
immediate and wrong: pause it, reallocate, move on. The problem is that 1.9× is not a result.
It is a snapshot of a number still being written.
Short answer
Meta ROAS looks worse in the morning because attribution is not finished. Spend is already counted,
but many of the conversions it earned have not been credited yet: Meta's 7-day click window keeps
attaching them for days. So you are dividing a complete cost by an incomplete revenue. The number
reads pessimistic by construction, and almost always revises up.
Meta attributes conversions on a 7-day click, 1-day view basis by default. A purchase that happens
today can be credited to an ad someone clicked six days ago. Day-one ROAS is therefore missing
conversions it will eventually earn and almost always revises up .
Why the morning read is the worst read
Early in a metric's life, the denominator (spend) is complete but the numerator (attributed revenue)
is not. You are dividing a finished number by an unfinished one. The result reads pessimistic by
construction, and it reads most pessimistic first thing in the morning, before the day's conversions
have landed.
The rule, in one line
A number inside the attribution window is not a verdict. It is a question that has not finished
being answered.
How to read a number that is not done
You do not need to stop looking at fresh data. You need to stop trusting it like mature data. Three
habits make the difference:
Mark the window. Treat anything inside 7 days as provisional. Flag it visually so
no one reacts to it as final.
Compare like-aged data. Judge a day-one read against other day-one reads, not
against a 30-day average that has fully matured.
Wait for the floor, not the ceiling. Make kill decisions when a metric has
stopped revising, usually day 3 to 4, not on the first reading.
The exception that costs real money
Waiting is not free. A genuinely broken campaign (wrong audience, broken landing page, creative that
misses) burns budget every hour you give it the benefit of the doubt. The discipline is not “never act
early.” It is knowing which signals mature and which do not.
Click-through rate, CPM and cost per click are effectively final within hours. They do not wait on
attribution. If CTR is a third of your account average on day one, that is a real signal and you can
act on it. Revenue-side metrics (ROAS, CPA, conversion rate) are the ones still being written. Kill on
the fast signals; wait on the slow ones.
Adgent is a team of AI agents working toward your marketing goals, and this judgement is built into
how it reads an account. It re-pulls a trailing window every day, 28 days on Meta and 14 on Google, and
the window always ends on the last full day, so a revision lands in the read instead of ambushing it.
And when the measurement behind a ROAS or CPA figure cannot support a call, the Trust Gate lets it raise a finding but never an action.
What the 7-day window actually does to your numbers
The default setting on most Meta accounts is 7-day
click, 1-day view . In plain terms: if someone clicks your ad and buys any time in the next
week, that sale gets credited back to the ad, and back to the day the spend landed. That is why
yesterday's ROAS keeps changing today, and the day after, and the day after that. You are not watching
a stable number wobble; you are watching an incomplete number fill in.
The shape of that fill-in is predictable. A large share of a cohort's eventual conversions typically
lands in the first 24 hours, then the curve tapers: day two adds less, day three less again, until by
day four or five the number has mostly stopped moving. How large that first-day share is depends on
the account and on how long your buyers deliberate. Overlay that on the morning read and the effect
compounds: at 9am you are not even seeing a full day-one figure, you are seeing the overnight slice of
it. The denominator, spend, is already whole. The numerator is a few hours old. No wonder ROAS looks
thin.
This is also why day-one comparisons across campaigns are treacherous. A campaign whose buyers convert
fast will look like a hero at breakfast; one whose buyers deliberate for three days will look like a
dog, and by Friday they can swap places entirely. The settling window delays the number and can reorder
the rankings.
Which metrics mature slowly, and which are already final
The trap is not fresh data; it is treating every metric on the dashboard as if it matured at the same
speed. It does not. Split your KPIs into two buckets and the morning stops lying to you.
Effectively final within hours. CPM, CPC, click-through rate, hook rate,
frequency, impressions. These are delivery metrics: they do not wait on a purchase to be attributed,
so what you see in the morning is close to what you will see at the end of the window.
Still being written. ROAS, CPA, conversion rate, cost per purchase: anything with
attributed revenue or conversions in it. These live inside the window and revise for days, almost
always upward.
The rule that falls out of this is clean: kill on the fast signals, wait on the slow
ones. If day-one CTR is a third of your account average, that is a real, mature signal: the
creative is not landing and you can act now. If day-one ROAS is a third of your account average, that
is mostly the window talking, and pausing means you will never see the conversions that were about to
land. Whether you run CBO or ABO, Advantage+ or Performance Max, the maturity split is the same: the
platform structure changes how budget flows, not how fast attribution settles.
How to decide before the window closes
Waiting a full seven days for certainty is not a real option, because a genuinely broken campaign
burns budget every hour you give it the benefit of the doubt. The discipline is deciding on the right
evidence early, not deciding blind. Three moves make that possible.
First, act on the mature metrics immediately. Broken landing page, mistargeted
audience, a creative with a dead hook rate: these show up in delivery data that is already final on
day one. You do not need attribution to catch them, and you should not wait for it.
Second, compare like-aged data. Never judge a day-one read against a 30-day average
that has fully matured. Line it up against other day-one reads: the same campaign last week, or a
sibling campaign at the same age. Same-age comparison strips the window out of the picture and shows
you the real difference.
Third, wait for the floor, not the ceiling. Make your kill-or-scale call when a
revenue metric has stopped revising, usually day three to four, rather than on the first reading. By
then the curve has flattened enough that the number is close to true, and you have still acted well
before the window formally closes. It is the same discipline that keeps a blended average from hiding a placement leak : the
aggregate looks calm while the truth sits one layer down. If you want the mechanics of pulling those
layers apart by hand, the Google Ads audit playbook
walks the same read across search.
The discipline is simple to state and hard to hold under pressure: a number inside the window
is a draft. Read it as one.
Frequently asked
Q: Why does my Meta ROAS look low in the morning?
A: Because spend is fully counted but the conversions it earned are not all credited yet. Meta's 7-day click window keeps attaching purchases for days, so at 9am you are dividing a complete cost by an incomplete revenue. The figure reads pessimistic by construction and almost always revises up.
Q: How long does Meta attribution take to settle?
A: The default window is 7-day click, 1-day view, but most of the movement is over sooner. A large share of conversions typically lands in the first 24 hours, then the curve tapers; by day three to four a revenue metric has usually stopped revising.
Q: Which metrics mature slowly and which are final?
A: Delivery metrics (CPM, CPC, CTR, hook rate, frequency) are effectively final within hours. Revenue-side metrics (ROAS, CPA, conversion rate) live inside the attribution window and revise for days. Kill on the fast signals, wait on the slow ones.
Q: Should I pause a campaign on day-one data?
A: Only on mature signals. A dead hook rate, a mistargeted audience or a broken landing page shows up in day-one delivery data, and you should act. But pausing on day-one ROAS means killing conversions that were still about to land.
Q: What is the 7-day attribution window?
A: It is Meta's default rule for crediting sales to ads: if someone clicks and buys within seven days, the purchase is credited back to the ad and to the day the spend landed. That is why yesterday's ROAS keeps filling in for a week.
Q: How do I decide before the window closes?
A: Act immediately on mature delivery metrics, compare only like-aged data instead of a matured average, and make revenue-based kill decisions once a metric stops revising, usually day three to four. That is early enough to protect budget, late enough to be true.

# Can AI audit your ad accounts? · Adgent

Blog Explainer
Can AI audit your ad accounts?
Yes, and for the tedious, high-volume checks it does better than a person. But an audit is
more than a checklist, and there is a ceiling where judgment takes over. What AI catches, and what still
needs you.

Where AI helps
Where it hits a ceiling
Installed is not useful
Catches and misses
The Adgent example
All articles
“Is there an AI that audits ad accounts?” Yes, and the plain version of that answer is more useful than
the marketing version. AI does part of an audit better than any person and part of it not at all.
Knowing where the line sits is what lets you trust the output, so here it is: where AI genuinely helps,
and where it hits a wall.
Short answer
Yes, AI can audit ad accounts. It reads Meta and Google through their APIs, runs the
checks a senior buyer would (wasted spend, placement leakage, tracking gaps, ROAS drift) and ranks
findings by what they cost, without anyone opening a tab. It is strongest on the tedious, high-volume
checks. It hits a ceiling on judgment: the strategic call, the business context, deciding whether an
ambiguous number is real. The strongest audit AI makes that boundary visible and returns the evidence
a person needs to interpret the finding.
Where AI genuinely helps in an audit
An audit is mostly reading: every campaign, ad set, placement, search term and conversion setting,
looking for the leaks. That is high-volume, rule-based, tedious work, and it is exactly where AI
outperforms a tired person on the fortieth ad set.
Wasted spend. Wasted search terms, leaked placements, duplicate retargeting, budget
stuck in something that stopped converting: the line-item leaks that reopen week after week. AI reads
all of them, every time, without skimming.
Reading both platforms. Meta and Google in one read instead of two tabs. Run it
over several accounts and each one is still audited on its own.
ROAS leaks hiding in the average. A healthy blended 3.8× can conceal a placement
running at 1.1×. AI breaks the average apart and finds the leak the summary number hides.
Tracking gaps. A broken pixel, a double-counted event, a misconfigured conversion:
measurement problems that quietly poison every decision downstream. Flagging these is often the single
most valuable thing an audit does.
Ranking by what each finding costs. Not a 40-item report of everything, but the
handful of findings that actually move money, ordered by impact. That prioritisation is analysis, not
just detection.
And unlike a one-off audit, AI keeps the read current. The high-drift checks (wasted terms, placement
leakage, pacing) change week to week, so a continuous read beats a scheduled review that is stale the
day after it is delivered. For the full manual version of these checks, see the
Google Ads audit checklist and its Meta twin,
the Meta Ads account audit .
In one line
Detection is where AI wins. Interpretation is where it needs you.
Where AI hits its ceiling
An audit combines leak detection with judgment. AI is strong at the first and limited at the second.
Business context it can't see. A “wasteful” campaign might be a deliberate brand
play, a promo period, or feeding an offline conversion the API never reports. AI flags the anomaly;
only you know it was intentional.
Strategic calls. “Is this even the right channel mix?” or “should we be on this
platform at all?” are questions above the account. An audit reads what is there; it does not decide
the strategy that put it there.
Numbers that aren't safe yet. Yesterday's ROAS is still revising inside its
attribution window; a confident-looking metric can be fiction from a broken tag. AI can
flag that a number is not safe to act on yet, but the final call on whether it is real stays
with a person. More on that in why day-one data
lies .
The account move. Finding the leak and choosing the right fix are different acts.
A useful audit turns the finding into a concrete next move while keeping the business decision with
the account team.
None of this makes AI a weak auditor. It makes it a partial one, and the right partial, if you point
it at detection and keep a person on interpretation.
“Is the pixel installed” is not “is the pixel useful”
One tracking check deserves its own section, because most audits stop one question short of it.
Confirming a pixel is installed and firing is a green tick. Whether it produces a signal an optimiser
can actually learn from is a different question, and the answer can be no while every tick stays
green.
A live account we read shows the gap. Thirty days of pixel data looked busy:
Custom events 65,042
Initiate checkout 16,404
Add to cart 515
Lead 216
Purchase 4
Meta pixel events over 30 days. One live account (hotel group), 11 August 2026.
Installed, firing, plenty of volume. Then the row that matters: 4 purchases . Meta's
own guidance is to structure ad sets for
a
minimum of 50 events over a 7-day period . Put both on the same window and four purchases in a month
is about one a week against a floor of fifty, roughly 2% of it. That is not a thin signal. It is below
the point where a conversion campaign can learn anything at all.
The distinction
Installed and firing is a tracking check. Whether the event that pays fires often enough to train on is
a signal-quality check. An audit that only does the first one hands you a green tick over an account
that cannot optimise.
Asked to build a sales campaign on that account, Adgent checked the pixel first and declined to build
on it: the setup was technically possible, but there was no purchase signal to learn from. The useful
finding was not “your pixel is broken”, because it was not. It pointed at fixing the purchase event
before building anything that optimises toward it. That check costs nothing before spend and is
expensive to discover after. Ask it of any audit, human or automated: does it read conversion counts
against what the platform needs to learn, or does it stop at “firing”?
Catches and misses, side by side
Audit task AI A person
Wasted search terms and placements Catches it Not needed
ROAS leaks inside a blended average Catches it Not needed
Tracking and conversion gaps Catches it Confirms
Conversion volume against the learning floor Catches it Not needed
Is a flagged number trustworthy yet? Flags it Decides
Business context behind an anomaly Can't see it Owns it
Strategy and the right channel mix Can't decide it Owns it
Choosing the account move Prepares the evidence Owns the business decision
The split is clean: AI owns detection at scale; a person owns context, trust and the final call.
What a good audit AI looks like: the Adgent example
To make it concrete, here is how the audit works inside Adgent. Every connected Meta and Google Ads
account is read every day, with GA4, Search Console and Merchant Center alongside. Ten specialists each
read the account from their own angle: Measurement Integrity looks for tracking and attribution
problems that make every other number suspect, Delivery & Burn Watch for spend with near-zero return,
Audience-Overlap Detector for ad sets competing in the same auction. What comes back is a ranked set of
decisions, each with evidence and an estimated monthly amount, not a 40-page report.
On one live account (19 campaigns, 47 ad sets, 75 ads), the full analysis took 1 hour 49 minutes, run
without anyone at the keyboard (28 September 2026).
Two behaviours make the output useful. First, findings are ranked by what they cost, so the account
team starts with the leak that matters instead of a flat checklist. Second, when a metric window cannot
carry a decision yet, Adgent changes the basis of the diagnosis instead of turning a still-settling
number into an account move.
So, is there an AI that audits ad accounts? Yes, and the good ones are clear about the line: they catch
the leaks a person would miss on the fortieth ad set, and they hand the judgment calls back to you.
Who wrote this Written by the people building Adgent, the AI employee that carries brand context into every growth decision. Related product: the Decisions screen .
Bring the same question to your own account. Adgent returns its position, the evidence underneath and what the finding is worth a month.
Pricing
Frequently asked.
Q: Is there an AI that audits ad accounts?
A: Yes. AI tools can read Meta and Google through their APIs, check the signals a senior buyer would (wasted spend, placement leakage, tracking gaps, ROAS drift) and rank findings by what they cost. The stronger ones read both platforms together, pull context from GA4 and Search Console, and return the evidence and next move instead of a flat checklist.
Q: Can AI audit a Google Ads or Meta Ads account?
A: Yes. AI reads the account through the platform API and runs the checks a manual audit would (conversion tracking, search-term and placement waste, budget pacing, bid strategy) and keeps them current instead of running once. Where it wins over a person is coverage and consistency: it reads every line, never gets bored on the fortieth ad set, and re-runs on schedule.
Q: What can AI catch in an ad account audit?
A: AI is strong on the rule-based, high-volume checks: wasted search terms and leaked placements, budget-pacing problems, duplicate retargeting, ROAS leaks hidden inside a healthy blended average, tracking gaps like a broken pixel or a misconfigured conversion, and conversion volume too low for the platform to learn from. It is also good at reading Meta and Google together, work that is tedious and error-prone by hand.
Q: What can't AI catch in an ad account audit?
A: AI hits a ceiling on judgment and context. It can flag that a number looks wrong but cannot always know the business reason behind it: a planned promo, a seasonal shift, a brand-safety constraint, an offline conversion it cannot see. It struggles with strategic calls (is this the right channel mix at all?), with data it has no access to, and with deciding whether an ambiguous number is real enough to act on. It surfaces the finding; a person still owns the interpretation and the final call.
Q: How long does an AI ad account audit take?
A: A manual audit of a mid-sized account takes a senior buyer a few hours to a day. Software reading through the API runs unattended: on one live account of 19 campaigns, Adgent's full analysis took 1 hour 49 minutes (September 2026), and it repeats every day, so the read stays current as the account drifts week to week.
Q: How does an AI audit become ongoing account work?
A: The audit should not end as a PDF. Each material finding becomes a ranked decision with its evidence and next move, then returns on later reads with the result attached. That turns a one-off leak hunt into a current account history.
Q: Can AI audit multiple ad accounts at once?
A: Yes, in the sense that matters for an agency: every connected account is read every day and gets its own ranked decisions, so a roster gets read without anyone opening a tab. Be precise about what “at once” means, though: each account is audited on its own, and what it remembers about one account never reaches across to another.
