# Can AI run your ad account? Where it stops · Adgent
URL: https://adgent.app/can-ai-run-your-ad-account

Blog Essay
Can AI run your ad account?
The honest answer to the “hand it your accounts and go home” pitch. AI can do the reasoning
and the busywork, but it should not hold the last click on live spend. The judgment automates; the
accountability stays human.
Adgent · Notes from building the analyst
Type
Essay
Reading time
7 min
Published
22 July 2026
Updated
31 October 2026
On this page
What AI does well
What still needs a human
In practice
The wrong promise
The right design
Frequently asked
All articles
Every second ad-tech pitch this year makes the same promise: hand the AI your accounts and go home, no
people required. It is a great demo and a bad idea, not because the AI is weak but because it is aimed at
the wrong job. So let's be honest about the split: what can AI genuinely run in an ad account, and what
still needs a human with a hand on the switch?
Short answer
Mostly, yes, but not alone. AI can do the reasoning and the busywork: daily reads,
diagnosis, drafting fixes and whole campaigns. What it should not do is hold the last click on
live spend. Advertising runs on numbers that mislead (attribution windows, broken conversions) and the
human is the one accountable for catching them. The judgment automates. The accountability stays human.
What AI genuinely does well
Start with the part that isn't hype. The reasoning-heavy, repetitive core of managing Meta and Google
is exactly what modern AI is good at, and it is good enough now that pretending otherwise is its own kind
of dishonesty.
It reads the whole account. Every campaign, ad set, placement and creative across
Meta and Google, without getting bored on the 40th ad set. A human buyer skims; AI actually reads all
of it.
It diagnoses why . It traces a ROAS drop to a placement, a tired creative
or CPM inflation on Audience Network, then ranks that cause by impact.
It drafts the fix, and the campaign. A budget shift, a CBO-to-ABO restructure, a
whole new build with copy and targeting. It writes the change so you are editing, not starting from a
blank page.
It never skips a day. No weekends, no “I'll check Monday”. The anomaly that would
have cost you three days of wasted spend gets raised at the next read.
Add it up and that is most of the hours a media buyer used to spend. If someone tells you AI can't do
the reading, the diagnosis or the drafting, they haven't used a good one. This is the real, unglamorous
bulk of the job, and AI runs it well.
The short version
The busywork was never the hard part. The hard part was knowing which number to trust.
What still needs a human
Here is where the hands-off pitch quietly breaks. The remaining slice of the job is small in hours but
enormous in consequence, and it is precisely the part AI should not own.
The final call on live spend
Drafting a change and committing it to a live account are two different acts with two different risk
profiles. The draft is reversible thinking; the commit moves real money. Keeping a human on that last
click isn't distrust of the AI. It is an accountability boundary. Someone has to own the decision, and
“the model did it” is not an answer you want to give a client whose CPA doubled overnight.
Judgment on untrustworthy numbers
This is the deep reason, and it is worth sitting with. Ad platforms hand you numbers that are often not
true yet, or not true in the way they look:
Attribution windows. Yesterday's ROAS will keep revising upward for a week as
conversions land. Act on day-one data and you will cut a winner. A human learns to wait; a system
optimizing for a fixed reward does not.
Misconfigured conversions. A broken pixel or a double-counted event can make ROAS
literally unmeasurable, or twice reality. The number looks confident. It is fiction.
Credit that isn't performance. A “great” placement can be view-through credit in
disguise, taking the bow for conversions it didn't cause.
A good AI can flag all of these, and the good ones do. But the final judgment on whether a
number is real enough to bet spend on belongs with a person, because catching a misleading number takes
suspicion the metric itself can't provide. For more on one of these traps, see
why day-one data misleads .
What that looks like in practice
An example from one live account, a hotel group, in August 2026. Before writing a single campaign,
the agent checked whether the account could actually teach one. Over thirty days the pixel had fired
plenty: 65,042 custom events and 16,404 initiate-checkouts , and 4
purchases . Meta's delivery system needs about 50 optimization events a week to
leave the learning phase ( Meta's
developer documentation ). Four a month isn't a slow start; it is below the floor where the algorithm can
learn anything at all.
Adgent Meta campaign pre-check · one live account, August 2026 · translated from Turkish
“The setup is technically possible: the page and pixel exist, and the create would not be
rejected. But there is no real purchase signal a conversion-focused sales campaign could learn
from.”
So the answer wasn't “here is your conversion campaign”. Building it anyway would have spent budget
teaching a model on four data points. That is the reasoning half of the job doing its work: not drafting
faster, but noticing that the thing you asked for shouldn't be built yet, and showing you the account's
own numbers as the reason. The human still makes the call. The point is that the call arrives before the
spend, not after.
Why “set it and forget it” is the wrong promise
The autonomy pitch borrows its confidence from games. AI conquered chess and Go because those are
closed systems: fixed rules, a clean reward, and every input is true. Advertising is none of that.
Advertising is an open game played on a leaky scoreboard. The reward function, ROAS or CPA, is
measured by instruments that break, lag and mislead. So when a system acts on those numbers with nobody
in the loop, it doesn't remove risk. It removes the one thing standing between a bad number and your
budget: the human who would have caught it. Autonomy doesn't make the numbers more
trustworthy. It just deletes the check.
That is the limit of “set it and forget it” on a live ad account. Platform data can still be settling,
misconfigured or credited on the wrong window. The product has to expose that uncertainty before it
becomes a budget move.
The right design: AI does the work; the owner makes the live-spend call
Give AI the daily reading, diagnosis and drafting. Keep execution as a named owner decision. That is
how Adgent is built: its agents work toward your marketing goals, remember what you confirm about the
brand and bring the next account move forward with the evidence attached.
It reads and ranks
Every connected account is read every day, before you open your laptop. Each decision carries an
estimated monthly amount, and the list is ranked by what it costs, so you start with the verdict, not a
wall of charts.
It explains, with evidence
You ask “why did Meta ROAS drop?” and get a strategist's answer with the evidence from your own account,
including the awkward truth when a number is still inside its attribution window and shouldn't be acted on
yet.
It prepares the account move
When a fix is ready, its card shows the current state, proposed state and reason. Once the owner accepts
it, the change executes and lands in the ledger with the value it replaced. For supported reversible
changes, the agent can prepare the inverse from that row for approval.
Here is the split, laid out plainly: where AI does the work, and where the human stays on the
click.
Task in running an ad account AI does it Human still owns it
Daily read of the whole account Yes n/a
Diagnosing why a metric moved Yes n/a
Drafting fixes and new campaigns Yes n/a
Spotting anomalies Yes n/a
Flagging untrustworthy numbers Yes Confirms
Final call on ambiguous data No Yes
The last click on live spend No Yes
Read it left to right and the pitch inverts: AI does almost all of it, and the human keeps
the two rows that carry the accountability. Not less automation: automation aimed correctly.
Can AI run your ad account? It can run the work. The judgment automates well. But the accountability,
the last click and the call on a number you can't trust, is the part worth keeping human, and a tool that
is honest about that is the one you can actually put on a client account.
Frequently asked
Q: Can AI fully run a Google Ads account?
A: AI can do almost all of the work (daily reads, diagnosis, drafting campaigns and fixes),
but it shouldn't run the account unsupervised. The last click on live spend belongs to a human,
because Google Ads numbers can be untrustworthy in ways only judgment catches: attribution windows,
misconfigured conversions, view-through credit. The judgment automates; the accountability stays
human.
Q: Should I let AI change my campaigns automatically?
A: Not without a named account owner. The AI should do the analysis and prepare the exact
move; execution should remain an explicit owner decision, with the before-state recorded. That keeps
the speed of automation and a clear line of accountability.
Q: Does AI replace a media buyer?
A: No. It automates the reasoning and the busywork (account reads, diagnosis, drafting) so
the buyer gets back time for strategy, creative direction and the business calls account data
cannot make.
Q: Is it safe to give AI access to my ad account?
A: Assess the connection scopes, credential storage, vendor access, write controls and
audit trail. A credible tool states each one precisely and records every account move with its
before-state. See Adgent's current controls on Security and data .
Q: What can AI not do in ad management?
A: AI shouldn't hold the last click on live spend, and it shouldn't be the final judge of
whether the numbers underneath a decision are real: an attribution window that will revise for a week,
a misconfigured conversion, view-through credit dressed as performance. It can flag those, but the
final call on ambiguous data stays human.
Q: Can AI manage Meta and Google together?
A: It can read them together, which is where AI is strongest: one pass across both
platforms, with GA4 and Search Console alongside, and one ranked list of decisions instead of
separate tabs. Account work still executes per platform, while one history keeps the evidence.
Q: What does read-only mean here?
A: It means the AI can inspect account data but cannot mutate the account through that
connection. Execution access is a separate product state for account moves.

# CBO vs ABO vs Advantage+ in 2026: which to use? · Adgent
URL: https://adgent.app/cbo-vs-abo-vs-advantage-plus

Blog Comparison
CBO vs ABO vs Advantage+: which budget model in 2026?
For years the argument was CBO vs ABO. Then Advantage+ made it a three-way question,
because now you can hand Meta the budget, the split and the whole structure. How to pick by what you are
actually trying to buy.
Adgent · Notes from building the analyst
Type
Comparison
Reading time
12 min
Published
22 July 2026
Updated
31 October 2026
On this page
The one question
The three side by side
ABO: a fair test
CBO: scaling a winner
Where CBO quietly fails
The volume question
Advantage+: trusting the signal
The decision guide
Moving from ABO to CBO
The same decision on Google
Only half the job
All articles
The old fight was simple: do you set budgets at the ad-set level (ABO) or let Meta split one budget
across ad sets for you (CBO)? Reasonable people argued both sides for years. Advantage+ rewrote the
question by taking over audiences, placements and structure along with the budget split. So “CBO or
ABO?” is now “how much of the campaign do I want to run myself?”
Short answer
Pick by what you are buying . Use ABO when you need a fair test of each
audience or creative, or run under about 50 conversions a week: every option gets its own budget. Use
CBO to scale known winners
at volume, letting Meta push spend to whatever is performing. Use Advantage+ when you
want Meta to run the entire structure and you trust your signal enough to hand it over.
That reframing is the whole point. These three are not three flavours of the same thing ranked best to
worst. They are three different amounts of control, and the right one depends on what you are trying
to do that week: testing, scaling, or handing the wheel to Meta. Each one in turn, then a decision guide
you can use.
The one question that picks for you
Before the definitions, the shortcut: what are you buying with this campaign? Not
“which is best”, but best at what?
Buying a clean read on which audience or creative wins? That is
ABO .
Buying volume from things you have already proven work? That is
CBO .
Buying Meta's judgment across the whole structure because your signal is strong?
That is Advantage+ .
Almost every “which should I use” question dissolves once you answer that. Now the detail.
The three side by side
The comparison across the dimensions that actually change your decision: who holds the controls, what
each is best for, how it learns, when it wins, and where it bites you.
Dimension ABO (ad-set budget) CBO (campaign budget) Advantage+ (Meta runs it)
Control level You set every ad-set budget by hand You set structure, Meta splits budget Meta owns budget, audience and placement
Best for Fair, comparable testing Scaling proven winners Hands-off scale on a strong signal
Learning behaviour Each set learns on its own fixed budget Meta reallocates toward the day's winners Meta learns across the whole account
When it wins You need to know which option earns You have winners and want volume Clean conversion signal, broad catalogue
Risk Manual, slow, easy to over-fragment Meta can starve a set you wanted to test You lose control; it can chase the wrong signal
Read the table as a spectrum of control, not a leaderboard: left is you driving, right is Meta driving. The right-hand column is not “best”; it gives up the most control, which is right for some accounts and wrong for others.
ABO: when you need a fair test
ABO (ad-set budget optimisation) gives every ad set its own fixed budget that you set
by hand. That single fact is its whole reason to exist: because you control the money per set, every
audience and every creative gets a guaranteed shot at delivery . Nothing gets starved
by Meta's early guesses before it has had a chance to prove itself.
That is what makes ABO the testing tool. If you are comparing five audiences, you want each one to
spend real money before you judge it, not have Meta pour most of it into the audience that happened to
convert first on thin data. ABO forces the fair fight. You read clean, comparable results per set, then
decide what graduates.
The cost is that ABO is manual and slow to scale. You are the one moving budgets around, and it is easy
to over-fragment: split into so many small ad sets that none of them exits the learning phase. ABO is a
scalpel for finding the truth, not a machine for pushing volume. Use it to learn, not to scale.
One more thing people forget: ABO's fairness only holds if you gave each set
enough
budget to exit learning . Five ad sets on $10 a day each is not a fair test. It is five under-powered tests that all
read as noise. If you test in ABO, fund each set to clear its optimisation event a handful of times per
day, or you are paying to learn nothing slowly.
CBO: when you want to scale a winner
CBO (campaign budget optimisation) flips the control: you define the ad sets, but Meta
owns one campaign-level budget and pushes it toward whichever sets are performing that day. You are no
longer hand-tuning each set. Meta does the reallocation, in real time, based on live delivery. Meta now
calls it Advantage campaign budget; the mechanics are the same.
It works for a real reason: the algorithm sees auction dynamics at a resolution and frequency no human
can match, and it keeps rebalancing while you are asleep. It needs two conditions to do that well:
enough conversion volume for the signal to be trustworthy, and comparable ad
sets so the comparison it is making is a fair one. Give it both and it will beat your manual
allocation reliably.
That is exactly what you want once you already know what works. With proven audiences and proven
creative, CBO scales the pool at volume without you watching every set. The winners get fed, the
laggards get throttled, and you do not have to log in at 8am to move the money yourself. It is the
natural next step after ABO has done its job.
The risk is the same mechanism running against you: CBO will starve a set you actually wanted data on.
Drop an unproven audience into a CBO campaign next to a known winner and Meta feeds the winner, so the
newcomer never gets a fair read. That is why CBO is a poor testing tool and a great scaling one. Do not
test in CBO. Scale a winner in it, carefully , without
breaking the thing that was working.
The other CBO trap is scaling too fast. When you raise a CBO budget, you can reopen the learning phase
for the whole campaign, and Meta reshuffles delivery against the new number. Triple it overnight and you
can knock a stable winner off its footing for days. Step budgets up gradually and let each increase
settle: the reallocation engine that makes CBO powerful is the same one that punishes sudden shocks.
On one live account, a request to lift a CBO budget by a third in one go returned this warning before
the budget shifted:
Adgent Account move · one live account, Meta, 30 September 2026
“33% in one step (300.00 → 400.00) is beyond the 20% band: a jump this size can reset the
ad set's learning phase.”
The card named the budget as a campaign (CBO) budget that governs spend across all its ad sets, and
suggested a smaller step of 360 TRY a day (about $7.44, +20%) instead of 400 ($8.26). The 20% band is
Adgent's own ceiling, not a Meta rule.
Where CBO quietly fails you
The failure is not that CBO underperforms. It is that it does its job so well it destroys your ability
to learn anything.
The catch, in one line
CBO optimises for the campaign's total result. If what you need is an answer about one ad set, it will
efficiently deny you that answer.
Put five audiences in a CBO and Meta will find the cheapest one quickly and starve the other four. You
will see one ad set with the overwhelming majority of the spend and four with statistical dust. Now
answer: were those four audiences bad, or did they just never get a fair trial? You cannot
know. The system optimised away the experiment you were trying to run.
The same dynamic bites when your ad sets are not comparable. A $200 cold prospecting set and a $20
retargeting set in the same CBO is not an allocation decision; it is a rigged comparison. Retargeting
will always look cheaper, CBO will always feed it, and you will wake up to an account that has stopped
acquiring anyone new.
Does CBO actually scale better? The volume question
The strongest case for CBO is scale, and it is a real case, but only above a threshold most people do
not check before they flip the switch. CBO's edge comes from having enough conversion signal to
reallocate on. Meta sets the learning threshold at about 50 optimization events per ad set over
7 days ; when the whole campaign produces fewer than that, the algorithm is
making high-stakes decisions on a handful of events, and the variance in that little data will send
your budget chasing noise. It will pile spend onto whichever ad set got lucky on Tuesday, then yank it
away on Thursday, and you will mistake that thrash for optimisation.
Above the threshold, CBO scales genuinely better than manual allocation because it is rebalancing at a
frequency and resolution you cannot. But “scales better” is conditional on the ad sets being
comparable: same funnel stage, same optimisation event, roughly similar economics. Hand CBO a healthy
volume of look-alike ad sets and it will outrun your spreadsheet every time. Hand it volume plus the
prospecting-next-to-retargeting mix above and it will scale you straight into a wall. Volume is
necessary for CBO to win. It is never sufficient on its own.
Advantage+: when you trust your signal
Advantage+ is the newest and the most misunderstood, because people file it next to
CBO when it is a bigger move. CBO hands Meta the budget split . Advantage+ hands Meta the
whole structure : budget, audiences, placements, often the creative combinations too. You bring
the creative and the conversion goal; Meta runs the campaign.
And here is the part the CBO-vs-ABO crowd sometimes will not say: Advantage+ is genuinely good
for some accounts. If you are an ecommerce brand with a broad catalogue and a strong, consistent
conversion signal, Advantage+ frequently beats a manually structured campaign, because Meta's model has
more real purchase data to learn from than your hand-built audiences do. For those accounts, fighting
Advantage+ with manual structure leaves money on the table.
The catch is in the word signal . Advantage+ is only as good as the data it optimises
toward. If your conversion event is noisy, misconfigured or measuring the wrong thing, Advantage+ will
confidently chase it, and you have handed the whole campaign to a model optimising the wrong target. It
also gives you the least visibility into why it is doing what it does. Trust it when you trust
your signal. Be careful when you don't.
In one line
CBO hands Meta the budget. Advantage+ hands Meta the whole campaign. The question is whether your signal
has earned that.
The decision guide
Stop asking “which is best” and run the if/then. Match the situation you are actually in:
Testing new audiences, creative angles or offers? ABO. You need each one to get a
fair, comparable shot. You are paying for an answer, not for efficiency.
Proven what works, healthy volume, similar audiences? CBO. Let Meta push budget to
the winners.
Ad sets with genuinely different jobs, prospecting next to retargeting? ABO, or
separate campaigns. Never make the algorithm choose between two things you need both of.
Ecommerce with a strong, clean conversion signal? Try Advantage+. It may well beat
your manual build.
Signal thin, noisy, or not sure it is tracked right? Stay on ABO or CBO, where you
keep control.
Small budget, or a campaign that cannot reach about 50 conversions a week? ABO first, to
force spend onto the one thing you need to learn, then consolidate. Below that volume a pooled budget
is guessing with your money.
Want the full picture? Run ABO to test and CBO or Advantage+ to scale.
They are stages, not rivals.
That last point is the one most people miss: the best accounts do not pick one. They run a pipeline,
ABO as the testing lane and CBO or Advantage+ as the scaling lane, and graduate what proves out. CBO is
not better than ABO. It is better at a different job. CBO buys efficiency; ABO buys
answers.
Moving from ABO to CBO without resetting learning
The real skill is not picking a structure. It is noticing when an ad set has finished being an
experiment and become a known quantity. A winner that has cleared its testing phase (stable
CPA, enough conversions to trust, a creative that is not fatiguing yet) is ready to graduate into a CBO
built for efficiency. The mistake is switching before the answer is in, which throws away the fair
trial ABO was buying you.
Two practical cautions on the switch itself. First, changing budget structure is an edit Meta treats
as significant, and it can briefly re-enter a learning phase, so migrate when you can absorb a few
unstable days, not the week before a launch. Second, do not drop three freshly tested winners of very
different scale into one CBO and expect a fair split; the same comparability rule that governed the
test governs the scale campaign. Group like with like. Carrying a proven winner across the line without
spooking the algorithm is its own discipline: see how to
scale a winner without breaking it .
Spotting statistical maturity is a judgement call, and it is the kind of call Adgent is built to put
in front of you. On one live account, a single sentence asking it to referee the agency's work produced
three standing findings: campaigns stuck in learning, losing campaigns still being scaled, and a
lopsided budget split. It then proposed a weekly agent to keep checking them, every Monday at 09:00
(30 September 2026).
The same decision on Google, and why attribution decides it
The CBO-versus-ABO instinct is not Meta-only. On Google the equivalent tension is Performance Max,
which pools budget and hides the structure the way CBO does, against tightly scoped campaigns you can
actually read. Performance Max is CBO's logic taken further: maximum delegation, minimum visibility. It
is the right tool once you trust the signal and the wrong one the moment you are trying to learn where
results actually come from, because it will happily credit itself for
demand you already owned .
Underneath both platforms sits the same unglamorous decider: attribution. CBO,
Advantage+ and Performance Max are only as smart as the conversion signal you feed them. If that signal
is inflated (view-through credit dressed up as incremental, a number still moving inside its
attribution window, a blended ROAS hiding a placement leak), automated allocation does not fix the
problem, it scales it. The budget flows toward whatever looks cheapest on paper, which is often
whatever is best at claiming credit rather than creating it. Before you trust any budget-pooling
structure to allocate for you, the question is not “CBO or ABO?” It is “do I believe these numbers
enough to hand over the wheel?”
Why the budget model is only half the job
Here is what all three share, and why picking the model is where most people stop when it
should be where they start. Whichever you choose, the model is a machine that acts on your conversion
signal, and it can only be as smart as that signal is honest. CBO reallocating to a “winner” that is
really an attribution-window mirage , or Advantage+
optimising to a broken purchase event, will fail confidently and fast.
So the real skill is not memorising which budget model to click. It is watching what each one is
actually optimising toward, catching when the signal it chases is bad, and knowing when to move a proven
audience from the testing lane to the scaling lane. That is judgment work: reading the account across
the whole structure, every day, and knowing which number can be trusted.
Adgent takes on this account-level judgment. The Budget Allocator looks for money split by history
rather than by result; Measurement Integrity looks for tracking problems that make every other number
suspect. When a conversion signal is inflated (more than about 90% of the reported ROAS coming from
checkouts or add-to-carts with zero purchases behind them), the ROAS- and CPA-ranked moves in that run
are held back.
The structure you chose, with the exception you made last quarter, becomes confirmed brand context
that account memory carries into the next read. To build the structure
itself, describe it and the campaign is drafted whole , field by field,
with the reason under each value.
Who wrote this Written by the people building Adgent, the AI employee that carries brand context into every growth decision. Related product: campaign build .
Bring the same question to your own account. Adgent returns its position, the evidence underneath and what the finding is worth a month.
Pricing
Frequently asked.
Q: Is Advantage+ better than manual campaigns?
A: Sometimes. It is genuinely good for accounts with a strong, consistent conversion signal and a broad catalogue, especially ecommerce. It is worse when you need to control which audience or creative gets tested, or when your signal is thin. It is not universally better or worse; it trades your control for Meta's scale, and whether that is a good deal depends on how much you trust your data.
Q: When should I use CBO vs ABO?
A: Ask what you are doing. Use CBO to scale a proven winner with healthy volume and comparable ad sets: let Meta allocate. Use ABO when you are testing audiences, creatives or offers, running low volume, or mixing ad sets with different jobs. CBO buys efficiency; ABO buys answers.
Q: Is CBO better than ABO?
A: Neither is better outright; they are better at different jobs. CBO beats manual allocation when you have volume and comparable ad sets. ABO wins when you are learning something, because it guarantees each option a fair sample instead of starving it. Match the tool to the task.
Q: CBO or ABO for scaling?
A: CBO to scale a known winner. Once you have proven which ad sets earn, CBO pushes budget toward the ones performing that day and scales the pool at volume without you watching every set. That holds above roughly 50 conversions a week with comparable ad sets; below that, or with mismatched ad sets, it chases noise. ABO is for the test that finds the winner in the first place; it is a worse scaling tool because it cannot reallocate on its own.
Q: When should I use ABO?
A: When you need a fair test. ABO gives every ad set its own fixed budget, so each audience or creative gets a guaranteed shot at delivery instead of being starved by Meta's early guesses. Use it to compare audiences, validate new creative or offers, run under roughly 50 conversions a week, or keep ad sets with different jobs (prospecting next to retargeting) from being judged against each other.
Q: Can I switch from ABO to CBO?
A: Yes, once an ad set has stopped being an experiment and become a known quantity: stable CPA, enough conversions to trust. Migrate when you can absorb a few unstable days, since changing budget structure can re-enter learning, and group only comparable winners together.
Q: Does Advantage+ replace CBO?
A: For some accounts, effectively yes: Advantage+ extends the CBO model to audiences and placements as well as budget. It does not replace CBO where you still want to define the ad-set structure yourself. CBO keeps that structure in your hands; Advantage+ gives Meta the wider job. If you trust your signal, Advantage+ can absorb the CBO role.
Q: Which is best for a small budget?
A: On a small budget, ABO usually wins early because you can force spend onto the one or two things you actually want to learn from, instead of letting CBO or Advantage+ spread thin and never exit the learning phase. Once one ad set proves out, consolidate into CBO or Advantage+ so the budget is not fragmented.
Q: Can I mix CBO and ABO?
A: Yes, and most good accounts do. Run ABO campaigns as your testing lane to find winners on fixed budgets, then graduate the proven audiences and creative into CBO or Advantage+ to scale. They are stages in a pipeline, not rivals: testing in one, scaling in the other.
Q: Is Advantage+ good for lead gen?
A: It can be, but it is less of a sure thing than for ecommerce. Lead-gen signal is often noisier (a form fill is not a purchase, and lead quality varies), so Advantage+ optimising to raw lead volume can flood you with cheap, low-intent leads. Feed it a clean qualified-lead or revenue signal and it works better. Without that, ABO or CBO gives you more control over quality.

# Ad fatigue starts in CPM, not frequency · Adgent
URL: https://adgent.app/cpm-is-the-early-creative-fatigue-signal

Blog Field note
Frequency is a lagging indicator. Watch CPM.
Frequency tells you an audience has seen your ad too often. CPM tells you the auction
already noticed. One of those is news; the other is a receipt.
Adgent · Notes from building the analyst
Type
Field note
Topic
Creative fatigue
Reading time
5 min
Published
2 April 2026
Updated
31 October 2026
On this page
Why frequency arrives late
What the CPM curve knows first
No universal fatigue number
Fatigue vs auction pressure
How often to refresh
Why it is hard by eye
Questions
All articles
The standard fatigue check is frequency. Watch it climb past 2, past 3, and somewhere in there you
refresh the creative. It is a reasonable habit built on a flawed instrument: frequency is an
average, and it is slow. Meta itself defines frequency as
the
average number of times each person saw your ad .
Short answer
The earliest sign of creative fatigue is a rising CPM paired with a falling CTR : the
auction repricing your ad within hours because engagement is decaying. It shows up days before a
frequency average moves, because frequency is a slow, backward-looking summary and CPM is a live
signal.
Why frequency arrives late
Frequency is impressions divided by reach over a window. To move meaningfully, it needs volume to
accumulate. By the time a 7-day frequency ticks from 2.1 to 2.8, the fatigue that caused it started
days ago. You are reading a summary of last week's problem.
Worse, it averages over the whole audience. A frequency of 2.4 can mean everyone saw the ad twice,
or it can mean your core 20% saw it nine times and the rest saw it once. Those are different problems
and the metric cannot tell them apart.
The difference in one line
Frequency is the audience telling you it is tired. CPM is the auction telling you it already priced
that in.
What the CPM curve knows first
Meta's auction is continuously repricing your ad against how people respond to it. As engagement
decays, your effective quality signal drops and you pay more for the same placement. That repricing
shows up in CPM within hours , long before enough impressions pile up to move a
frequency average.
The diagnostic pattern to look for is CPM rising while CTR falls. Read them together:
CPM up, CTR down: creative fatigue. The audience has stopped responding and the
auction is charging you for it. Refresh.
CPM up, CTR flat: auction pressure, not fatigue. A competitor moved in, or it is
Black Friday. Your creative is fine; your market got expensive.
CPM flat, CTR down: audience mismatch, usually after a targeting or placement
change. The creative is not tired, it is in the wrong room.
None of the three patterns can be read from a single metric. Each one is a
relationship between two curves, judged against what is normal for that account,
and “normal” is different for a $5k-a-month DTC brand and a $500k-a-month retailer.
Frequency is not useless. It is confirmation. By the time it agrees with you, you have
already paid for the lesson.
What frequency number actually signals fatigue
People want a threshold, so here is the honest version: there is not one that holds across accounts.
A prospecting audience of two million cold users can run at a frequency of 4 or 5 for weeks without
fatigue, because the impressions are spread thin across a huge pool. A retargeting audience of eight
thousand warm users can be cooked at a frequency of 2: they have all seen the ad twice in three days,
and the auction knows it before the average does.
That is the trap in the “refresh at frequency 3” rule of thumb. The same number means burnout on one
ad set and plenty of runway on another. What matters is not the absolute frequency but the
rate of change against that ad set's own baseline , and whether CPM is climbing while
response falls. A frequency of 3.5 that has been stable for two weeks with flat CPM is fine. A
frequency of 2.2 that jumped from 1.6 in four days while CPM ticked up is the one to worry about.
There is no universal fatigue frequency. There is only your ad set's normal, and the moment CPM
starts pulling away from it.
Fatigue vs auction pressure: don't refresh the wrong thing
The most expensive mistake here is not missing fatigue. It is misreading a cost spike as
fatigue when it is really the auction getting crowded. If you swap out a perfectly good
creative because CPM jumped over Black Friday, you have thrown away a proven asset and reset the
learning phase for nothing. The tell is CTR. Fatigue means the audience stopped responding, so CTR
falls with CPM. Auction pressure means the market got expensive while your audience still likes the
ad, so CTR holds steady even as CPM climbs.
This is the same class of problem behind a CPA that jumps
overnight : the number moved, but the number alone does not tell you which lever to pull. Read CPM
in isolation and every cost spike looks like fatigue. Read it against CTR, seasonality and what
competitors are doing in your placements, and the three causes separate cleanly. Only one of them is
fixed by new creative.
How often you should actually refresh
Refresh on the signal, not the calendar. A fixed cadence (“new creative every two weeks”) either
churns out winners before they have peaked or lets losers rot past the point of profit, because ad
sets do not fatigue on a schedule. The right cadence is whatever your CPM and CTR relationship tells
you, and that varies with audience size, budget and how distinctive the creative is. A high-budget ad
set pounding a small retargeting pool needs new frames far more often than a lean prospecting campaign
against a broad Advantage+ audience.
What you can standardise is the pipeline , not the timer: always have the next
variation ready, so that when the signal turns you swap without going dark. Keep a small stable of
proven angles in rotation so no single execution carries the whole ad set. And when you do scale a
winner, watch the fatigue curve steepen: bigger budgets burn a fixed audience faster, which is exactly
the failure covered in scaling a winner without
breaking it .
Why this is hard to do by eye, every day
Everything above is readable in principle. The problem is doing it across dozens of ad sets, every
day, before the spend compounds. You would have to hold each ad set's CPM and CTR against its own
trailing baseline, separate a fatigue slope from an auction spike from a targeting miss, and do it fast
enough to act while the creative still has salvageable reach. By hand that is an hour of squinting at
exports, and it is the hour most teams skip until the CPA report forces it.
Adgent is a team of AI agents working toward your marketing goals, and this read is shared between
two of its specialists. Creative-Fatigue Scout looks for single ads wearing out and
for a whole account running out of fresh creative. CPC-Spike Autopsy takes a cost
spike apart into its driver: CTR, CPM, bid or auction competition. In creative analysis , every concept carries a verdict (still scaling,
wearing out, testing), and a falling number is checked for where it actually broke before anything
goes on the refresh list:
Adgent Creative review · one live account (e-commerce), 30 September 2026 · translated from Turkish
“This creative's CTR rose 29.5% while its purchase conversion rate fell 62.3% (15 to 9
conversions, p = 0.015). That is not creative fatigue. It is a funnel problem, from message to
landing page, so I left it off the refresh list.”
Higher CTR, worse conversion: new creative would have fixed nothing. Adgent analyses creative; it
does not make it. When a refresh is the right call, it names the tired ad, explains why and carries
that evidence into the next creative review.
Frequently asked
Q: What is the earliest signal of creative fatigue?
A: A rising CPM alongside a falling CTR. The auction reprices your ad within hours as engagement decays, so cost climbs while response drops, days before enough impressions accumulate to move a frequency average.
Q: Why watch CPM instead of frequency?
A: Frequency is impressions over reach: a slow average that needs volume to accumulate, so it reports last week's problem. CPM reflects the auction repricing your ad almost immediately, which makes it the leading indicator, not the receipt.
Q: How do I tell fatigue from auction pressure?
A: Read CTR alongside CPM. Fatigue is CPM up with CTR down: the audience stopped responding. Auction pressure is CPM up with CTR flat: a competitor or seasonality made the market expensive while your creative still works.
Q: What frequency means creative fatigue?
A: There is no universal number. A broad prospecting audience runs fine at 4–5; a small retargeting pool can be cooked at 2. What signals fatigue is the change against that ad set's own baseline, read together with CPM.
Q: How often should I refresh creative?
A: On the signal, not the calendar. Fixed cadences churn winners early or let losers rot. Refresh when the CPM and CTR relationship turns for that ad set, which comes sooner for high-budget campaigns against small audiences.
Q: Does rising CPM always mean fatigue?
A: No. CPM up with CTR flat is auction pressure: your creative is fine, your market got expensive. CPM flat with CTR down is usually a targeting or placement mismatch. Only CPM up with CTR down means refresh.

# Meta says 4.2×, Google says 3.1×. Both are right. · Adgent
URL: https://adgent.app/cross-platform-comparability-meta-google

Blog Comparison
Meta says 4.2×, Google says 3.1×. Both are right.
Two platforms, two ROAS figures, one budget decision. The numbers are not measuring the
same thing, and moving money between them as if they were is the most common expensive mistake in
multi-channel accounts.
Adgent · Notes from building the analyst
Type
Comparison
Topic
Attribution
Reading time
7 min
Published
26 February 2026
On this page
Three ways they disagree
The double-counting problem
A comparability boundary
Why platforms won't fix it
Windows are most of the gap
The view-through trap
How to allocate
Questions
All articles
You are running both. Meta reports 4.2×, Google reports 3.1×, and the conclusion writes itself: move
budget to Meta. It is the most natural decision in the account, and you have almost no
evidence for it.
Short answer
Not directly comparable. Meta and Google measure ROAS with different attribution windows, credit
models and conversion definitions, so 4.2× and 3.1× are not the same unit. To compare them, match the
windows, check both against the revenue your analytics recorded, and read direction over level.
Three ways the numbers disagree
Meta and Google are not reporting the same metric under
the same name. They are reporting three different disagreements at once.
Different windows. Meta defaults
to 7-day click, 1-day view. Google Ads runs its own
windows , commonly 30-day click. A longer window catches more conversions mechanically, not
because the channel worked harder.
Different models. Google's data-driven attribution spreads credit across the
path. Meta credits its own touchpoints on a last-touch basis. One is sharing credit; the other is
claiming it.
Different definitions. A “purchase” fired by Meta's pixel and a “conversion”
counted by a Google tag can be counting different events, deduplicated differently, at different
points in the funnel.
The point, in one line
Both platforms are honest. Neither is comparable. The dishonesty is in the subtraction you do between
them.
The double-counting problem
Here is the tell that something is broken. Add up platform-reported revenue across your channels and
compare it to what your store or GA4 says you actually made. In most multi-channel accounts, the
platforms claim more revenue than the business earned.
That is not fraud, it is arithmetic. A customer who saw a Meta ad on Monday and clicked a Google
search ad on Wednesday is one purchase, and both platforms will report it, because from where each one
sits it is true. Sum them and you have counted the same money twice.
Building a comparability boundary
You cannot make the platforms agree. They are structurally incapable of it, and each has an interest
in claiming the conversion. What you can do is decide, deliberately, what you are willing to
compare. That is a comparability boundary, and it is built the same way every time:
Anchor on ground truth. Your store or your GA4 knows what you actually sold. That
is the denominator every platform claim gets checked against, not the other way round.
Match the windows. Pull both platforms on the same lookback before you compare.
It will not be perfect, but it removes the most mechanical distortion.
Compare direction, not level. Meta at 4.2× and Google at 3.1× tells you little.
Meta trending up 15% while Google is flat, at matched windows and against what your analytics
recorded, tells you where the next dollar goes.
Watch the blended number. Total spend against the revenue your analytics recorded
is the only figure that cannot be double-counted. If your channels look great and blended is flat,
the channels are eating each other.
Why the platforms will never fix this
It is worth being clear about the structural reason. Each platform measures its own contribution
with its own ruler and reports it in good faith, and neither has any incentive to calibrate its ruler
against a rival's. Google can now bring other platforms' ad cost into GA4 and will even model the
cross-channel split for you. But it grades that model with its own attribution, and its own
documentation draws the line:
Google Analytics Help About cross-channel budgeting · re-read 4 October 2026
“These tools are for planning purposes only and won’t affect budgets or spend in your
connected accounts.”
So the cross-platform allocation call, the one that decides where your marginal dollar actually goes,
is one the platforms will model but not make. They plan; they do not execute. That
call stays with you, and it is only as good as the comparison underneath it.
Two platforms reporting different numbers is not a bug to be resolved. It is the permanent
condition of running more than one channel , and the work is building a view that is honest
about it.
Windows are not a detail: they are most of the gap
If you only fix one thing, fix the window. It is the single largest mechanical source of the
disagreement, and it has nothing to do with which channel is actually working. Meta's default 7-day
click, 1-day view means a purchase only counts if it lands within a week of a click, or a day of a
view. Google Ads commonly runs a 30-day click window on the same account. Give any channel four times
as long to catch a conversion and it will catch more of them: the same buyers, credited later, on a
longer clock.
This is why matching the lookback before you compare does more work than any other
single move. Pull both platforms on a matched window (7-day click on each, say) and a chunk of the
4.2× vs 3.1× gap simply evaporates, because you have stopped comparing a sprint to a marathon. It will
not make the numbers identical; the models and definitions still differ. But it removes the
distortion you can actually remove, and what is left is a more honest starting point. We go deeper on
this in why the 7-day window is lying before noon : the
same clock problem, one channel at a time.
The view-through trap: not all credit is earned
There is a subtler distortion hiding inside the window difference, and it flatters whichever platform
leans on view-through credit. A view-through conversion counts a purchase because someone
saw an ad: no click, no deliberate action. On Meta, that is the 1-day view leg of the default
window; on placements like Audience Network it can quietly inflate reported ROAS with impressions that
scrolled past unnoticed. When you compare a channel earning mostly click credit against one padded
with view credit, you are not comparing performance. You are comparing how generously each platform
counts a glance as an outcome.
The practical guard is to inspect both the amount of credit and how it was earned. A channel showing
high ROAS on mostly view-through conversions is making a weaker claim than a channel showing the same
number on clicks, even at a matched window. A raw platform export hides that distinction; an AI media buyer worth the name reads the account like a strategist
instead of repeating the dashboard's headline figure.
What this means for how you allocate
Put it together and the allocation rule changes shape. You stop asking “which platform has the higher
ROAS?”, an unanswerable question across incompatible units, and start asking “at a matched window,
checked against what my analytics recorded, which channel is trending up and which is flat?” Level is
noise between platforms; direction survives the comparability boundary because it is measured inside
each channel's own consistent ruler over time.
Then you let the blended number keep everyone honest. Total spend against the revenue your analytics
recorded is the one figure that cannot be double-counted, because there is only one denominator: what
the business actually earned. When your channels each look strong but blended ROAS is flat, that is
the signature of channels claiming the same conversions and eating each other. The comparability
boundary is not a report you build once; it is a discipline you hold every time a platform hands you
a confident number and invites you to move budget on it.
Adgent is a team of AI agents working toward your marketing goals. It reads Meta and Google Ads
through their own APIs every day, with GA4, Search Console and Merchant Center read-only alongside,
so the two rulers and your own analytics sit in one place when you ask the question. Before it ranks
anything by ROAS or CPA, it checks that the conversion signal underneath is real: if more than about
90% of reported ROAS comes from add-to-cart or begin-checkout events with zero purchases, every
ROAS- or CPA-ranked action in that run is held back. The allocation between the two platforms stays
your call. See what it reads next to the platforms .
Frequently asked
Q: Can I compare Meta and Google ROAS directly?
A: Not directly. The two numbers use different attribution windows, credit models and conversion definitions, so they are not the same unit. Match the windows, check both against the revenue your analytics recorded, and compare direction over level.
Q: Why are Meta and Google ROAS different?
A: Three disagreements at once: different windows (Meta's 7-day click vs Google's common 30-day), different credit models (Meta last-touch, Google data-driven), and different definitions of what counts as a conversion. Each platform is honest inside its own ruler.
Q: How do attribution windows differ between platforms?
A: Meta defaults to 7-day click, 1-day view. Google Ads commonly runs a 30-day click window. A longer window mechanically catches more conversions, the same buyers credited later, which inflates reported ROAS without the channel working any harder.
Q: What is the double-counting problem?
A: A buyer who sees a Meta ad on Monday and clicks a Google ad on Wednesday is one purchase, but both platforms report it, since from each seat it is true. Sum platform-reported revenue and you count the same money twice, claiming more than the business earned.
Q: How do I build a comparability boundary?
A: Anchor on ground truth: your store or GA4 revenue is the denominator every platform claim checks against. Match both platforms to the same window, compare direction rather than level, and watch the blended number that cannot be double-counted.
Q: Which platform reports higher ROAS?
A: Usually whichever runs the longer window or leans on view-through credit. Often that is Meta on default settings, but it varies by account. That is exactly why a higher reported number proves nothing until you match windows and check both against what your analytics recorded.

# Google Ads account structure 2026: how to audit it · Adgent
URL: https://adgent.app/google-ads-account-structure-2026

Blog How-to
Google Ads account structure in 2026 (and how to audit yours)
The old rules of structure were about manual control. In 2026 they are about signal
quality: building an account so Smart Bidding has
enough clean conversion data to learn. Here is the modern default, and how to audit whether yours
measures up.
Adgent · Notes from building the analyst
Type
How-to
Reading time
8 min
Published
23 July 2026
On this page
The hierarchy, level by level
STAGs: the ad group rule
The campaign split
The signal threshold
Signal, not control
How to audit yours
Reading it all at once
Questions
All articles
For fifteen years, account structure was how you controlled Google Ads by hand. You split campaigns
to control budgets, split ad groups to control bids, and the buyer with the most granular structure
usually won. That advice is now actively wrong. Smart Bidding sets the bids; your structure's only job
is to feed it clean, concentrated signal. Build for that and you win. Build the old way (a hundred
single-keyword ad groups, a campaign per product) and you starve the algorithm across so many thin
units that it never learns.
Short answer
In 2026, Google Ads structure is about signal quality, not manual control : give Smart
Bidding enough conversions per unit to learn. The modern default is Single Theme Ad Groups
(STAGs) of 3 to 10 tight keywords, a Brand / Core non-brand / (optional)
Competitor campaign split, and 30+ conversions a month per campaign so bidding
has signal. Structure to feed the algorithm, not to fight it.
This is the 2026 default as an audit: four checks for whether your existing structure still feeds
Smart Bidding clean signal. Most accounts were built correctly for 2018 and never re-cut for how
bidding works now.
The hierarchy, and what each level is for now
The four levels have not changed. What each one is for has changed completely:
Account. The billing and conversion-tracking boundary. One conversion action set,
one source of truth. This is where signal is defined: if your conversion tracking is wrong here,
nothing below it can be right.
Campaign. The bidding unit. This is where budget lives and where Smart
Bidding learns. The campaign is now the thing you must feed with enough conversions; it is the level
the algorithm optimises against.
Ad group. The relevance unit. Its only remaining job is keeping keywords,
ads and landing page tightly matched. It no longer controls bids at all. This is where STAGs
live.
Ads and keywords. The message and the trigger. Keywords tell Google what intent you
want; responsive search ads answer it. Quality Score still rides on how well the two align.
The shift in one line: campaigns are for bidding, ad groups are for relevance. Every
structural mistake in 2026 is really a confusion of those two jobs: either splitting bidding units so
fine they cannot learn, or lumping unrelated intents into one ad group so no ad can answer them.
STAGs: the one rule that governs ad groups
A Single Theme Ad Group is exactly what it says: an ad group where every keyword
shares one intent. Three to ten keywords, all so closely related that a single ad and a single landing
page can answer every one of them. That is not a style preference. It is the mechanism that drives
relevance and Quality Score, and Google itself reports that raising ad relevance and landing-page
experience is one of the largest levers on
Quality Score ,
which in turn discounts your cost per click.
The rule is a single test, and it decides without mercy:
The STAG test
Every keyword in an ad group must be answerable by the same ad and the same landing page. If you
cannot write one ad for all of them, the group is too broad. Split it.
Take “running shoes.” If your ad group holds running shoes , trail running shoes ,
marathon shoes and waterproof running shoes , ask whether one headline can answer all
four. It cannot. Someone searching “waterproof running shoes” who lands on a generic running-shoe page
bounces, and that bounce teaches Smart Bidding that the whole group converts worse than it should.
Split them into four STAGs, each with its own ad and its own page, and every impression now carries a
clean signal.
The 2018 version of this advice was SKAGs: Single Keyword Ad Groups, one keyword each. Close-variant
matching ended that. Google now serves your ad on dozens of variants regardless, so a one-keyword group
buys you nothing but fragmentation. The STAG is the correction: tight enough for relevance, broad
enough that conversions concentrate instead of scattering across a hundred starved groups.
The campaign split: isolate brand, above all
At the campaign level, split by intent , not by product line or geography or anything
else that fragments signal. The modern default is three buckets:
Brand. People searching your name. High intent, high conversion rate, low CPA: a
different economy entirely.
Core non-brand. Your real prospecting: category and problem-aware searches where
the money is actually won or lost.
Competitor (optional). Bids on rival names. Expensive, low conversion rate, and
worth isolating so its poor efficiency never contaminates non-brand targets.
The non-negotiable one is brand . Brand searches convert at rates that dwarf
non-brand, often several times higher at a fraction of the CPA, because the person already decided to
buy from you. Leave brand mixed into non-brand and those cheap conversions flatter the blended average,
hiding the fact that your actual prospecting is losing money. Worse, a single target CPA cannot serve
both economies at once: set it for brand and non-brand starves; set it for non-brand and you overpay
for traffic you would have won for free. Isolating brand is the structural change that pays back most
in the average account. The full case for it, including how Performance Max quietly takes brand
credit, is in why brand must be isolated from
Performance Max .
The signal threshold: 30+ conversions a month, or bidding thrashes
Here is the number that quietly governs everything above.
Google's own guidance
is to judge a Target CPA campaign over a period carrying at least 30 conversions in the last 30
days . Target ROAS is
eligible from 15 conversions in 30 days
on Search and Shopping, but that is an eligibility floor, not a stable model, and it has to learn
conversion values too, so we treat 30 a month as the working minimum for both. Below that,
Smart Bidding is fitting a curve to noise. It over-reacts to a lucky week, pulls back after a random
dead Tuesday, and never settles. That is the thrash: bids swinging not because the market moved, but
because the algorithm cannot tell signal from randomness on too few data points.
This is why granular structure now backfires. Split one healthy campaign carrying 90 conversions a
month into six tidy product campaigns and you have made six units of 15: all below threshold, all
thrashing, all worse than the one you started with. The instinct to organise neatly is exactly the
instinct to resist. Consolidate until each campaign clears the threshold, then stop. If
you are weighing how to group budgets for this, the mechanics are in
CBO vs ABO vs Advantage+ ; if you are trying to grow a campaign that is already
learning without resetting it, see how to scale a winner
without breaking it .
Structure for signal, not control: the 2026 shift
Everything above collapses into one mental model, and it is the whole point of this piece. The old
question was “how do I structure this so I can control every bid?” The new question is “how do I
structure this so the algorithm has the cleanest, most concentrated signal to learn from?”
Those two questions produce opposite accounts. Controlling by hand pushes you toward more units,
finer splits, single-keyword groups: maximum granularity. Feeding signal pushes you toward fewer,
denser units, with enough separation to keep intents clean and enough consolidation to keep every
bidding unit above threshold. In 2026 the second account wins every time, because you are no longer
the bidder. You are the person who decides what the bidder gets to see.
You do not structure a Google Ads account to control the bids anymore. You structure it to
control what the algorithm can learn.
How to audit your existing structure
Now the part most guides skip. You almost certainly already have an account. The question is not how
to build one from scratch; it is whether the one you have is quietly leaking signal. Run these four
checks, in order of how much damage they do:
1. Are any ad groups too broad?
Open your biggest ad groups and apply the STAG test to each: could one ad answer every keyword in
here? If the group mixes intents you could not write a single relevant headline for, it is too broad,
and every mismatched impression is teaching Smart Bidding the wrong thing. This is the most common leak
and the easiest to fix.
2. Are any campaigns below the conversion threshold?
Sort campaigns by conversions over the last 30 days. Anything under about 30 is a thrashing bidding
unit. It either needs consolidating into a sibling, or its bid strategy needs to move up to a portfolio
that pools signal across campaigns. Thin campaigns underperform because each one has too little clean
signal to learn from.
3. Is brand mixed into non-brand?
Check whether brand terms live in the same campaign as prospecting. If they do, your reported CPA is
a fiction: cheap brand conversions are subsidising losing non-brand targets, and you cannot see it.
Pull brand into its own campaign and watch the non-brand numbers tell the truth, often for the first
time.
4. Is Performance Max overlapping Search?
If you run both, Performance Max will happily serve on queries your Search campaigns should own,
brand included, and take the credit. That overlap makes both structures unreadable. Two deeper
walkthroughs cover the full sweep: how to audit a Google
Ads account end to end, and how to audit Performance
Max specifically for cannibalisation.
Structural check The old rule (manual control) The 2026 rule (signal quality)
Keywords per ad group 1 (SKAG) 3 to 10, single theme (STAG)
Campaigns per account Many, granular Few, above threshold
Split campaigns by Product or geo Intent (brand / non-brand)
Bids set by You, by hand Smart Bidding
Conversions per campaign Not a concern 30+ a month, tCPA and tROAS alike
Same four levels, opposite instincts. In 2026, granularity is the failure mode.
The close: let something read the whole structure at once
The hard part of a structure audit is not any single check. It is holding all four in your head at
once, across every campaign, and seeing how they interact. A broad ad group inside a thin campaign
that Performance Max is also cannibalising is three problems compounding, and a person scanning the
interface at 8am rarely catches the compound.
That is the kind of read an AI media buyer is for. Adgent is
a team of AI agents working toward your marketing goals, and one of its ten specialists, Account
Architect, reads for exactly this layer: duplication, fragmentation and naming you cannot report on,
across campaigns. On one live account in September 2026, its first run flagged four campaigns
competing for the same goal, with an estimated $310 (₺15,000) a month attached. The finding, evidence,
next move and later account history stay together.
Frequently asked
Q: What's the best Google Ads account structure in 2026?
A: Single Theme Ad Groups of 3 to 10 tightly related keywords, grouped into a small number of campaigns split by intent (Brand, Core non-brand, and optionally Competitor), with each campaign carrying 30+ conversions a month so Smart Bidding has enough signal to learn. Structure for signal, not manual control.
Q: What is a Single Theme Ad Group (STAG)?
A: A STAG is an ad group where every keyword shares one intent, so a single ad and a single landing page can answer all of them. The test: if you cannot write one relevant ad for the whole group, it is too broad and needs splitting.
Q: How many ad groups per campaign?
A: There is no fixed number: enough to keep each ad group a single tight theme, few enough that the campaign still clears the conversion threshold. In practice that is a handful to a couple of dozen STAGs, consolidated so budget and signal are not spread too thin.
Q: Should brand be a separate campaign?
A: Yes. Brand traffic converts at a far higher rate and lower CPA than non-brand, so mixing them lets cheap brand conversions flatter the average and hide non-brand losses. Isolating brand keeps its efficiency out of your prospecting numbers and stops Smart Bidding from over-crediting it.
Q: How many conversions does Smart Bidding need?
A: Google's guidance is to judge a Target CPA campaign over at least 30 conversions in the last 30 days; Target ROAS is eligible from 15 conversions in 30 days on Search and Shopping, which is a floor rather than a stable model. We treat 30 a month per campaign as the working minimum for both. Below that the algorithm thrashes, chasing noise, so consolidate campaigns to clear the threshold.
Q: How do I audit my Google Ads account structure?
A: Check four things. Are any ad groups too broad to answer with one ad? Are any campaigns below about 30 conversions a month? Is brand mixed into non-brand? Is Performance Max overlapping and cannibalising Search? Each is a structural leak that quietly starves Smart Bidding of clean signal.
Q: Does account structure still matter with AI bidding?
A: More than ever; it just changed jobs. You no longer structure to control bids by hand; you structure to feed the algorithm clean, concentrated conversion signal. Bad structure now degrades what Smart Bidding can learn.

# Google Ads CPA rose? The Aug 2026 Target CPA change · Adgent
URL: https://adgent.app/google-ads-target-cpa-roas-change-2026

Blog Explainer
Why your Google Ads CPA rose: the August 2026 Target CPA change
On 17 August, Google changed how target-based bidding works, and on many accounts actual CPA
climbed without anyone touching a campaign. What changed, who it hit, and how to tell that rise from a
real one.
Adgent · Notes from building the analyst
Type
Explainer
Reading time
7 min
Published
23 July 2026
Updated
17 August 2026
On this page
What changed on 17 August
Who it hits hardest
Why nothing broke
What to do now
Reading the rise
All articles
Most Google Ads changes are quiet: a label moves, a report gets a new column, nobody notices. This one
was not. On 17 August 2026 , Google changed the mechanics of target-based bidding in a
way that lifted actual CPA on many accounts, whether or not anyone touched a setting. If your CPA jumped
in late August, this is very likely why. Your campaign did not break. The rules changed underneath it.
Short answer
Since 17 August 2026, Google makes budget-limited campaigns on target-based bidding perform more
consistently toward the target you set. If your campaigns had been beating their
target, with actual CPA sitting below your Target CPA , the change lets Google spend up
to the target, which raised both your actual CPA and your spend. Audit your targets now.
The frustrating part is that the accounts most affected are often the well-run ones: the ones that
were quietly beating their targets. So before you spend a morning hunting for a broken pixel,
understand what actually moved.
What changed on 17 August
Google's own framing is that target-based bid strategies make budget-limited campaigns
perform more consistently toward the target you set , including after budget adjustments.
Before the 17th, a campaign constrained by budget could drift well under its target, because Google
was not pushing to fill every dollar toward that goal. Now it does. The strategy steers delivery back
up to the target you have told it to hit.
The clearest way to see it is Google's own example:
Google Ads Help Center Target-based bidding update, effective 17 August 2026
“If your Target CPA is $10 but recent actual CPA is $5, after August 17 the campaign will
deliver closer to a $10 actual CPA if you make no changes.”
Read that again, because the direction matters. A campaign acquiring conversions at $5 against a $10
target was not underperforming. It was outperforming, comfortably. The change told Google to stop
leaving that room on the table and spend up toward the $10 you set. Your acquisition volume may rise,
but so does the price you pay per acquisition, and so does total spend. The number you set as a ceiling
became, in effect, the number Google aims for.
Alongside the mechanics, Google renamed the strategies. “Maximize conversions with a Target
CPA” becomes simply “Target CPA” , and “Maximize conversion value with
a Target ROAS” becomes “Target ROAS” . Same underlying strategy, cleaner
label. The rename is still a good reminder to go and look at what each target is actually set to.
Change date 17 August 2026
Bid strategies Target CPA, Target ROAS
Campaign types Search, Shopping, Performance Max, Demand Gen, Display, Hotel, Travel
Hit hardest Budget-limited campaigns beating their target
Target review tool Bid Target Adjustment Tool, since 6 July 2026
The change at a glance. Source: Google Ads Help Center .
Who this hits hardest
The single biggest tell is the gap between your target and your real delivery. If your actual CPA has
been sitting comfortably below your Target CPA , or your actual ROAS comfortably above
your Target ROAS, you had been leaving delivery on the table, and the change is designed to fill exactly
that gap. The bigger the gap, the bigger the move you saw.
Budget-limited campaigns feel it most sharply. They are the ones where Google now has
explicit room to spend up toward the target after adjustments, so the effect concentrates there. If you
run tight daily budgets on Search, Shopping, Performance Max or Demand
Gen with a target-based strategy, assume you are in scope. The change applies across Search,
Shopping, Performance Max and Demand Gen, and also Display, Hotel and Travel campaigns using Target CPA
or Target ROAS.
Accounts already delivering right at their target will not see much: there is no gap for Google to
close. It is the outperformers, the accounts that set a target with headroom and then beat it, who got
the surprise.
Why your CPA looked like it jumped, though nothing broke
Here is the diagnostic trap. Someone opens the account in late August, sees CPA up thirty or forty
percent, and starts pulling levers: pausing campaigns, cutting budgets, blaming the creative. None of
that is the right response, because none of that is the cause. This is a settings and system
change on Google's side , not a campaign problem. The funnel did not break. The auction did not
turn. Google changed what your target means .
That distinction is the whole game. A CPA rise that comes from the auction, a tracking break or
creative fatigue demands one kind of response, and a rise that comes from a bidding-rule change demands
a completely different one. If you cannot tell them apart, you will react to the wrong thing. For the
general version of that diagnosis, the usual causes of a CPA spike and how to rank them, see
why did my CPA suddenly jump . This change is one more cause worth
adding to that list for the second half of 2026: the target itself moved.
What to do now
The change went live on 17 August 2026, so the checklist below is no longer preparation. It is a
catch-up audit. The window to prepare has closed; the tool has not. Google's Bid Target
Adjustment Tool , available since 6 July 2026 , still lets you review and reset
targets by hand.
Audit target against true break-even. Compare each Target CPA or Target ROAS
against the most you can actually afford to pay, not your comfortable recent actual. If your target
was set with slack, that slack has already become spend. The
break-even ROAS calculator gives you the floor.
Use the Bid Target Adjustment Tool. If you do not want the higher CPA, lower your
Target CPA (or raise your Target ROAS) to your real ceiling now, rather than leaving Google to spend
up to a loose target.
Flag your budget-limited campaigns. These move most. Know which campaigns are
capped: that is where the CPA rise concentrated.
Do not panic-edit. If CPA rose after the 17th, resist reworking bids and budgets
in a hurry. Big edits reset learning and cost you more. If you do need to scale, do it deliberately:
scale a winner without breaking it .
The one decision that matters is whether your target is a real ceiling or a loose placeholder. If it
is your genuine break-even, leave it: the change is bringing delivery up to a number you can live with.
If it was set once and forgotten, fix it, because Google is already acting on it.
Reading the rise before reacting to it
A number moving because Google changed the rules is exactly the kind of thing that should be
explained before anyone touches the account. A CPA up in late August is not automatically a fire. If it
lines up with the 17th, your campaigns are target-based, and actual CPA moved toward your target rather
than past it, the cause is this change.
The same discipline runs the other way: a target only means something if the account can reach it.
On one live account, Adgent was asked to set a target CPA the numbers could not support:
Target CPA requested ₺250 ($5.16)
Actual cost per booking about ₺4,028 ($83)
What it did declined the target and explained why
One live account (hotel group), 11 August 2026. TRY converted at 48.4069 per USD.
A target set far from what the account delivers, in either direction, is an instruction the bidding
system will follow literally. That is the work the Trust Gate exists for:
checking a request against the account's own numbers before the budget moves.
Adgent reads every connected Google Ads and Meta account each day, carries the brand and confirmed
targets into the analysis, and puts an estimated monthly amount on each decision. The target gap,
evidence and proposed move arrive together; after the account changes, the result returns to the same
history. If you want that read on your own targets now the change has landed, start with the audit.
Google's own announcement of the change is
in the Google Ads Help Center .

Bring the same question to your own account. Adgent returns its position, the evidence underneath and what the finding is worth a month.
Pricing
Frequently asked.
Q: What changed with Google Ads Target CPA on 17 August 2026?
A: Google changed target-based bid strategies so that budget-limited campaigns perform more consistently toward the target you set, including after budget adjustments. In practice, a campaign that was beating its target is now steered to deliver closer to it. Google's example: if your Target CPA is $10 but recent actual CPA is $5, after 17 August the campaign will deliver closer to a $10 actual CPA if you make no changes.
Q: Will this raise my CPA?
A: For accounts that have been beating their target, yes: that is the point of the change. If your actual CPA has been comfortably below your Target CPA, Google was leaving delivery on the table. Since 17 August it fills that gap by spending up to your target, so both your spend and your actual CPA rise toward the number you set. Accounts already delivering at their target will not see much movement.
Q: Which campaigns are affected?
A: Any campaign using a target-based bid strategy, Target CPA or Target ROAS. That covers Search, Shopping, Performance Max and Demand Gen, and also Display, Hotel and Travel campaigns. Budget-limited campaigns are hit hardest, because they are the ones where Google now has room to spend up toward the target.
Q: What is the Bid Target Adjustment Tool?
A: A tool Google made available on 6 July 2026 so you can review and adjust your targets by hand. The 17 August change has landed, but the tool still works: if you do not want Google spending up toward a target higher than your true break-even, use it to lower your Target CPA or raise your Target ROAS to your real ceiling.
Q: Should I lower my Target CPA now?
A: Only if your current target sits above your true break-even. Many accounts set a Target CPA with headroom and then quietly delivered well under it. Since 17 August, that headroom is spend. If your target is genuinely the most you can pay per conversion, leave it. If it was set loosely and your real ceiling is lower, use the Bid Target Adjustment Tool to bring the target down to that ceiling.
Q: Is my CPA jump a bug or this change?
A: If your CPA rose around 17 August, your campaigns use a target-based strategy, and your actual CPA moved toward your Target CPA rather than past it, this change is the most likely cause, not a bug and not a broken campaign. If the jump does not line up with the date or overshoots your target, run the general CPA diagnostic before blaming the change.
Q: Do I need to do anything if my CPA already matches my target?
A: Probably not. The change moves budget-limited campaigns toward the target you set; if you are already delivering at that target, there is little gap for Google to fill, so your CPA and spend should stay roughly where they are. It is still worth a quick check that your target really is your break-even and not a number you set once and forgot.
