# How much ad budget is wasted? And how to find it · Adgent
URL: https://adgent.app/how-much-ad-spend-is-wasted

Blog How-to
How much of your ad budget is wasted (and how to find it)
The best-documented study puts the typical account near a third of budget wasted. Most
of that waste has a name and an address, and you can find it in an afternoon.
Adgent · Notes from building the analyst
Type
How-to
Reading time
9 min
Published
22 July 2026
Updated
11 October 2026
On this page
1. Wasted search terms
2. The location default
3. Placement leakage
4. Device bids
5. Audience exclusions
6. Branded double-pay
Attach a number to every leak
What one run surfaced
When the leak is elsewhere
Once is not enough
Questions
All articles
Ask a room of media buyers how much of the average account is wasted and you get a shrug and a
range. The best-sourced figure we know of is WordStream's: about $1,127 a month spent
on clicks that did not convert, against a median monthly spend of about $3,127. Roughly a third of
the budget, going to queries nobody meant to buy, placements nobody chose and audiences you are
paying twice to reach.
Short answer
WordStream's
study , published in February 2026, of 15,666 Google Ads accounts graded during
2025 found the typical account spending about $1,127 a month on clicks that did not
convert, roughly a third of the median account's $3,127 monthly spend. Your own share depends on how
much of the account runs on defaults. Most of it is findable in an afternoon: junk search terms, a
location-targeting default, placement leakage, careless device bids, missing audience exclusions and
branded-search double-pay. Each leak can carry a monthly price you work out yourself.
Read that number as context, not as a diagnosis. The accounts in the study came through a free
grading tool, so they likely lean toward the unoptimised end, and “wasted” there means clicks that
did not convert, which is a loose definition. Your account is not the median. The useful part is the
shape underneath: the waste is not hiding in some sophisticated attribution model. It is sitting in
reports you already have access to. Here is the playbook, roughly in the order the leaks tend to give
money back.
In one line
Waste isn't a mystery. It's a set of reports nobody has time to read.
1. Wasted search terms: the largest pool you can stop today
Start here, because it is usually the biggest single pool and the fastest to fix. Broad and phrase
match keywords pull in queries you never intended to bid on. The search terms report is where you see
what people actually typed to trigger your ad, and it is routinely full of junk: wrong intent,
“free”, “jobs” and “DIY” modifiers, and searches for products you don't sell.
Every click on one of those is spend you can stop today with a negative keyword. Pull the search
terms report over the last 30 to 60 days, sort by cost, and read down until the queries stop looking
like buyers. On a neglected account this is where the afternoon pays for itself.
How to price it: total the cost of the queries you are about to add as negatives
over the window, and scale it to a month. It runs larger on a broad-match-heavy account that has
never been groomed and smaller on one that is already tightly matched.
2. The location default: “interest” vs “in”
This one is a single setting, and it quietly bleeds local and regional accounts. The location
option Google recommends for Search, Presence or interest , shows your ads to people
who are physically in your target area or who have merely shown interest in it. For a
plumber in Manchester, that can mean paying for clicks from someone in another country googling
“Manchester” for a trip.
Switch it to Presence: people in or regularly in your targeted locations and you
cut the tourists and the researchers. Google's own location
targeting help says to consider Presence when you only want to reach people in specific
locations. The broad option widens reach, and for a business that serves only one area, that extra
reach is mostly people who cannot buy.
How to price it: segment by user location and total the spend that came from
outside the area you serve. It is negligible for genuinely national or global advertisers, which is
exactly why it is easy to miss on the accounts it hurts most.
3. Placement leakage: the leak in the average
Display, video and Performance Max spread your budget across placements you never hand-picked:
apps, made-for-ads sites and low-quality partner inventory that eats impressions and returns nothing.
A healthy blended number can hide a placement quietly burning cash underneath it, which is the exact
dynamic in placement drift: the leak hiding in
your average .
Pull the placements report (or the Performance Max placement and channel reporting), sort by cost,
and look for spend with clicks but no conversions. Exclude the worst offenders, and exclude app
placements if you are not deliberately advertising in apps. On accounts running Display or
Performance Max at scale, this is often the second-biggest pool after search terms. How to audit a Performance Max campaign walks through where
that spend hides.
How to price it: the spend on placements with clicks and no conversions over the
window, scaled to a month.
4. Device bids: paying a premium for the worse device
Segment any mature campaign by device and the conversion rates rarely match. Mobile often converts
worse than desktop for considered purchases; the reverse is often true for impulse and local. If
your bids treat every device the same, you are overpaying on the one that converts worse and
underbidding the one that converts better.
On manual bidding, look at cost per conversion by device over a meaningful window and adjust to
match reality: down on the laggard, up on the leader. It is a smaller pool than the first three, but
it is pure margin, because you are not cutting volume, just repricing it. On Smart Bidding (Target
CPA, Target ROAS, Maximize conversions or conversion value), Google's bid
adjustment rules ignore manual device adjustments except −100%, which switches a device off, and
Target CPA treats a device adjustment as a change to the target. There the lever is the target and
the conversion data you feed it, not the bid.
How to price it: the gap between each device's cost per conversion and the
account's, times that device's conversions, over a month.
5. Audience saturation: paying full CPA to reach converters
If you have no audience exclusions, you are paying full price to show ads to people who already
bought. Retargeting that keeps chasing existing customers, prospecting that re-serves recent
converters, and broad campaigns with no exclusion list all spend real money reaching people who are
done. You pay the full CPA to acquire someone you already acquired.
Add exclusions: existing-customer lists, recent purchasers out of prospecting, and converters out
of top-of-funnel campaigns. Retargeting is not wrong. Unbounded retargeting saturates, and the
incremental return collapses while the spend does not.
How to price it: the spend that reached people who had already converted, over the
window. It concentrates in accounts leaning hard on retargeting.
6. Branded-search double-pay
The most argued-about leak on the list. When someone searches your brand name, they were likely
going to find you organically, so a branded click can be spend for a visit you would have had for
free. Not always: if others bid on your name, or your organic listing is buried, branded search
earns its keep. But a lot of accounts run it on autopilot and never test whether the paid clicks
are incremental. Performance Max can blur this further by taking credit for branded demand .
The test is simple: pause branded search for a controlled window and watch whether total branded
traffic and conversions actually drop, or just shift to organic. If they shift, you were
double-paying.
How to price it: only the test prices it. The leak is the branded spend whose
conversions moved to organic when you paused, which is why it is a test, not a rule.
Attach a number to every leak
Here is the framing that turns a checklist into a decision: every leak above can carry a monthly
price, and the only question worth asking is which one gives back the most, first. A generic “you
have wasted spend” is noise. “Your search terms are leaking this much a month, and your location
setting is on the wrong default” is something you can act on before lunch.
That is the whole idea behind recoverable spend : not a vague health score, but a
ranked list of leaks with a dollar figure and a fix attached to each. It is how you decide what to
touch, and it is the framing our product is built around. Don't tell someone their account is
unhealthy; tell them where the money is and what closing the gap is worth.
Leak Where it hides How to spot it How to price it
Wasted search terms Search terms report Junk queries, no intent Cost of the new negatives
Location default Location settings “Interest”, not “presence” Spend from outside your area
Placement leakage Placements, Performance Max Spend, no conversions Spend on those placements
Device bids Device segment Flat bids, uneven conversion rate Cost-per-conversion gap by device
Audience saturation No exclusions Retargeting converters Spend on people who already bought
Branded double-pay Branded campaigns Non-incremental clicks A pause test
These overlap, so you won't recover every leak additively. Price each one as a range for
your own account; there is no honest category-wide percentage per leak.
Pricing also disciplines whoever produced the list. In rough order of money recovered per hour
spent:
Check the signal before anything else. If the conversion the account optimises
toward is not the conversion the business cares about, every efficiency number downstream is a
proxy, and the ranked list you build on it is ranked wrong.
Price each candidate leak as a monthly range. Spend in the window, times the
share you would actually reclaim, scaled to a month. Write both ends of the range down; if you
cannot, you do not understand the leak yet.
Put what you can't price on a watch list. Write down the condition that would
make each one worth acting on, so it comes back when the condition is met instead of nagging you
every week.
Re-run the same list a month later. A leak that reappears unchanged is not a
finding any more. It is money that has already gone.
A 60% swing on a campaign spending $50 a day is noise wearing a large percentage; a 4% drift on
the campaign carrying half the budget is the thing that matters. That is why the price comes before
the percentage.
What one run surfaced on a live account
Here is what that method looks like when software runs it. A single run on one live account
produced 60 decisions , each with evidence attached and each priced. Not “issues
found”: decisions, sorted by what they are worth per month, so the list ranks itself and you work
top down instead of reading all of it.
One run · one live account $2,892–5,867 a month, priced across 60 items
Fix now 34
Opportunity 13
Experiment 7
Watching 6
Evidence items attached 192
One live account, run of 7 September 2026, 28-day window. ₺140,000–284,000 a month, the model's estimate, converted at 48.4069 per USD. A range, not a point estimate.
It is a range. $2,892 to $5,867, not a single figure. The spread is the honest
expression of what the account's own history can support: pricing a leak requires assuming what
happens to the money afterwards, and that assumption has a floor and a ceiling.
Only 34 of 60 are “fix now”. Thirteen are opportunities, seven are experiments,
and six are being watched rather than acted on. A tool that returns 60 urgent problems has not read
an account; it has run a checklist.
192 pieces of evidence for 60 decisions. Roughly three per decision. Every
verdict names the rows it came from, which is the only reason you can argue with it in your own Ads
Manager instead of taking it on faith. It is one account's output, not a benchmark for yours.
Sometimes the leak is somewhere else
The most useful output we have seen on a second live account was a diagnosis that moved the
problem. On a Google read of 61 campaigns and $7,825 (₺378,800) over 28 days, in August 2026:
Adgent Google budget analysis · one live account · translated from Turkish
“Pacing is 34–86% but impression share is 10–43%. Not a budget problem: a rank wall.”
Both of the obvious “recover wasted spend” moves were available, and neither fit: nothing was
over-pacing, so there was no case to cut, and adding budget to campaigns held at 10% impression
share buys a larger share of the same loss. The money was not being wasted at the budget layer at
all. A waste percentage that cannot reach that conclusion is measuring the wrong thing
confidently.
The catch: doing this once isn't enough
You can work this list in an afternoon and claw back a chunk of budget. The problem is that waste
regenerates. New junk search terms accumulate every week. Performance Max drifts toward cheap
inventory the moment you stop feeding it exclusions. A new campaign launches on the location default
because that is what defaults are for. The afternoon audit is a snapshot; the leak is a stream.
This is where continuous beats periodic. An AI media
buyer reads these reports the way you would (search terms, placements, location, device,
audiences), but on a schedule rather than once a quarter. It ranks each leak by what it is costing
now and keeps the evidence, next move and later result together. It removes the hours of digging that
stop you doing this as often as you should.
If you would rather run the manual version first, the step-by-step is in how to audit a Google Ads account , and the Meta
equivalent is the Meta Ads account audit .
Frequently asked
Q: How much ad spend is typically wasted?
A: WordStream's study of 15,666 Google Ads accounts, published in February 2026, found a typical account wasting about $1,127 a month on clicks that did not convert, against a median monthly spend of about $3,127: roughly a third. Two caveats matter: those accounts came through a free grading tool, so they likely lean toward the unoptimised end, and “wasted” is defined loosely as clicks that did not convert. Your own figure depends on account maturity, how much runs on defaults, and whether anyone reviews search terms and placements.
Q: How do I find wasted ad spend?
A: Work the leaks in order: pull the search terms report for junk queries, check whether location targeting is set to “interest” rather than “in” your area, review placement and Performance Max reporting, sanity-check device bids, add exclusions for existing converters, and test whether branded search is incremental. Most of it is findable in an afternoon.
Q: What is the biggest source of wasted spend?
A: Wasted search terms are usually the largest pool you can stop today: broad and phrase match pull in queries with no buying intent, and every click on them is spend you can stop with a negative keyword. Location and placement defaults are close behind, and they compound because nobody looks at them.
Q: Can AI reduce wasted ad spend?
A: Yes. The repetitive part of finding waste is what an AI media buyer is good at. It reads search terms, placements, location and device reports on a schedule, ranks each leak by what it is costing you and keeps the evidence and next move together. It removes the hours of digging that stop a team checking often enough.
Q: How often should I check for waste?
A: Search terms and placements deserve a weekly pass on active accounts, because that is where new junk queries and bad placements accumulate fastest. Location, device and audience settings change less: audit them at launch and re-check quarterly. If software is watching for you, the cadence becomes “whenever something crosses a threshold” instead of a calendar chore.
Q: Does Performance Max waste budget?
A: It can. Performance Max spreads spend across Search, Display, YouTube and partner placements with limited visibility, so budget can drift toward cheap, low-intent inventory unless you feed it exclusions and audience signals. It is not waste by design, but the leaks are harder to see, which is why the placement and audience checks matter more, not less.
Q: How do I know if a campaign is wasting money?
A: Look for spend with no conversions attached: search terms that cost money and convert nothing, placements or locations with clicks but zero sales, and audiences you pay full CPA to reach after they have already converted. If a slice of the account has spend but the conversion column is empty, that is the campaign telling you where the leak is.

# How to audit a Google Ads account: 12-point checklist
URL: https://adgent.app/how-to-audit-a-google-ads-account

Blog How-to
How to audit a Google Ads account, properly
Most account audits are a 40-point checklist that produces a 40-point to-do list. This
one is shorter and ordered differently: the checks that move money first, ranked by recoverable spend,
not by how thorough the report looks.
Adgent · Notes from building the analyst
Type
How-to
Reading time
9 min
Published
21 July 2026
On this page
Start with measurement
The 12-point audit
Rank, don't just list
Why it doesn't stay done
Red flags
Manual vs continuous
How often to audit
Common audit mistakes
Questions
All articles
A Google Ads account audit is supposed to answer one question: where is this account leaking
money, and what is the cheapest thing to fix first? Yet most audits bury that answer under a
hundred green ticks. So here is the version that leads with impact: the checks that actually recover
spend, in the order a senior buyer runs them.
Short answer
To audit a Google Ads account, work in order of recoverable spend. First verify conversion
tracking (a broken signal corrupts everything downstream), then check
wasted search terms , placement
leakage , bid-strategy fit and budget pacing . Attach a money
estimate to each finding and fix the highest-value leak first. A useful audit ranks by impact, not by
how many boxes it ticks.
Start with the number you can't trust
Before you judge a single campaign, judge the measurement. An account optimising toward a
misconfigured or value-less conversion will make every downstream number lie, and no amount of bid
tuning fixes a broken signal. So the first check is not performance; it is whether performance is
even measurable.
An audit that trusts a broken number just optimises the account deeper into the wrong
thing.
This is the same discipline behind leading with the
verdict : say what you can stand behind, flag the numbers you cannot, and never manufacture
confidence.
The 12-point audit, ranked by recoverable spend
Conversion tracking integrity. Are conversions firing once, with the right value,
on the right action? Duplicate or value-less conversions corrupt every optimisation downstream. Verify
against Google's
conversion tracking setup .
Wasted search terms. Pull the search terms report and find spend on queries that
will never convert. This is usually the single largest pool of instantly recoverable budget.
Placement leakage. On Display, Video and Performance Max, spend drifts to
low-quality placements at a fraction of core performance: the Google-side twin of the
placement drift that hides inside a blended
average .
Bid strategy fit. Is the strategy matched to the data volume? Target CPA and ROAS
need enough conversions to learn; below that threshold they thrash.
Budget pacing. Which campaigns are capped while winners starve? Reallocation is
free performance.
Search vs Performance Max overlap. Performance Max can cannibalise your branded and
high-intent search. Check where they compete for the same query.
Negative keyword hygiene. Missing negatives let broad match bleed into irrelevant
queries, which compounds with check 2.
Audience and geo signal. Are you feeding the algorithm useful audience signals, or
letting it guess?
Ad strength and asset coverage. Thin responsive assets cap reach and quality, but
chase this after the money checks, not before.
Landing page and tracking parity. Do the pages match the promise, and does
analytics agree with Ads on conversions?
Attribution maturity. Recent numbers are still settling. A campaign judged inside
its window reads pessimistic: the Google cousin of Meta's 7-day
window problem .
Cross-platform comparability. If you also run Meta, remember the two
cannot be compared directly before you shift
budget between them.
Rank, don't just list
The difference between a useful audit and a report nobody acts on is ordering. Every finding should
carry an estimate of recoverable spend so the account owner knows what to do on Monday morning, not a
flat list where a $12,000-a-month leak sits next to a cosmetic asset warning.
Attach a number to each finding. “Wasted search terms: about $9,000 a month” beats
“improve keyword targeting.”
Sequence the fixes. Some changes reset learning; order them so you do not undo one
fix with the next.
Make every figure verifiable. Each number should point back to where you can
confirm it in the account. Trust is the whole point.
What a ranked audit looks like when it comes out of the account itself rather than a template: one
run on one live account, every item priced and sorted into classes before anyone opened a
spreadsheet.
One run · one live account $2,892–5,867 a month, priced across 60 items
Fix now 34
Opportunity 13
Experiment 7
Watching 6
Evidence items attached 192
One live account, run of 7 September 2026, 28-day window. ₺140,000–284,000 a month, the
model's estimate, converted at 48.4069 per USD. A range, not a point estimate.
Why this doesn't stay done
The catch with a one-off audit is that accounts drift. Search terms shift weekly, placements leak
again, pacing changes with seasonality. A PDF from last quarter describes an account that no longer
exists. The real fix is not a better audit template; it is a standing
analyst that keeps re-reading the account and flags what changed.
That is the job Adgent is built for. It is a team of AI agents working toward your marketing goals,
and it reads every connected Google and Meta account each day. Several of its ten specialists map
straight onto this list: Measurement Integrity on tracking, Placement & Network Optimizer on
placements, CPC-Spike Autopsy on bidding, Budget-Pacing Cop on budget exhaustion, and Account Architect
on structure. What they find comes back ranked by an estimated monthly amount, with the evidence and
next move attached.
Red flags: what a broken account looks like
Some findings you have to calculate. Others you can spot in thirty seconds: the tells that an account
has been left on autopilot. If you see any of these, you have found recoverable spend before you have
done a single sum.
Conversion action set to “Every” instead of “One.” A lead form counting every
submission inflates your conversion count and teaches Smart Bidding to chase repeat form-fillers. For
lead gen, this single toggle can materially overstate conversions.
No audience exclusions on retargeting or Performance Max. You are paying full CPA to
re-serve ads to people who already converted. On accounts with a healthy return rate, that is spend
re-buying customers you already have.
Performance Max with zero audience signals. An empty signal means the algorithm
cold-starts on your money. Performance Max will find the cheapest conversions it can, usually your
existing branded traffic, and take credit for demand you would have captured for free.
A search terms report nobody has opened in 90 days. Broad match without weekly
negative-keyword pruning bleeds into junk queries continuously. If the last negative was added six
months ago, assume a meaningful share of search spend is landing on queries that will never
convert.
Target CPA or ROAS running on under 30 conversions in 30 days.
Google's own guidance
is to judge a Target CPA campaign over at least 30 conversions in the last 30 days. Below that, per
campaign, Smart Bidding does not have enough signal to learn: it thrashes, and CPA swings wildly week
to week.
One catch-all ad group with 50+ keywords. Structure this loose means no query gets
a relevant ad or landing page. Quality Score suffers, CPCs climb, and you cannot diagnose anything
because everything is averaged together.
Auto-applied recommendations turned on. Google's auto-apply will quietly expand
match types and raise budgets on its own schedule. An account where Google is making the changes is
not an account you are auditing; it is one you are discovering.
Display and Search fused in one campaign. “Search with Display Select” pools two
different funnels under one budget and one CPA target. The Display half almost always drags, hidden
inside the blended number: the same trap as placement
drift inside an average .
Ads-reported conversions that do not match analytics. When Google Ads claims 400
conversions and GA4 sees 250, someone is optimising on a number that is not real. Past roughly 15 to
20% (our working threshold for investigate versus ignore), we treat it as a measurement problem to fix
before the bids; inside that band, call it attribution noise.
Manual audit vs continuous audit
The format of the audit decides what it can actually catch. A person running a checklist once a
quarter and software reading the account through the API every day are looking for the same leaks,
but they see very different amounts of them.
Manual audit Automated, continuous audit
Time to run A few hours to a full day per account Runs on its own, without anyone's afternoon
Frequency Quarterly, if you are disciplined Every day
What gets read What the auditor has time to sample What the API exposes, on every run
Catches drift No; it is a snapshot that ages fast Yes; flags what changed since the last read
Best at Judgment calls, strategy, context High-drift leaks: search terms, placements, pacing
Cost An agency fee per one-off audit A software fee, then nothing extra per re-run
Neither wins outright. A manual audit brings judgment a script cannot; a continuous one catches the
leaks that reopen the week after a manual audit ships. The strongest setup is a standing analyst for
the high-drift checks and a person for the strategy calls, which is exactly what
an AI media buyer is meant to be.
How often should you audit?
Audit cadence should match how fast each check goes stale. Some things barely move; others rot within
a week. A single quarterly review treats them all the same, which is why so many audits feel out of
date the moment they land.
Full audit: quarterly. The complete 12-point pass: structure, bid strategy,
attribution, account hygiene. These are slow-moving and worth a deep, unhurried look four times a
year.
Light review: monthly. A focused pass on budget pacing, ad strength and the
campaigns that shifted most. Thirty minutes to catch anything the quarter would let drift too
far.
Continuous: for the high-drift checks. Wasted search terms, placement leakage and
budget pacing move week to week. These want watching, not scheduling: the moment they slip, spend
leaks, and a quarterly cadence means you find out 89 days late.
The blunt version: audit the slow things on a calendar and watch the fast things continuously.
Anything you only check quarterly, you are effectively not checking.
Common Google Ads audit mistakes
A bad audit can be worse than an incomplete one: it draws confident conclusions from bad inputs.
These are the mistakes that turn a review into a list of wrong decisions.
Auditing before you have checked conversion tracking. Every performance judgment
rests on the conversion signal. If you rank campaigns before verifying it fires once, with the right
value, you are ranking noise. Measurement is step one for a reason.
Treating small-sample placements as decisions. A placement with 40 impressions and
one conversion is not a winner, and one with 200 clicks and no sale is not dead: it is just noise.
Cutting or scaling on samples this thin creates the very volatility you were trying to fix.
Ignoring the attribution window. Recent conversions are still landing. Judge a
campaign from inside its window and it always reads pessimistic: the Google cousin of Meta's
day-one data problem . Let the window close before you
call a verdict.
Comparing across platforms as if they measure the same thing. Google and Meta count
conversions differently, so a raw ROAS comparison is apples to oranges. Understand how each one counts
before you move budget between them.
Producing a to-do list instead of a ranking. A flat 40-point list where a
$12,000-a-month leak sits beside a cosmetic asset warning gets skimmed, not acted on. Rank by
recoverable spend, or the audit changes nothing.
Run the audit
Worked end to end, this checklist is a solid afternoon, and the account starts drifting again the next
morning. That makes a standing read more useful than a quarterly one: the same checks run every day on
Google and Meta, ranked by recoverable spend, with the evidence and next move attached. Later reads
bring the result back to the same account history.
Frequently asked
Q: What is a Google Ads account audit?
A: A structured review of how an account is built and spending (conversion tracking, search terms, placements, bid strategy, budget pacing and measurement) to find wasted spend and missed opportunity. A good audit ranks findings by recoverable spend, not by how many boxes it ticks.
Q: How often should you audit a Google Ads account?
A: A full audit quarterly, a lighter review monthly. But the highest-value checks drift week to week, so the ideal is continuous watching rather than a one-off review.
Q: How long does a Google Ads audit take?
A: A manual audit of a mid-sized account takes a senior buyer a few hours to a day. Software that reads the account through the API surfaces the same kind of findings without taking anyone's afternoon, and keeps them current.
Q: Can an AI audit a Google Ads account?
A: Yes. An AI ad account audit reads the account through the platform API, checks the same signals a senior buyer would, ranks findings by recoverable spend and flags any number it cannot yet stand behind. The strongest tools keep the evidence, recommendation and later account history together.
Q: How long does a PPC audit take?
A: For a mid-sized Google Ads account, a thorough manual PPC audit runs a few hours to a full day, longer if the account is large or the tracking is messy. Agencies often quote a one-to-two-week turnaround because the report has to be written up. Software that reads the account through the API does the reading on its own and, unlike a document, keeps the findings current.
Q: What tools do you need to audit Google Ads?
A: The account itself gets you most of the way: the search terms report, the placements and asset reports, the change history, and the conversion and attribution settings. Pair it with GA4 to compare conversions, and Google Tag Assistant to confirm tags fire correctly. Beyond that, a spreadsheet to rank findings by recoverable spend, or a continuous tool that does the reading and ranking for you.
Q: How much can an audit recover?
A: It depends entirely on how neglected the account is, but on accounts that have not been pruned in a while, wasted search terms, leaked placements and duplicate retargeting are where recoverable spend usually sits. The bigger, quieter win is measurement: fixing a misconfigured conversion often reshapes every downstream decision, which is worth more than any single line-item cut.
Q: Can you automate a Google Ads audit?
A: The high-drift checks (wasted search terms, placement leakage, budget pacing) automate well, because they are rule-based and change constantly, so continuous watching beats a scheduled review. Judgment calls like strategy and structure still benefit from a person. The best setup automates the leaks that reopen weekly and keeps a person on the calls that need context.

# How to audit a Performance Max campaign · Adgent
URL: https://adgent.app/how-to-audit-performance-max

Blog Playbook
How to audit a Performance Max campaign (the black box)
Performance Max either becomes your best campaign or your biggest waste source, and Google
won't tell you which. Here are the checks that open the black box, ranked by how much money they recover,
in the order you should actually run them.
Adgent · Notes from building the analyst
Type
Playbook
Reading time
9 min
Published
22 July 2026
Updated
31 October 2026
On this page
1. Brand-spend detection
2. Conversion tracking
3. Channel breakdown
4. Asset groups and signals
5. Landing pages
6. Search overlap
Manual vs continuous
Where an AI media buyer fits
Frequently asked
All articles
Performance Max is the campaign type Google most wants you to run and least wants you to see inside.
You hand it budget, assets and a goal; it decides where the money goes across Search, Display, YouTube,
Gmail, Discover and Maps, and reports back a single ROAS number that, more often than you would like, is
flattering. The good news: the black box has seams. This is the audit, ranked by how much money each check
tends to recover.
Short answer
Performance Max becomes your best campaign or your biggest waste source, and the
difference is setup plus a few checks. Audit in this order: brand-spend detection first, then
conversion-tracking quality, then the channel and placement breakdown, then asset-group signals,
landing-page experience, and finally Search overlap. Fix the leaks Google hides, and PMax earns its
budget.
PMax doesn't fail loudly. It fails by spending your budget in the one place you would
never have chosen, and taking credit for the sales you would have made anyway.
1. Brand-spend detection: the check that pays for the audit
Start here, always. The most common way Performance Max looks like a hero is that it is serving on your
own brand terms (people already searching “[your company]”) and booking those near-certain conversions as
its own work. Your reported ROAS goes to the moon; your incremental ROAS barely moves.
The tell is a search term or asset group with a ROAS wildly out of line with everything else: 15× when
the account average is 3×. That is almost never a demand-gen miracle. It is branded traffic PMax is
intercepting on the way to a click you already owned. Pull the search-terms and asset-group breakdown,
find the outlier, and check whether the winning queries contain your brand name.
If they do, the fix is a brand exclusion (an account-level negative keyword list or
a brand
list applied to PMax ) so the campaign competes for demand you don't already have. It is worth its own deep dive, see
Performance Max brand cannibalization , but for the
audit the rule is simple: any asset group with abnormal ROAS is guilty until the search terms prove
otherwise.
2. Conversion-tracking quality: garbage in, garbage out
Performance Max leans on your conversion data more heavily than any other campaign type. It has no
manual levers: no keywords, no placements you pick, no bids you set. All it has is the goal you give it
and the conversion signal it optimizes toward. If that signal is wrong, every decision downstream is
wrong, and no amount of asset tweaking will save it.
So before you touch anything else, verify the tracking is clean:
One primary conversion, counted once. Double-firing tags and duplicate conversion
actions teach PMax that a purchase is worth two, and it overspends accordingly.
Values that reflect real revenue. If you pass a static value instead of dynamic
cart value, PMax optimizes for volume of cheap orders, not margin. Check the values against GA4 and your
store's own numbers.
No soft goals as primary. “Add to cart” or “page view” as a primary conversion turns
PMax into a traffic firehose chasing the easy signal, not the sale.
Consent mode and modelling sanity. If a big share of conversions are modelled
rather than observed, the ground under every decision is softer than the ROAS number admits.
Garbage in, garbage out isn't a cliché here; it is the whole mechanism. PMax is a signal-following
machine, so the signal is the product.
3. Channel and network breakdown: where it's actually spending
Now find out where the money physically went. The channel-level split (Search vs Display vs Video vs
Shopping) is in the Channel performance report under Insights and reports, for data from June 2025 onward;
a script or the Google Ads API gives the same split in bulk or for older periods, and the placement
report shows the actual apps and sites.
What you are looking for is the classic PMax leak: budget draining into cheap Display impressions and
auto-playing Video that generate impressive reach and almost no revenue, while the Search and Shopping
slices quietly do the real work. If 60% of spend is Display and 5% of conversions are, you have found a
large recoverable chunk.
Two exclusions do most of the cleanup:
Junk placements. Pull the placement report, find the mobile games and
made-for-advertising sites eating budget, and add them to an account-level placement exclusion
list. Google
confirms Performance Max respects account-level placement exclusions.
Mobile-app inventory. A mobile-app category exclusion removes a large share of the
accidental-tap traffic that flatters your click numbers and converts at nothing.
4. Asset-group strength and audience signals: don't cold-start on your money
Every asset group is a mini-campaign, and PMax launches each one into a cold start while it learns.
What shortens the cold start is audience signals : your customer lists, high-intent
segments and custom audiences telling Google where to begin looking. Leave them empty and you are paying
full price for the machine to guess from scratch.
In the audit, check that every asset group has a genuine audience signal (not blank, not “all users”),
the full complement of assets so Google isn't starved for creative to test, and enough conversion volume
to have actually exited learning. A thin asset group with no signal is a cold start you are funding
indefinitely.
5. Landing-page experience per asset group
PMax uses your final URLs, and unless you turn it off, final URL expansion sends traffic to whatever
page on your site Google thinks fits the query. That means an asset group themed around one product can
be sending paid clicks to a stale blog post or an out-of-stock page.
Audit the landing experience per asset group: are the URLs the ones you intended, is final URL
expansion doing something sensible or something feral, and does each page match the promise of the asset
group's creative? A great asset group pointed at a slow, off-message page is spend you are wasting at the
last step.
6. Search vs PMax overlap and cannibalization
Finally, zoom out to how PMax coexists with your standard Search campaigns. Google's serving priority
means PMax can win queries your Search campaigns would have won anyway, including brand, and the two can
end up bidding against your own account. The result is the same conversions attributed twice and a
blended picture that hides which campaign actually earned them.
Check the overlap: are PMax and Search competing for the same high-intent queries, is PMax siphoning
credit from a well-built Search campaign, and would tighter brand exclusions plus clearer campaign roles
stop the two from cannibalizing each other? This closes the loop back to check one: brand spend and
Search overlap are the same leak seen from two angles.
Manual audit vs continuous monitoring
Here is the uncomfortable truth about everything above: a manual PMax audit is a snapshot, and PMax is
a moving target. Brand-spend creep, a tracking break, placement drift: none of them wait for your monthly
review. A once-a-month audit catches the leak weeks after it started spending. Side by side:
What the audit needs Manual monthly audit Continuous monitoring
Catches a tracking break At the next review At the next daily read
Spots brand-spend creep early No Yes
Pulls the channel and placement split By hand Yes
Flags a new cold-start asset group No Yes
Ranks findings by recoverable spend No Yes
Runs while you sleep No Yes
The manual audit tells you what was true last month. Continuous monitoring tells you what is
leaking now, and how much.
Where an AI media buyer comes in
Every check in this playbook rewards running continuously and suffers when run monthly. That is the
case for handing it to an AI media buyer : one that pulls the
channel and placement breakdown, catches the brand term with abnormal ROAS, raises the tracking break at
the next daily read instead of in next month's report, and ranks every finding by recoverable spend, so
you fix the biggest leak first instead of the most visible one.
PMax isn't the only black box worth this treatment. The same discipline applies to the whole account,
which is why it pairs with a broader Google Ads account
audit .
Adgent is a team of AI agents working toward your marketing goals on Google Ads and Meta. They read
every connected account each day, put an estimated monthly amount on every decision and rank the list
by what it costs. Each leak arrives with the evidence, next move and later result attached.
Frequently asked
Q: Why is Performance Max spending but not converting?
A: Usually one of three things: conversion tracking is broken or double-counting, so PMax
is optimizing toward bad signals; the campaign is pouring budget into cheap Display and Video
placements that impress but don't convert; or the asset groups are so thin that Google is still in
cold start, buying junk inventory while it learns. Audit tracking first, then the channel
breakdown.
Q: How do I see where Performance Max spends?
A: Open the Channel performance report under Insights and reports to see the Search,
Display, Video and Shopping split (data from June 2025 onward), and the placement report to see the
actual apps and sites. A script or the Google Ads API gives the same split in bulk, for older periods
or across many accounts at once.
Q: Can you exclude placements in Performance Max?
A: Partially. You can apply account-level placement exclusions, exclude mobile-app inventory
via a mobile-app category exclusion, and add brand-safety and content exclusions. You can't hand-pick
placements the way you can in a Display campaign, but the account-level exclusion list and the
mobile-app exclusion together remove most of the wasted junk inventory.
Q: Is Performance Max cannibalizing my search?
A: Often, yes. PMax can serve on search queries, including your brand terms, and Google's
priority rules mean it can outrank or overlap your standard Search campaigns. The tell is a PMax term
or asset group with a wildly higher ROAS than the rest: that is usually branded search PMax is taking
credit for, not new demand it created.
Q: How often should I audit Performance Max?
A: A full manual audit is worth doing monthly, and always after a big budget change, a new
asset group or a tracking change. But the checks that matter (brand-spend creep, tracking breaks,
placement drift) move daily, so the honest answer is that PMax wants continuous monitoring, not a
monthly snapshot. A once-a-month audit catches the leak weeks after it started.
Q: What's the most important Performance Max setting?
A: Clean conversion tracking, followed closely by a brand exclusion. PMax leans entirely on
your conversion data to decide where to spend, so if tracking is wrong every downstream decision is
wrong. After that, excluding your brand terms stops PMax from taking credit for demand you already own
and inflating its reported ROAS.
Q: Can AI audit Performance Max?
A: Yes, and PMax is exactly the kind of black box AI is good at. An AI media buyer can pull
the channel and placement breakdown, detect a brand term with abnormal ROAS, raise a tracking break at
the next daily read and rank each finding by recoverable spend, continuously rather than once a
month.

# How to choose an AI media buying tool · Adgent
URL: https://adgent.app/how-to-choose-an-ai-media-buying-tool

Blog How-to
How to choose an AI media buying tool
“AI ad tool” describes four different products solving four different problems. This is a
neutral map of the categories (creative generation, bid automation, analysis and diagnostics, and DSPs)
and a framework for picking the one that fixes your actual bottleneck.
Adgent · Notes from building the analyst
Type
How-to
Reading time
7 min
Published
25 July 2026
On this page
The four categories
A comparison by capability
If you need X, look for Y
Four things to check
Where Adgent fits
Questions
All articles
Search for the “best AI media buyer tool” and you will get a list that mixes ad-copy generators,
automated bidding bots, reporting dashboards and enterprise programmatic platforms as if they were
rivals. They are not. They are four different products aimed at four different jobs, and a ranked list
that pretends they compete tells you nothing about which one you should buy. So before the shortlist,
the map.
Short answer
There is no single “best” AI media buying tool, because AI ad tools split into four
categories : creative generation, bid automation, analysis and diagnostics, and programmatic
buying (DSPs). The right one matches your bottleneck. Need more ads: pick generation . Cannot
tell why a metric moved: pick analysis and diagnostics . Buying display or CTV at scale: pick a
DSP . And remember that the bid AI is probably already running, free, inside Meta and Google.
The four categories of AI ad tools
Almost every tool marketed as “AI for media buying” fits one of these buckets. Knowing the bucket
tells you what the tool is actually for.
1. Creative generation
Creative-generation tools make the assets: ad copy, image and video variations, hooks and headlines at
volume. The pitch is speed: turn one concept into forty variants and let testing sort them. Meta's own
Advantage+ creative lives here, and so do general-purpose image and text models used for ad output.
You want this category when your constraint is producing enough creative to test , not
understanding what is already running.
2. Bid and budget automation
These act on the auction: setting bids, shifting budget, expanding audiences toward a target ROAS or
CPA. The crucial thing to know is that you almost certainly already own the best of
these . Meta's Advantage+ and Google's Performance Max are AI bid-automation tools that ship
inside the platforms for free. Third-party rules engines add triggers on top. Buy into this category
deliberately, because a standalone bidding tool often duplicates what the platforms do natively.
3. Analysis and diagnostics
These read the account and explain it: why ROAS moved, where spend leaks, which placement is dragging
the average, whether the tracking can be trusted at all. They do not generate ads and they do not buy
inventory; they turn a wall of metrics into a ranked verdict. This is the category the platform AI
leaves wide open: Advantage+ optimises the auction but will not tell you why it is
underperforming. Tools here range from BI-style dashboards and attribution suites to AI analysts that
reason across an account. Adgent sits in this row , as a daily read of each account
that ranks findings by an estimated monthly amount. Reach for analysis and diagnostics when your
bottleneck is understanding, not making or buying .
4. DSPs (demand-side platforms)
These are programmatic-buying infrastructure, such as Google's Display & Video 360 or Amazon's DSP,
that bid on inventory across display, video and connected-TV exchanges in real time. The AI here is in
the bidding algorithms and inventory selection. It is a different sport from managing Meta and Google
campaigns: DSPs are about reach and buying at scale across the open web. You want one when you are
buying programmatic inventory , not when you are optimising social and search
accounts.
The question is not which tool is best. It is which of the four jobs is the one slowing you
down.
A comparison by capability
Here are the same four categories read across the jobs that matter, so you can see at a glance what
each does and, just as usefully, what it does not.
Capability Creative generation Bid automation Analysis and diagnostics DSP
Produces ad variations Yes No No No
Sets bids and budgets No Yes Prepares the move Yes
Explains why a metric moved No No Yes No
Reads Meta and Google side by side No Some Yes No
Buys open-web or CTV inventory No No No Yes
Flags wasted spend and tracking gaps No Partial Yes No
Already inside Meta and Google, free Partly Yes No No
Read down the analysis column and it does the thing the others cannot: tell you why, on every
account you connect, and what to do about it. It sits on top of the platform bid AI, not against
it.
A decision framework: if you need X, look for Y
Skip the ranked lists. Start from what is actually slowing you down, and the category picks
itself.
If you cannot make enough creative to test, look at a generation
tool. Your constraint is output volume, and this is the one category that adds it.
If you want the auction managed automatically, first check what Advantage+ and
Performance Max already do. A third-party bid-automation tool only earns its price if it
adds logic the platforms cannot.
If you are drowning in reports and cannot tell why numbers moved, look at an
analysis and diagnostics tool. This is the most common real bottleneck, and the one the
platform AI leaves unsolved.
If you are buying display, video or CTV at scale, you need a DSP .
Nothing in the other three categories buys open-web inventory.
If you are an agency stretched thin across many accounts, look for an
analysis layer that reads each client every day and gives each one a ranked verdict.
The auction is already automated per platform; the scarce resource is senior attention, and that is
what this scales.
Four things to check on any tool
Whichever category you land in, four questions cut through the marketing. First: does it
duplicate the platform AI you already have? A lot of “AI media buying” is a paid wrapper over
bidding that Meta and Google do for free. Second: does the decision continue into finished
work? A tool that diagnoses the problem and leaves the team to rebuild the report, plan or
account move has only moved the bottleneck. See how the layers compare .
The last two are harder to fake in a demo, which is exactly why they are worth asking.
Does it check your request against the account's own numbers?
Ask for something the account cannot support: a target CPA well below anything it has ever produced,
or a conversion campaign on an event that barely fires. A tool that reasons will push back and show its
work: your history at this stage sits here, your target sits there, and here is the gap. A tool
that only executes will build it, cheerfully, and let you find out in four weeks. The reason matters as
much as the answer: “not recommended” with no numbers behind it is a shrug, not an analysis. Run this
test in the demo, on a real account, and see whether the answer comes with the account's own
figures.
Does it tell you the account isn't ready before you spend, or after?
Every account has preconditions: enough conversion volume for the optimiser to learn from, tracking
that is not broken, a signal that maps to something the business actually sells. A tool that checks
those first will sometimes tell you the setup is technically possible but the learning signal is not
there yet, and name the fix. A tool that checks them afterwards reports the same fact as a performance
problem a month later, once the budget has already taught the algorithm nothing. Same finding, very
different price. Ask which one you are buying.
What the first kind looks like in practice: asked to set up a sales campaign on one live account (a
hotel group, August 2026), Adgent read what the pixel had actually recorded over 30 days before
building anything. It found 16,404 initiate-checkout events and 4 purchases.
Adgent Pre-build check · one live account (hotel group), August 2026 · translated from Turkish
“The account is ready, but not ready for an efficient Sales conversion event.”
Where Adgent fits
To be plain about our own place on this map: Adgent sits in analysis and diagnostics that
continues into account work . It is not a creative generator and not a DSP. It reads Meta and
Google every day, with GA4, Search Console and Merchant Center alongside, and turns what it finds into
ranked decisions with evidence and an estimated monthly amount. The same decision can become a report,
media plan, campaign build, recurring agent or account move. It reads the creative you already run; it
does not make it.
It does not replace the categories above. You will still want creative tools, and you will still run
the platforms' bid AI. It fills the row those leave open: telling you why , on each account, and
what to do next.
So which AI media buying tool is best? The one that fixes your bottleneck. Map your constraint to a
category, check that it is not reselling the platform AI, and inspect what happens after the diagnosis.
If your constraint is understanding why performance moved and where spend leaks, ask for a demo of
the ranked decisions and their supporting evidence.
Frequently asked
Q: What is the best AI media buyer tool?
A: There is no single best AI media buyer tool, because AI ad tools solve four different problems: creative generation, bid automation, analysis and diagnostics, and programmatic buying (DSPs). The best tool is the one that matches your bottleneck. If you are drowning in reporting and cannot tell why a metric moved, you want an analysis and diagnostics tool. If you need more creative variations, you want a generation tool. If you are buying display or CTV at scale, you want a DSP. Pick by the job, not by the label.
Q: What are the best AI tools for performance marketers?
A: Performance marketers typically layer three kinds of AI: the platform's own bid automation (Advantage+, Performance Max) that ships inside Meta and Google, a creative tool to produce ad variations faster, and an analysis or diagnostics tool that reads accounts and explains why numbers moved. The platform AI is usually already running; the two you actively choose are creative and analysis. Which matters more depends on whether your constraint is making ads or understanding them.
Q: What's the best AI tool for a media buying agency?
A: For an agency, the constraint is usually senior attention spread across many client accounts, not the auction; every platform already runs its own bid AI. So the AI worth buying is an analysis and diagnostics layer that reads each account every day and gives each client a ranked verdict, letting junior teams work at senior output. Creative generation tools help volume; a DSP helps if the agency buys programmatic. The account-diagnostics layer is what holds the same standard on every client in the book.
Q: Does the AI already inside Meta and Google count as an AI media buying tool?
A: Yes. Advantage+ and Performance Max are AI bid-automation tools, and they are already running in most accounts. That is why buying a separate bid-automation tool often duplicates what the platforms do for free. The gap the platform AI leaves is explanation: it optimises the auction but will not tell you why your ROAS dropped or which placement is leaking. That is the analysis and diagnostics category, which sits on top of the platform AI rather than replacing it.
Q: What should happen after an AI tool diagnoses the account?
A: The decision should continue into the work it creates: a report, plan, campaign build, recurring check or account move. Check whether the evidence and later result stay attached. If the output ends as a paragraph the team must copy into another tool, the operational bottleneck remains.
Q: What's the difference between a DSP and an AI media buyer?
A: A DSP (demand-side platform) is programmatic-buying infrastructure: it bids on inventory across display, video and CTV exchanges in real time. An AI media buyer works on top of your existing platform accounts (Meta, Google), reading and reasoning about performance rather than buying inventory. They solve different problems: a DSP is about reach and buying at scale; an AI media buyer is about understanding and acting on what you are already running.
Q: How do I choose between all the AI ad tools?
A: Start from your bottleneck, not the tool list. Ask what is actually slowing you down: producing enough creative, understanding why performance moved, buying inventory at scale, or managing many accounts at once. Each maps to one category: generation, analysis and diagnostics, DSPs, or an agency-oriented analysis layer. Then check the access model and whether the tool duplicates the platform AI you already have. Buy the layer that fixes your constraint, not the one with the broadest feature list.

# The Meta Ads audit: ten checks that recover spend · Adgent
URL: https://adgent.app/meta-ads-account-audit-checklist

Blog How-to
The Meta Ads account audit: the ten checks that recover spend
Most Meta audits are a screenshot tour of the dashboard. This one is ordered by impact:
the checks that recover spend first, and the signal check that has to come before all of them, because
a broken pixel makes every other number a guess.
Adgent · Notes from building the analyst
Type
How-to
Reading time
7 min
Published
22 July 2026
On this page
Start with the signal
The ten checks
Rank, don't just list
Red flags
Manual vs continuous
A standing audit
All articles
A Meta Ads audit is supposed to answer one question: where is this account leaking money, and
what is the cheapest thing to fix first? Yet most audits bury that answer under a screenshot
tour of Ads Manager. This is the version that leads with impact: the checks that actually recover spend,
in the order a senior buyer runs them. It is the Meta twin of
how to audit a Google Ads account : same discipline,
different platform.
Short answer
To audit a Meta Ads account , work in order of recoverable spend, and verify the signal
first. Confirm pixel and Conversions API health before you judge a single campaign,
because a broken signal corrupts everything downstream. Then check attribution, CBO leakage, Audience
Network placement drift, frequency and creative fatigue. Attach a dollar figure to each finding and fix
the biggest leak first.
Start with the signal you can't trust
Before you judge a single ad set, judge the measurement. On Meta more than anywhere, the number you
optimise toward is only as good as the pixel and Conversions API feeding it. A misconfigured event, a
browser pixel firing without a CAPI match, a purchase event that double-counts: any of these makes ROAS
and CPA read like fiction, and no amount of budget tuning fixes a broken signal.
In one line
An audit that trusts a broken pixel just optimises the account deeper into the wrong thing.
So the first check is not performance. It is whether performance is even measurable. Open Events
Manager, confirm events fire once per action, check event match quality, and make sure the browser pixel
and CAPI events deduplicate on a shared event ID. It is the same discipline behind
leading with the verdict : say what you can stand behind,
flag what you can't, and never manufacture confidence.
The ten Meta audit checks, ranked by recoverable spend
Ten families of check, ordered so the money moves first and the hygiene comes last. Each is a place
spend hides on Meta specifically:
Pixel and Conversions API health. Events firing once, with the right value, on the
right action? Confirm browser and CAPI events deduplicate, and check event match quality against
Meta's
Conversions API setup . A broken signal corrupts every optimisation downstream.
Attribution setting. Is the account on 7-day click, or the default 7-day click /
1-day view? Ad sets judged on different windows are not comparable, and view-through credit inflates
the wrong winners. Judge it on settled data, too: an ad set read on
day-one data looks pessimistic and gets paused before it
has finished reporting.
CBO budget leakage. Under Campaign Budget Optimisation, Meta pools the budget and
often starves a proven ad set to feed a cheaper but worse one. Check where the money actually landed
against where the conversions did.
Audience Network placement drift. Spend quietly drifts to Audience Network and Reels
at a fraction of feed performance: the Meta twin of
the placement drift that hides inside a blended
average .
Frequency and creative fatigue. Rising frequency with climbing CPM is the account
telling you the creative is spent.
CPM is the early creative-fatigue signal , well
before ROAS drops.
Audience overlap. Ad sets bidding against each other in the same auction drive up
your own CPMs. Run the overlap tool on your prospecting sets.
Retargeting exclusions. Are purchasers and recent converters excluded from
prospecting and retargeting? Missing exclusions mean paying full CPA to re-buy customers you already
have.
Catalogue and feed health. For commerce accounts, a stale or partly rejected
catalogue silently caps Advantage+ Shopping reach. Check feed freshness, rejection rate and required
fields.
Learning-phase status. Ad sets stuck in learning, or endlessly re-entering it after
edits, never stabilise. Count how many are learning-limited and why.
Ad-account structure. Too many overlapping ad sets fragment the signal below the
conversion volume Meta needs to learn. Consolidation is often free performance.
Rank, don't just list
The difference between a useful audit and a report nobody acts on is ordering. Every finding should
carry an estimate of recoverable spend so the account owner knows what to do on Monday morning, not a
flat list where a $10,000-a-month leak sits next to a cosmetic naming warning.
Attach a number to each finding. “Audience Network drift: about $6,000 a month”
(an example figure) beats “review placements”.
Sequence the fixes. Editing an ad set can reset the learning phase; order changes so
you don't undo one fix with the next.
Make every figure verifiable. Each number should point back to where to confirm it
in Ads Manager. Trust is the whole point.
Red flags: what a neglected account looks like
Some findings you have to calculate. Others you can spot in thirty seconds: the tells that an account
has been left to run itself. If you see any of these, you have found recoverable spend before you have
done a single sum.
Frequency above 5 on a prospecting audience. A cold audience seeing the same ad five
or more times in a week is fatigued and getting more expensive to reach. Rising frequency with climbing
CPM is the clearest early fatigue tell there is: act before ROAS confirms it.
No retargeting exclusions. If purchasers and recent converters are not excluded
from prospecting, you are paying full CPA to re-serve ads to people who already bought.
A backend versus Ads Manager revenue gap wider than roughly 15–20%. That is our
working threshold for investigate versus ignore. When Ads Manager claims, say, $40,000 in sales and
your store or GA4 sees $30,000, someone is optimising on a number that is not real. Inside that band,
call it attribution noise; past it, your pixel and CAPI setup is the first thing to fix, not your
bids.
Audience Network eating a big share of a placement-optimised budget. When automatic
placements let Audience Network absorb a large slice of spend at a fraction of feed performance, the
blended ROAS looks fine while the leak sits hidden inside the average.
Ad sets still in the learning phase after five days. Learning-limited ad sets never
stabilise, usually because conversion volume is too low or edits keep restarting the clock. If half
the account is perpetually learning, the structure is fragmenting the signal.
One giant CBO campaign with every audience inside it. Pooling prospecting,
retargeting and lookalikes under one budget lets Meta chase the cheapest conversions, usually warm
retargeting, and take credit for demand you would have captured anyway.
Default attribution, and nobody knows which window. An account reported on 7-day
click / 1-day view while the team quotes numbers as if they were click-only is comparing ad sets that
were never on the same footing.
Manual audit vs continuous audit
The format of the audit decides what it can catch. A person running this checklist once a quarter and
software reading the account through the API every day are looking for the same leaks, but they see
very different amounts of them.
Dimension Manual audit Continuous audit
Time to run A few hours to a full day per account Runs unattended, then re-runs on its own
Frequency Quarterly, if you are disciplined Every day
Coverage What the auditor has time to sample Every campaign, ad set and ad it can read
Catches drift No: a snapshot that ages fast Yes: reads what changed since the last run
Best at Judgment calls, strategy, creative direction High-drift leaks: placements, frequency, CBO pacing
Cost An agency fee or a day of senior time, each time A subscription, nothing extra per re-run
Neither wins outright. A manual audit brings judgment a script can't; a continuous one catches the
leaks that reopen the week after a manual audit ships. The strongest setup is a standing analyst for the
high-drift checks and a person for the strategy calls, which is what
an AI media buyer is built to be.
The real fix is a standing audit
The catch with a one-off Meta audit is that accounts drift. Frequency climbs daily, placements leak
again, creative fatigues, CBO re-pools the budget overnight. A PDF from last quarter describes an account
that no longer exists. The real fix is not a better template. It is a standing analyst that re-reads the
account continuously and brings what changed.
Adgent is a team of AI agents working toward your marketing goals, and its ten specialists each read
the account from their own angle. Several line up with this list: Measurement Integrity with the signal
check, the Budget Allocator with CBO leakage, the Placement & Network Optimizer with placement drift,
the Creative-Fatigue Scout with fatigue, the Audience-Overlap Detector with overlap and exclusions, and
the Account Architect with structure. Every connected Meta and Google Ads account is read every day, and
every decision carries an estimated monthly amount, so the list arrives ranked with its evidence and
next move attached.
Who wrote this Written by the people building Adgent, the AI employee that carries brand context into every growth decision. Related product: the Decisions screen .
Bring the same question to your own account. Adgent returns its position, the evidence underneath and what the finding is worth a month.
Pricing
Frequently asked.
Q: How do I audit a Meta (Facebook) ads account?
A: Work in order of recoverable spend, not report length. First verify the signal (pixel and Conversions API health, deduplication and event match quality), because a broken signal corrupts every number downstream. Then check your attribution setting, CBO budget leakage, Audience Network placement drift, frequency and creative fatigue, audience overlap, retargeting exclusions, catalogue health, learning-phase status and account structure. Attach a dollar estimate to each finding and fix the highest-value leak first.
Q: How often should I audit Meta ads?
A: Match the cadence to how fast each check goes stale. Run the full ten-check audit quarterly, a light monthly review on pacing, frequency and the ad sets that shifted most, and monitor the high-drift checks (placement drift, frequency, audience overlap and CBO leakage) continuously, because those reopen within a week of any manual pass.
Q: What are the red flags in a Meta ads account?
A: Frequency above 5 on a prospecting audience, no retargeting exclusions, a backend versus Ads Manager revenue gap wider than roughly 15–20%, Audience Network eating a large share of a placement-optimised budget, and ad sets stuck in the learning phase after five days. Any one of these is recoverable spend you can find before you do a single calculation.
Q: How do I check if my pixel is working?
A: Open Events Manager and confirm events fire once per action with a healthy event match quality score, that browser pixel and Conversions API events deduplicate on a shared event ID, and that your key conversion carries the right value. Use the Meta Pixel Helper on live pages and compare Ads Manager conversions against GA4 or your store. A gap wider than roughly 15–20% means the signal, not your bids, is the first thing to fix. Then check volume: Meta's guidance is a minimum of 50 events over 7 days for an ad set to learn.
Q: What attribution setting should I use?
A: For most direct-response accounts, 7-day click is the sensible default: it captures the buying window without over-crediting view-through. The trap is judging performance on the default setting without knowing which window it uses, or comparing ad sets on different windows. Pick one attribution setting, apply it consistently, and remember recent numbers are still settling inside the window and read pessimistic.
Q: Can AI audit Meta ads?
A: Yes, and it suits the high-drift checks better than a quarterly human pass. An AI media buyer reads the account through the API every day, ranks findings by what they cost and keeps the evidence and next move together. More in can AI audit your ad accounts .
Q: How long does a Meta audit take?
A: A thorough manual audit of a single account takes a few hours to a full day, depending on how many campaigns and creatives it holds. A continuous, API-driven audit runs unattended and repeats every day, so a leak is read the day after it opens, not at the next quarterly review.
