# Meta vs Google Ads: which for your first $10k? · Adgent
URL: https://adgent.app/meta-vs-google-ads-which-first

Blog Comparison
Meta vs Google Ads: which platform for your first $10k?
It is not the fight you think. Google Ads captures demand that already exists; Meta
creates demand that does not. Which you start with comes down to one question: do people already search
for what you sell?
Adgent · Notes from building the analyst
Type
Comparison
Reading time
7 min
Published
22 July 2026
Updated
31 October 2026
On this page
The one distinction
Side by side
Google Ads
Meta Ads
The ROAS trap
Which to start with
The measurement problem
All articles
“Meta or Google?” is the first budget question every new advertiser asks, and it is usually framed as a
duel, as if one platform is simply better and the other is the runner-up. That framing is wrong, and it
quietly wastes a lot of first-$10k budgets. Meta and Google are not two teams playing the same game.
They play different games, and the one you should start with depends on your product, not on which
platform has the better reputation this quarter.
Short answer
It is demand capture versus demand generation . Google Ads captures intent people
already have: they are searching for what you sell. Meta creates intent by interrupting people who were
not looking. Most brands eventually need both, but start with Google if there is real search volume for
your product, and with Meta if you are introducing something nobody knows to search for.
The one distinction that decides everything
Here is the split that matters more than any CPM chart: demand capture versus demand
generation .
Google Ads is demand capture. When someone types “best running shoes for flat feet”,
they have already decided they want running shoes; you are competing to be the answer. The intent is
there before your ad ever loads. Your job is to show up and not fumble it.
Meta is demand generation. Nobody opens Instagram to buy your product. You interrupt
them mid-scroll and create the want on the spot. There is no existing intent to capture, so your
creative has to do the work of creating it.
In one line
Google catches the hand already reaching for the shelf. Meta puts the product in front of a hand that
was not reaching for anything.
Everything else (cost, creative load, how hard the platform is to measure) flows from that one
difference. So before you compare a single number, ask the only question that matters: do
people already search for what I sell? If yes, there is demand waiting to be captured on
Google. If no, you will have to generate it on Meta.
Google Ads vs Meta Ads, side by side
Here is the comparison across the five dimensions that actually change your outcome. Neither column is
the winner: each is better at a different job.
What matters Google Ads (demand capture) Meta Ads (demand generation)
Intent type Existing: people already searching Created: interrupts the scroll
Best for Products people search for by name or need Visual, impulse or new-to-market products
Typical CAC pattern Lower early on warm search intent; CPCs climb in competitive categories Higher until a creative lands, then scales further and cheaper
Creative demand Low: a plain text ad on the right keyword converts High: weak creative gets punished fast
Measurement difficulty Moderate: Google's own reporting flatters search Hard: view-through and 7-day windows over-credit Meta
Read the table as two jobs, not two rivals. The right first dollar depends on which job your product needs done.
Google Ads: capturing the demand that is already there
Google's advantage is that it does not have to convince anyone the problem exists. Someone searching
“emergency plumber near me” or “CRM for small agencies” has already identified themselves as a buyer.
You are one click from a warm lead. That is why Google is usually the shorter path to a first sale, and
why a first-time advertiser can get a plain search campaign profitable faster than a first Meta
creative.
The downsides: on high-intent commercial keywords in competitive categories, cost per click can be
brutal, because you are bidding against everyone else who wants the same warm buyer. And Google's
automated products can drift. Performance Max in particular will spend your budget
across channels most accounts never break out, crediting itself for conversions that would have happened anyway.
Google's own reporting also over-credits search: its data-driven default
spreads credit across Google ad interactions only, and ignores that Meta may have created the awareness that led to the search in the first place.
Start on Google when people search for your category by name, when your product solves an urgent or
well-defined problem, or when you are a local or considered-purchase business where intent is
explicit.
Meta Ads: creating demand that was not there
Meta's strength is reach into people who have never heard of you. If your product is visual,
impulse-friendly or genuinely new, the kind of thing nobody would think to search for, Meta is where you
build the want from scratch. Done well, it scales further than Google because the audience is not
capped by search volume. Only so many people search for your keyword each month; there is no such
ceiling on the scroll.
The downsides: Meta lives and dies on creative. A weak ad burns budget fast, and the platform punishes
fatigue: what worked last month stops working, and you are back to producing more.
Advantage+ automates a lot, but it optimises toward Meta's auction, not your margin.
And Meta's measurement is the hardest to trust: view-through attribution and generous 7-day windows mean
the platform routinely claims credit for sales it merely witnessed. A reported ROAS of
4.2× on Meta is not the same 4.2× you would get anywhere else.
Start on Meta when nobody searches for what you sell yet, when your product is visual or
impulse-driven, or when you are building a brand and need awareness before intent can exist.
The trap: the two ROAS numbers don't compare
Here is where most “Meta vs Google” decisions go wrong. You run both for a month, pull the reports,
and see, for example, Meta reporting 4.2× while Google reports 3.1×. Obvious call: cut Google, double
down on Meta.
Except the two numbers were never measured the same way. Meta counts a 7-day-click, 1-day-view window
and claims view-through conversions; Google credits only its own ad interactions, inside its own conversion window. They frequently
double-count the same sale: Meta created the awareness, the person searched, Google closed it,
and both platforms report the win. Stacking those raw figures against each other is comparing two
different rulers and trusting the one with the friendlier markings.
Before you move a dollar based on platform-reported ROAS, read
why Meta and Google ROAS aren't directly
comparable . It is the single most expensive mistake in this whole decision. The fix is to check both
against the revenue your own analytics recorded, in GA4 or your store, on the same window, so you know
which platform actually earned the conversion instead of which one claimed it most loudly.
So which do you start with?
Skip the platform loyalty and run the product through this:
Do people search for it? If there is real search volume for your category, start
with Google. You are capturing demand that already exists, which is cheaper and faster to
convert.
Is it visual or impulse? If the product sells on sight and nobody is searching for
it, start with Meta. The feed is built to sell things people did not set out to buy.
Are you a beginner? Google search is more forgiving. The intent does half the
work, and a plain ad on the right keyword can convert without a studio's worth of creative.
Genuinely can't tell? Default to Google for the first $10k. Warm intent is the
easier thing to learn on, and the lessons transfer.
Then, once the first channel is stable and profitable, add the second, because the real endgame is
both . Meta generates the awareness that becomes tomorrow's branded searches; Google
captures the intent Meta warmed up. They compound. But compounding is a phase-two problem. On your first
$10k, pick the one your product needs and prove it works before you split your attention.
The measurement problem underneath all of this
Whichever you start with, the hard part is not launching. It is knowing what actually worked. Both
platforms grade their own homework, and both grade generously. So the advice to act on a number has to
come with a check that the number can carry the decision.
On one live account in August 2026, the GA4 funnel broke. Adgent recommended holding back budget
and pause advice that depended on those conversion counts, and argued from impression share and
pacing instead. The recommendation was observed; an automatic hold was not. That is a useful test
for an AI media buyer : can it name the broken signal and
explain which evidence still supports a decision?
Adgent reads Meta and Google Ads every day, with GA4, Search Console and Merchant Center alongside,
and carries confirmed brand context into the comparison. It returns the allocation decision with the
evidence underneath, then turns that decision into a media plan the team can reopen and share. Deciding
how much of the next dollar goes to each platform stays connected to the account data that justified it.
Who wrote this Written by the people building Adgent, the AI employee that carries brand context into every growth decision. Related product: media planning in chat .
Bring the same question to your own account. Adgent returns its position, the evidence underneath and what the finding is worth a month.
Pricing
Frequently asked.
Q: Should I start with Meta or Google Ads?
A: Start with Google Ads if people already search for what you sell: you are capturing demand that exists, so the intent is warm and the path to a first sale is short. Start with Meta if you are introducing something people do not know to look for, or if your product is visual and impulse-friendly. When you are unsure, Google is usually the safer first dollar because search intent is easier to convert and cheaper to learn from.
Q: Is Google Ads better than Meta?
A: Neither is better in the abstract; they do different jobs. Google Ads captures existing demand from people already searching; Meta creates demand by interrupting people who were not looking. Google tends to convert warmer traffic at a lower cost per acquisition early on; Meta scales further once you have nailed creative. The right answer depends on whether search volume exists for what you sell.
Q: Can you compare Meta and Google ROAS?
A: Not directly. A 4.2× on Meta and a 3.1× on Google are measured by two different attribution systems on two different windows, often double-counting the same sale. Comparing the raw numbers is misleading: check both against the revenue your analytics recorded, in GA4 or your store, before you decide which platform actually earned the conversion.
Q: Which is cheaper, Meta or Google?
A: It depends what you mean by cheap. Meta usually has a lower CPM, so you pay less per thousand impressions, but Google often has a lower cost per acquisition on high-intent search terms because the traffic is warmer. Cheap CPMs do not help if nobody buys; cheap conversions are what matter. On non-brand search, Google's CPCs can be expensive in competitive categories.
Q: Do I need both Meta and Google Ads?
A: Eventually, most brands do: demand capture and demand generation compound each other. Meta creates awareness that later shows up as branded searches you catch on Google; Google catches the intent Meta warmed up. But you do not need both on day one. Start with one, prove it works, then add the second channel once the first is stable and you can afford to learn on a new one.
Q: Which is better for ecommerce?
A: For ecommerce with a visual, impulse-friendly product, Meta is often the stronger engine: the feed is built to sell things people did not set out to buy, and Advantage+ shopping campaigns scale well. But Google Shopping and search catch buyers with active purchase intent and usually convert at a lower cost. Most scaled ecommerce brands run both; if forced to pick one first, let the product decide. Visual and impulse leans Meta, considered and searched-for leans Google.
Q: Which is easier for beginners?
A: Google search is usually easier to start with because the intent does half the work: someone typing “buy running shoes” is already close to a sale, so a plain ad on the right keyword can convert. Meta demands more from your creative, since you are interrupting people, and it punishes weak creative quickly. Neither platform's reported numbers should be trusted without a cross-check against what your analytics recorded.

# Is Performance Max cannibalizing your branded search?
URL: https://adgent.app/performance-max-brand-cannibalization

Blog Playbook
Is Performance Max cannibalizing your branded search?
Performance Max loves a cheap conversion, and nothing is cheaper than someone typing your
brand name. Left unchecked, it absorbs demand you already own, takes the credit, and reports a ROAS
you can't actually bank. Here is how to catch it and shut it down.
Adgent · Notes from building the analyst
Type
Playbook
Reading time
7 min
Published
22 July 2026
Updated
31 October 2026
On this page
How it happens
How to spot it
How to fix it
Measuring incrementality
Reported vs incremental
Analyst vs dashboard
Frequently asked
All articles
You look at the account and Performance Max is the hero: a ROAS two or three times everything else,
scaling like it can't miss. It feels great until you ask the uncomfortable question: how much
of that would have happened anyway? For a lot of accounts the answer is “most of it”, because
PMax has parked itself on top of your branded search, converting people who were already coming to
buy.
Short answer
Often, yes. Performance Max frequently serves on your own branded queries, taking credit
for demand you would have captured for free or near-free. That inflates its apparent ROAS while adding
little incremental value. Spot it with impression-share and search-term reports, stop it with brand
exclusions and negatives, then measure what PMax actually contributes on top.
This isn't a bug. It's the auction working exactly as designed, and it's the most common way a Google
Ads account tells you a comforting story. Below: how it happens, how to spot it, and what to do about
it.
It matters more the better PMax looks. The accounts most exposed are the ones where PMax is the star
performer, because a big, shiny ROAS is exactly what a big pool of branded demand produces. If your PMax
numbers seem too good to argue with, that is the account most worth auditing, not the least.
How the cannibalization happens
Performance Max is a goal-seeking machine. You give it a target, usually ROAS or CPA, and it hunts
across every Google surface (Search, Shopping, YouTube, Display, Discover, Gmail, Maps) for the
conversions that hit that target most efficiently. And the most efficient conversion in your entire
account, every single time, is the person who searched your brand name.
Someone typing “ [your brand] running shoes ” has already decided. They know you, they want you,
and they were going to land on your site whether or not an ad greeted them. PMax doesn't have that
context. It sees a query with a sky-high conversion rate and a rock-bottom cost, and it does what it was
built to do: it bids, it wins, and it books the sale as its own.
The short version
PMax isn't creating that demand. It's standing in the doorway and taking credit for everyone who walks
through.
The result is a slow, invisible transfer. Traffic that would have arrived through organic listings or
a cheap branded search campaign gets rerouted through PMax, at a higher cost per click and with the
conversion credit reassigned. Your blended numbers might look fine. Underneath, you are paying a premium
to buy customers you already had.
There is a second-order effect worth naming. Because PMax optimizes toward your ROAS target, and
branded conversions make that target trivially easy to hit, the algorithm learns that the cheap path is
the winning path. It leans harder into brand, spends less effort on the genuinely hard prospecting that
grows the business, and reports back a number that says everything is wonderful. You end up rewarding
the campaign for the one thing you didn't need it to do.
How to spot it
Cannibalization hides inside a good-looking average, so you have to go looking for it deliberately.
Three signals give it away.
1. One asset group or channel with a wildly higher ROAS than the rest
Pull performance by asset group and by channel. If one slice is posting a ROAS three, five or ten times
the rest of the campaign, that is not brilliance. It is almost always brand demand hiding inside it. Real
prospecting performance is lumpy but earthbound. A single outlier an order of magnitude better than
everything around it is the tell.
2. A jump in branded impression share
Check your branded search impression share over time. If it climbed right as you launched or scaled
Performance Max, PMax is now competing in an auction you used to own outright. You are bidding against
yourself, buying clicks that used to be cheap or free at auction prices.
3. Your own brand name in the reports
Performance Max search-term visibility is thin by design, but it isn't zero. Dig into the search terms
and search categories reports, plus the insights surfaced for the campaign. If your brand name and its
obvious variants keep showing up as top converting terms, you have your answer in black and white.
None of these is conclusive alone. Together, they are a pattern. This is exactly the kind of thing
worth checking as part of a broader Performance Max audit :
cannibalization rarely travels alone, and the same review usually surfaces two or three other leaks.
How to fix it
You have a ladder of options, from light-touch to structural. Pick the rung that matches how much
control you need.
Account-level negative keywords. Add your brand terms as account-wide negatives.
Performance Max respects them, so this is the fastest way to fence PMax off your own name without
touching the campaign structure.
Campaign brand exclusions and brand lists. Google's
brand
exclusion feature lets you attach a brand list to the Performance Max campaign so it stops serving
on your brand (and, if you want, on other brands). It is the purpose-built lever for exactly this problem.
Split brand into its own campaign. The cleanest fix: run a dedicated branded search
campaign, exclude brand everywhere in PMax, and let each campaign do one job. Now you can see, and
control, exactly what you pay for branded versus non-branded demand.
For most accounts the right answer is a combination: brand exclusions on the PMax campaign
plus a dedicated branded search campaign to catch that demand cheaply and on purpose. You aren't
trying to stop capturing branded traffic. You are trying to stop overpaying for it and mislabelling where
it came from.
One caution before you flip everything at once: make the change deliberately and give it room to
settle. Performance Max re-learns after a structural change, so expect a week or two of noisy numbers
while spend redistributes. Change one lever at a time where you can, and note the date. You will want a
clean before-and-after when you measure, and a pile of simultaneous edits makes it impossible to tell
which one moved the result.
How to measure incrementality afterward
This is the part most people skip, and it is the whole point. Once you exclude brand, Performance Max's
reported ROAS will drop . That is not the fix failing; that is the fix working. You have
stripped out the cheap branded conversions that were flattering the number. What is left is closer to
PMax's true incremental contribution.
So watch the right things after you make the change:
Total sales, not campaign ROAS. If revenue holds while PMax's ROAS falls, the demand
simply shifted to a cheaper channel. You saved money and lost nothing.
Blended CAC across the account. The number that matters is what it costs you to
acquire a customer overall, not what any single campaign claims in isolation.
Branded vs non-branded split. Now that they live in separate campaigns, you can
finally read them separately, and make decisions on the non-branded number that actually reflects new
demand.
The honest framing: a campaign's reported ROAS is not the same as its incremental
value. Branded conversions are the cheapest in the account, so any campaign allowed to absorb
them will look like a star. Take them away and measure again. That is the only way to know what PMax is
really worth on top of the demand you already own.
Reported ROAS vs incremental value
It is worth seeing the two side by side, because this gap is the entire trap.
What you're looking at Reported PMax ROAS, with brand Incremental value, brand excluded
Counts branded conversions you'd win anyway Yes No
Reflects new demand PMax actually created No Yes
Looks impressive in the campaign view Yes Honest
Survives a “would this have happened anyway?” test No Yes
Safe to base budget decisions on No Yes
The left column is what the platform hands you. The right column is what you can actually
bank, and the only one worth scaling on.
This is the same discipline behind a proper Google Ads
account audit : never trust a headline number until you have asked what would have happened without
the spend. Branded cannibalization is just the most expensive place that question goes unasked.
Why an analyst catches this and a dashboard doesn't
A reporting dashboard will show you PMax's glorious ROAS and stop there. The number is technically
correct, so nothing flags. Catching cannibalization takes a step of reasoning a dashboard never makes:
cross-referencing impression share, spotting the outlier asset group, and asking whether the conversions
are incremental at all. That is judgment work, and it is the job an
AI media buyer is meant to do: read the whole account, distrust
the flattering number, and tell you where the credit is really coming from.
Adgent reads every connected Google Ads and Meta account each day, remembers what you confirm about
the brand, and returns the finding with the evidence and estimated monthly impact attached. The same
context continues into the next account move and the result that follows.
Frequently asked
Q: Does Performance Max cannibalize branded search?
A: Often, yes. By default Performance Max can serve on your own branded queries: demand you
would have captured for free or near-free through organic and brand search. It takes the conversion
credit, inflating its reported ROAS while adding little or no incremental sales.
Q: How do I stop PMax bidding on my brand?
A: Add your brand terms as account-level negative keywords, apply campaign brand exclusions
inside the Performance Max campaign, and use Google's brand list feature to keep the campaign off your
own name. For full control, pull brand into its own dedicated branded search campaign and exclude it
everywhere in PMax.
Q: Can you add negative keywords to Performance Max?
A: Yes. You can apply
account-level
negative keywords that Performance Max respects, and use campaign-level brand exclusions and brand
lists. This is the main lever for keeping PMax off your branded queries without turning the campaign off.
Q: How do I know if PMax is taking branded traffic?
A: Look for one asset group or channel with a ROAS wildly higher than the rest, a spike in
branded impression share, and search-term or category reports full of your own brand name. If PMax
scaled up right as your organic and brand-search clicks dipped, it is likely absorbing branded
demand.
Q: Does excluding brand hurt Performance Max?
A: Its reported ROAS will drop, because you are removing cheap branded conversions from its
credit. But total sales usually hold, because that demand shifts to a cheaper branded search campaign
or converts organically. You lose inflated numbers, not real revenue, which is exactly the point.
Q: Is PMax ROAS inflated by brand?
A: Frequently. Branded conversions are the cheapest in the account, so when Performance Max
absorbs them its blended ROAS looks far better than its true incremental performance. Exclude brand
and measure again to see what PMax is actually contributing on top of demand you already own.

Bring the same question to your own account. Adgent returns its position, the evidence underneath and what the finding is worth a month.

# Why Performance Max isn't spending your budget · Adgent
URL: https://adgent.app/performance-max-not-spending-budget

Blog Diagnostic
Why Performance Max isn't spending your full budget
You set the budget, the campaign is live, and it is spending a fraction of the cap. Before
you touch the budget slider: it is probably not the budget. Here is how to find the real constraint,
ranked by how often it is the culprit.
Adgent · Notes from building the analyst
Type
Diagnostic
Reading time
8 min
Published
23 July 2026
Updated
31 October 2026
On this page
Is it the budget?
1. Bid targets
2. Learning phase
3. Asset review
4. Thin signals and assets
5. Shared budgets
6. Conversion tracking
The Channel Performance report
One change at a time
Frequently asked
All articles
“Performance Max isn't spending my budget” is one of the most common panics in a Google Ads account,
and one of the most misdiagnosed. The instinct is to raise the budget, or to assume the campaign is
broken. Both are usually wrong. A PMax campaign that under-delivers is almost always
telling you something specific about its bid targets, its learning state or its inputs, and the fix
depends entirely on which one.
Short answer
Most of the time it isn't a budget problem. Far more often a bid target or Quality Score
constraint is choking delivery , and genuinely budget-limited cases are the minority. Check in
order: bid targets too aggressive, learning phase, asset approvals, thin signals, shared-budget
cannibalization, then broken conversion tracking. Loosen the target before you raise the budget.
So treat this as a diagnostic, not a checklist to blast through. Work the causes in order of
likelihood, confirm each one before you act, and change one thing at a time.
The short version
A campaign that won't spend is rarely short of budget. It is short of auctions it is allowed to win.
First: is it actually a budget problem?
Before anything else, read the campaign status. Google labels a campaign “Limited by
budget” only when it genuinely wants to spend more than the cap allows. If your status reads
eligible , limited by bid strategy , or shows a learning notice, the
budget is not your bottleneck, and raising it will do nothing except sit unspent.
That is the whole point. In practice, “PMax isn't spending” resolves to a bid or Quality Score
constraint far more often than to the budget itself; truly budget-limited cases are the minority. The rest
split across approvals, tracking and thin inputs. If you skip the status check and go straight to the
budget, you are fixing the wrong thing on most campaigns.
The same pattern shows up well beyond PMax. On one live Google Ads account, asked to analyse 61
campaigns carrying $7,825 (₺378,800) over 28 days, the read was:
Adgent Google budget analysis · one live account, August 2026 · translated from Turkish
“Pacing is 34–86% but impression share is 10–43%. Not a budget problem: a rank wall.”
More budget would have bought nothing there. The work was on rank, which is where the next section
starts.
1. Bid targets too aggressive (the most common cause)
Check this first, because it accounts for the largest slice. A tight Target ROAS or
Target CPA tells Smart Bidding to enter only the auctions it can win profitably at
that target . Set the ROAS target too high, or the CPA too low, and the algorithm walks away from most
of the auction ( Google
lists unrealistic targets as a reason a campaign stops spending). The result looks exactly like a budget
problem: spend flatlines well under the cap. It isn't. The campaign is behaving as instructed; you instructed
it to be picky.
The fix is counterintuitive: loosen or remove the target and let it learn . Start with
“Maximize conversions” (or “Maximize conversion value”) with no target, let the campaign gather
data and find volume, then introduce a target gradually once you can see what CPA or ROAS it actually
achieves. Setting an aggressive target on day one asks the system to optimize against a number it has no
data to hit yet.
Status reads “limited by bid strategy” or eligible, not “limited by budget”.
Your Target CPA sits below your recent historical CPA, or your Target ROAS above your recently
achieved ROAS.
Fix: drop the target, run Maximize conversions, reintroduce the target after 2–3 weeks of data.
2. You're still in the learning phase
For the first 7–14 days after launch, or after any significant edit, PMax delivers
slowly and conservatively while Smart Bidding calibrates. Under-spend in this window is expected, not
broken. The trap is impatience: you tweak the budget, then the target, then the assets, and each edit
resets the learning clock , so the campaign never gets a clean run to ramp.
The discipline is the same one that keeps a winning campaign winning: batch your changes, then leave it
alone. If you are mid-learning, the right move is often to do nothing for a week. The full version is in
how to scale a winner without breaking it ; the mechanics
of editing without resetting learning apply directly to a campaign still finding its feet.
3. Ad review delays and disapproved assets
New asset groups go through review, which typically takes up to 24–48 hours and can
run longer. Until assets are approved they can't serve, so a brand-new campaign that isn't spending may
simply be waiting. Worse is the silent case: some assets are disapproved (policy, trademark, a
low-quality landing page) while others are approved, so the campaign serves in a starved, partial state
and never reaches the channels the disapproved assets would have unlocked.
Check the asset group status and the policy column. A single disapproved video or a rejected final URL
can cap delivery on YouTube or Display while Search carries on, making the total look like a mysterious
under-spend.
4. Narrow audience signals or thin asset groups
PMax uses your audience signals as a starting hint and your assets as the raw material
to assemble ads for every channel. Give it too little of either and it has nothing to work with. A thin
asset group (one headline variant, no video, a single image) can't build a YouTube or Display ad at all,
so those channels stay dark and delivery concentrates on the one or two it can serve. Likewise, a narrow
or empty audience signal gives Smart Bidding a weak cold start.
Fill every asset slot: multiple headlines, descriptions and images, and at least one video. Google
will auto-generate a poor one if you don't, so supply your own.
Add strong audience signals, such as your customer lists and high-intent custom segments, so the
system has a warm start, not a cold one.
5. Shared-budget cannibalization with Search
If PMax and your Search campaigns sit in a shared budget pool , PMax can starve Search,
or the reverse can mask what is really happening. PMax has broader auction access than a standard Search
campaign: it can serve across Search, Shopping, YouTube, Display, Gmail and Discover, so in a shared pool
it often out-competes Search for the same money. The pool drains, and it looks like one campaign “won't
spend” when really another is eating the budget.
The fix is structural: give PMax and Search their own separate budgets so neither can
cannibalize the other. This is the flip side of a problem covered in depth elsewhere: PMax absorbing your
brand traffic and inflating its own numbers at Search's expense. If that is your situation, read
Performance Max brand cannibalization for how to
detect and fence it off.
6. Broken conversion tracking
This one is last by frequency but first by damage. Smart Bidding spends toward conversions it can
measure . If your conversion tag is broken, double-firing, mapped to the wrong conversion action,
or reporting zero, the algorithm has no signal to optimize against, so it does the safe thing and pulls
delivery back. From the outside it looks like a budget or bid problem; underneath, the campaign is flying
blind.
Before you conclude anything else, confirm conversions are firing cleanly and landing on the right
action. If you are not sure how to check end to end, the
Google Ads account audit walkthrough covers the tracking
checks that catch this. A misconfigured conversion event is one of the most common reasons a
healthy-looking campaign refuses to spend.
The diagnostic tool: the Channel Performance report
You don't have to guess which of these it is. Open the campaign, go to Insights , and
read the Channel
Performance report . It breaks delivery down by Search, Shopping, Display, YouTube, Gmail and
Discover, so you can see directly which channel is silent.
That silence is the tell. A dark YouTube row usually means a missing video asset or a disapproval. A
dark Shopping row points at feed or Merchant Center issues. Broad silence across everything but Search
points back at the bid target or the learning phase. The report turns “it won't spend” from a mystery
into a specific, addressable gap.
Work it in order, and change one thing at a time
The mistake that keeps campaigns stuck isn't missing a cause; it is fixing three at once, resetting
learning, and losing the ability to tell what worked. Read the status. Check the target. Give it time.
Confirm approvals and tracking. Read the Channel Performance report. Change one variable, then wait for
the campaign to respond before you touch the next.
This is the kind of ranked, evidence-first diagnosis an
AI media buyer is meant to do. Instead of you eyeballing six
possible causes, it reads the account, identifies which constraint is actually binding, ranks
the fix by impact, and shows its work: the status flag, the target gap, the silent channel. The
Performance Max audit guide shows what a full read looks
like.
Adgent reads every connected Google Ads and Meta account each day, puts an estimated monthly amount
on each decision, and returns the binding constraint with the evidence underneath. The diagnosis,
proposed move and later result stay together instead of becoming three separate pieces of work.
Frequently asked
Q: Why is Performance Max not spending my full budget?
A: Usually it isn't a budget problem at all. Far more often, a bid target or Quality Score
constraint is choking delivery; genuinely budget-limited cases are the minority. Check bid targets,
learning phase and asset approvals before touching the budget.
Q: Is it a budget problem or a bid problem?
A: Most often a bid problem. The status says “Limited by budget” only when the campaign
truly wants more spend. If it reads eligible or limited by bid strategy, a tight Target ROAS or CPA is
the real cap: loosen the target before you raise the budget.
Q: Does a tight tCPA or tROAS limit spend?
A: Yes, and it is the most common cause. An aggressive Target CPA or ROAS tells Smart
Bidding to enter only auctions it can win profitably, so it walks away from most of them. Start with
no target, let it learn, then tighten gradually.
Q: How long is the PMax learning phase?
A: Roughly 7–14 days after launch or a significant edit. During it, delivery ramps slowly
and is deliberately conservative. Any major change (budget, target, assets or audience signals) resets
the clock, so batch your edits and then leave it alone.
Q: Does Performance Max steal budget from Search?
A: In a shared budget pool, yes. PMax has broader auction access than a standard Search
campaign, so it out-competes Search for the same pool and can starve it. Give PMax and Search separate
budgets so one campaign's delivery can't cannibalize the other.
Q: How do I see where PMax is spending?
A: Open the campaign, go to Insights, and read the Channel Performance report. It breaks
delivery down by Search, Shopping, Display, YouTube, Gmail and Discover, so you can see which channel
is silent and whether an asset gap or a signal gap is the reason.
Q: Can broken conversion tracking stop PMax spending?
A: Yes. Smart Bidding spends toward conversions it can measure. If your conversion tag is
broken, double-firing, or reporting into the wrong action, the algorithm can't find signal to optimize
against and pulls back delivery. Audit tracking before you blame the budget.

# Audience Network: the leak hiding in your average · Adgent
URL: https://adgent.app/placement-drift-the-leak-in-the-average

Blog How-to
Placement drift: the leak hiding in your average
Your account is at 3.8× and everything looks fine. Inside that number, one placement is
returning 1.1× on a fifth of your budget, and the average is doing an excellent job of hiding it.
Adgent · Notes from building the analyst
Type
How-to
Topic
Attribution
Reading time
7 min
Published
19 March 2026
Updated
31 October 2026
On this page
How placements drift
Why the arithmetic hides it
Finding the leak
Drift, week to week
The attribution trap
Running the check
Questions
All articles
The most dangerous number in your account is the one that looks fine. A blended ROAS of 3.8× does not
prompt an investigation; it prompts a nod and a move to the next tab. An average is a summary,
and summaries are where problems go to hide.
Short answer
A blended ROAS is a weighted average, so strong placements carry weak ones. A Feed at 4.4× on most of
your budget hides an Audience Network at 1.1× on the rest, and the top-line 3.8× never moves. The
waste is real; the arithmetic just averages it out of sight until you break the number down by
placement.
How placements drift
Advantage+
placements let Meta's delivery system move your budget across Feed, Stories, Reels,
Audience Network and the rest, chasing whatever the optimisation signal says is cheapest. Usually that
is what you want; it is the whole point of letting the system optimise.
The catch is what “cheapest” is measuring. If the system is optimising toward a signal that fires more
easily in one surface than another, it will happily pour budget into placements that generate the
signal but not the outcome. Cheap impressions, cheap clicks, and revenue that never shows up. The
drift is gradual, it is automatic, and nothing in the interface announces it.
The point, in one line
The average did not lie to you. It just answered a different question from the one you were asking.
Why the arithmetic hides it
This is Simpson's paradox wearing a media-buying costume. A weighted average lets strong performers
carry weak ones, and the more strong performers you have, the more weakness they can carry before the
top-line number moves at all.
Feed and the placements carrying it · 81% of spend 4.4×
Audience Network · 19% of spend 1.1×
Blended, the number you watch 3.8×
Blended, leak cut and budget redeployed 4.4×
A worked sum, not an account: 0.81 × 4.4 + 0.19 × 1.1 ≈ 3.8.
Run the numbers: 81% of spend at 4.4× blended with 19% at 1.1× gives you 3.8×. Perfectly
healthy-looking. Cut the leak and redeploy that budget into the placements that were carrying it, and
you are at 4.4×: a 16% improvement that was invisible in the metric you were
watching.
Finding the leak
The mechanical part is easy: break down by placement, sort by ROAS, look at the bottom. The judgement
part is knowing what you are allowed to conclude from what you see.
Check the volume before the verdict. A placement at 1.1× on $80 of spend is noise.
At $4,000 it is a decision. Small slices produce wild ratios for the same reason small samples
do.
Check attribution before you cut. Upper-funnel placements often earn view-through
credit that a last-click read never shows. A weak Reels number can be a strong Reels contribution
being attributed to the Feed ad that closed it.
Check the trend, not the snapshot. Drift is a direction. A placement that has been
sliding for three weeks is a different animal from one that had a bad Tuesday.
Nobody breaks down every campaign by placement every day. It is twelve clicks per campaign, it is
boring, and it is usually nothing, which is exactly why it is usually missed. The check that only
matters one week in eight is the check that never gets done.
Averages are answers to questions about groups. Your budget is not spent by a group.
It is spent slice by slice, and that is where you have to look.
What drift actually looks like week to week
Placement drift is easy to miss because it does not arrive as an event. There is no alert, no red
number, no day where the account breaks. It is a slow reallocation. Week one, Audience Network is 12%
of spend at 2.9×. Week three it is 17% at 2.1×. Week five it is 21% at 1.4×. Every individual week
looks like noise, and the blended number barely twitches because the placements carrying it are
getting a little stronger at the same time. The trend only becomes obvious once you line up the weeks,
and nobody lines up the weeks for a metric that looks fine.
This is the same failure that shows up across the whole discipline: the summary number moves last. By
the time your blended ROAS dips enough to prompt a question, the leak has been growing for a month and
you have already spent the money. Meta's delivery system is not malfunctioning when this happens; it
is doing exactly what you told it to do. Advantage+ placements optimise toward the conversion signal,
and if that signal is cheaper to trigger on the Audience Network than on Feed, the system will keep
shifting budget there. Cheaper to trigger and cheaper to convert are not the same thing, and the gap
between them is where your money goes.
The attribution trap underneath the leak
Before you cut a low-ROAS placement, you have to be sure the number is telling the truth, and
placement-level ROAS is one of the easiest numbers to misread. A last-click model assigns the whole
conversion to the placement that closed it, which is almost always Feed or Search. Upper-funnel
surfaces like Reels and the Audience Network do the priming work and get none of the credit. So a
placement reading 1.1× on a last-click basis might be contributing far more once you account for the
view-through impressions that warmed the user up three days before they converted somewhere else.
That is the difference between a placement that is genuinely leaking and one that is simply
mis-credited by your attribution setup. Cutting the first recovers budget. Cutting the second quietly
kills your top of funnel, and your Feed ROAS drops a week later for reasons that look unrelated. It is
the same bookkeeping problem we dig into in Meta
says 4.2×, Google says 3.1× : the number you trust depends on the window and the model that
produced it, and two placements are rarely measured on the same one.
How to run the check without doing it by hand every day
The honest problem is that the placement breakdown is a chore that pays off maybe one week in eight.
Twelve clicks per campaign, sorted by ROAS, cross-referenced against volume, trend and attribution
window: done properly it is twenty minutes of tedium that usually turns up nothing. So it does not get
done, and the one week it would have mattered slides past.
The fix is not discipline; it is decomposition on every read. Adgent is a team of AI agents working
toward your marketing goals, and one of its ten specialists, Placement & Network
Optimizer , has exactly this job: inefficient placements, devices, geos, networks and channels,
each finding with an estimated monthly amount on it. On one live account, its screen held five open
placement findings worth an estimated $144 a month (₺6,950), carried over from an earlier read rather
than re-read in that day's run. Two of them:
Adgent Placement & Network Optimizer · one live account, September 2026 · translated from Turkish
“Reels is 43% cheaper, but 74.5% of the budget is in Feed.”
“In this ad set the Notifications placement doubles the CPA.”
The leak runs both ways: budget sitting on an expensive surface is the same problem as budget drifting
to a cheap one that does not convert. An AI media buyer turns
that decomposition into a ranked decision with the current mix, proposed move and monthly impact
attached. The boring check against slow leaks keeps running, and the finding stays open with an owner
until the account team closes it.
None of this means Advantage+ is a mistake or that you should hand-pick every placement. Letting the
system optimise is usually right. The move is to keep watching the decomposition underneath the
average, to treat the blended number as a headline and never as the story, so that when a placement
starts drifting you catch it in week two instead of paying for it through week six.
Frequently asked
Q: How can a good blended ROAS hide a leak?
A: A blended ROAS is a weighted average, so placements that perform well carry the ones that do not. When most of your budget sits at 4.4×, a slice at 1.1× barely moves the top-line 3.8×. The loss is real but averaged out of sight.
Q: What is placement drift?
A: The gradual, automatic reallocation of budget by Meta's Advantage+ delivery toward whatever surface is cheapest to trigger the conversion signal on, even when that surface converts poorly. It happens slowly, without any alert, and nothing in the interface announces it.
Q: How do Advantage+ placements drift?
A: Advantage+ moves budget across Feed, Stories, Reels and Audience Network chasing the cheapest optimisation signal. If that signal fires more easily on one surface than another, the system pours spend there: cheap impressions and clicks, but not always the revenue that should follow.
Q: How do I find a placement leak?
A: Break each campaign down by placement, sort by ROAS, and look at the bottom. Then check three things before you act: the spend volume behind the ratio, the attribution window feeding it, and the trend (a placement sliding for weeks, not one bad day).
Q: Why does averaging conceal wasted spend?
A: It is Simpson's paradox in a media-buying costume. A weighted average lets strong performers absorb weak ones, and the more strong performers you have, the more weakness they can carry before the top-line number moves at all. The waste never shows up in the summary.
Q: How do I fix placement leakage?
A: Confirm the leak is real (enough volume, a trusted attribution window, a directional trend), then cut it and redeploy that budget into the placements already carrying the account. In the 81%-at-4.4× example, that lifts blended ROAS from 3.8× to 4.4×.

# Scale a winner without resetting the learning phase
URL: https://adgent.app/scale-a-winner-without-breaking-it

Blog How-to
How to scale a winner without breaking it
You found a campaign that works. Now the hard part: adding budget without handing it
back to the learning phase. The rule is not about how much you add. It is about how fast.
Adgent · Notes from building the analyst
Type
How-to
Topic
Scaling
Reading time
6 min
Published
9 April 2026
On this page
What a budget change does
The 20% rule
When to go sideways
Why ROAS crashes
CBO, Advantage+ and the pool
A practical cadence
The part that is hard to hold
Questions
All articles
Every performance marketer knows the feeling. A campaign hits 4× and you want more of it, so you
triple the budget overnight. By Thursday it is at 1.8× and you are trying to work out what broke.
Nothing broke. You reset it.
Short answer
To scale a Meta campaign without a learning reset, raise the budget by no more than about 20%
every 48–72 hours instead of one big jump. An ad set re-enters the learning phase when a
budget change is large enough to count as a significant edit, so it is the size of the step, not the
final number, that triggers the reset. Scale in small steps and the ad set keeps what it learned.
What a budget change actually does
Meta's delivery system treats a significant budget change as a material change to the ad set. Cross
that line and the ad set re-enters the learning phase, where it needs roughly 50
conversions in 7 days to stabilise again. Everything it learned about who converts gets
re-litigated, and while it re-learns, your cost per result climbs.
The trap, in one line
You did not buy more of a working campaign. You bought a new campaign wearing its name.
This is the trap in scaling: the thing you are scaling stops being the thing that worked the moment
you scale it hard enough.
The 20% rule, and what it is really about
The widely used heuristic is to raise a budget by no more than about 20% every 48–72 hours. It is a
practitioners' rule of thumb, not a published platform limit, and the reason behind it matters more
than the number. You are not avoiding a big budget. You are avoiding a big step. An ad
set at $100 a day can reach $500 a day in about three weeks of 20% steps without tripping a reset.
Jump there in one move and you have thrown away three weeks of learning to save three weeks of
waiting.
When to go sideways instead of up
Vertical scaling, more budget into the same ad set, eventually hits a ceiling that has nothing to do
with learning phases. You saturate the audience. Frequency climbs, CPM follows, and each extra dollar
buys a worse impression than the last.
At that point the move is horizontal: duplicate into a new audience, a new placement mix or a new
geo, and let the winning creative do its work in front of fresh eyes. The signals that tell you the
ceiling is close:
CPM rising while CTR holds. You are paying more for the same interest. The
auction, not the creative, is the constraint.
Frequency past about 2.5 in a 7-day window. On a cold prospecting audience,
that is saturation, not reach.
Incremental spend at falling marginal ROAS. The blended number still looks fine
while the last $1,000 returns nothing. Read the margin, not the average.
Why ROAS crashes the moment you scale hard
A hard scale rarely fails for one reason. It fails for three at once, and they compound. The first is
the reset itself: the ad set is re-learning, so delivery is deliberately exploratory and inefficient
while it hunts for 50 conversions. The second is auction pressure. To spend three times the budget,
Meta widens delivery into more expensive inventory and more competitive slots, so CPM climbs
before your creative gets a fair test. The third is measurement lag: the ROAS you scaled on
may still have been inside its attribution window, so the “4×” you were chasing was never fully real
to begin with.
Stack those together and the crash looks mysterious. It is not. You changed the campaign, made it
more expensive to run, and did it on a number that had not matured. The fix is not a better bid
strategy; it is slowing down enough that only one variable moves at a time. If you are not sure the
ROAS was solid before you scaled, that is usually an attribution-window problem , not a scaling problem.
CBO, Advantage+, and where budget lives when you scale
Where you push the budget matters as much as how fast. Under ABO , you are editing an
ad set directly, so a large increase maps cleanly onto a single learning phase, and the 20% rule
applies exactly as written. Under CBO (and Advantage+ campaign budgets), you are
raising a shared pool that Meta redistributes across ad sets on its own logic. A big campaign-level
jump can quietly re-open learning on several ad sets at once, or starve the ad sets that were actually
carrying performance.
The safer pattern at the campaign level is the same principle applied to the pool: step the campaign
budget up gradually and watch how Meta reallocates before you add more. If you are deciding between
the two structures while you scale, the trade-offs are in CBO vs ABO
vs Advantage+ . And whatever the structure, do not stack a budget change on top of a creative swap or an
audience edit on the same day. Every simultaneous change is one more variable you cannot isolate when
the number moves.
A practical scaling cadence
Here is the loop that holds up across a whole account. Confirm the winner is real first: enough
conversions to be out of the learning phase, and a ROAS that has cleared its attribution window rather
than a day-one spike. Then raise the budget about 20%, and leave it alone for a full 48–72 hours so the
ad set can settle before the next step. Repeat only while the marginal ROAS on the last increase still
holds.
When vertical steps start returning less each time (CPM up, frequency past about 2.5, marginal ROAS
sliding), stop climbing and go sideways: duplicate the winning creative into a fresh audience,
placement mix or geo. Horizontal scaling resets the saturation clock without resetting the learning
you paid for. The discipline is boring on purpose: one change, then wait, then read the
result. It is the opposite of the overnight triple that started this post.
The part that is hard to hold
The rules above are easy to write down and hard to hold across thirty ad sets on a Tuesday. Each
scaling decision needs three facts at once: how long since the last change, where the ad set is in
its learning phase, and whether the ROAS you are scaling on has actually matured.
Adgent is a team of AI agents working toward your marketing goals, and it keeps those facts in view.
It records changes made on the platform itself, by people and by tools, so “when did this budget last
move?” has an answer. A proposed budget step arrives with its current value, new value and reason. On
one live account, a request for a 33% campaign-budget jump produced this warning:
Adgent Account move · Meta · one live account, 30 September 2026
“This is a CAMPAIGN (CBO) budget: it governs spend across ALL ad sets in the campaign.
33% in one step (300.00 → 400.00) is beyond the 20% band: a jump this size can reset the ad set's
learning phase.”
It suggested 360 TRY a day instead, a 20% step ($7.44 against the current $6.20), with the rest after
two or three days of settled CPA. The 20% band is Adgent's own ceiling, the same rule of thumb as above.
Every applied step lands in the Change Ledger with the budget it replaced;
the exact inverse starts from that recorded before-state and becomes its own row.
Scaling well is mostly patience with a system that punishes impatience. Add slowly, and you
keep what you built.
Frequently asked
Q: How fast can I scale a Meta campaign?
A: Raise the budget by no more than about 20% every 48–72 hours. That pace lets an ad set settle between steps, so a $100-a-day winner can reach $500 a day in roughly three weeks without tripping a learning reset.
Q: What is the 20% rule?
A: A scaling heuristic: increase an ad set's budget by no more than about 20% every 48–72 hours. It works because you are limiting the size of each step, not the final budget. Small steps stay under the line that re-opens the learning phase.
Q: Does increasing budget reset the learning phase?
A: Only if the change is large enough to count as a significant edit. A modest step of about 20% usually does not; a big overnight jump does, sending the ad set back into learning, where it needs roughly 50 conversions in 7 days to stabilise again.
Q: When should I scale horizontally instead of vertically?
A: When vertical steps stop paying off: CPM rising while CTR holds, frequency past about 2.5, marginal ROAS falling. That is audience saturation, not a learning issue. Duplicate the winning creative into a fresh audience, placement or geo instead of adding more budget.
Q: How much budget increase is safe?
A: About 20% per step is the widely used ceiling for a single ad set. The exact figure matters less than the principle: keep each step small enough to count as a tweak, not a material change, and wait 48–72 hours between steps.
Q: Why does my ROAS crash when I scale?
A: Usually three things at once: a learning reset from too big a jump, rising CPM as Meta buys pricier inventory to spend more, and a ROAS that had not matured past its attribution window. Scale slowly so only one variable moves at a time.

# What is an AI media buyer? A plain-language guide · Adgent
URL: https://adgent.app/what-is-an-ai-media-buyer

Blog Definition
What is an AI media buyer?
The term is new, the job isn't. An AI media buyer reads your ad accounts like a senior
strategist, explains what changed and why, then carries the decision into the next piece of account
work. Not a dashboard with a chatbot bolted on.
Adgent · Notes from building the analyst
Type
Definition
Reading time
8 min
Published
21 July 2026
Updated
11 October 2026
On this page
The short definition
What it is not
Side by side
How the category got here
What a real one does
Three tests on a demo
From decision to account work
How to choose one
Where Adgent sits
Questions
All articles
Search “AI media buyer” and you'll find two kinds of answer: hype that promises to do your team's job for you, and tools that are really dashboards with a chat box. Neither describes the job. So here is a
plain-language definition, an honest map of what the category contains, and a test you can run on
any demo.
Definition
An AI media buyer is software that reads your ad accounts like a senior strategist,
states what should change and why, and carries that decision into reports, plans, campaign builds or
account moves while keeping the result attached. Unlike a dashboard, it commits to a conclusion;
unlike platform automation, it works for the advertiser, not the auction.
The short definition
An AI media buyer is software that does the reasoning part of a media buyer's job. It reads your ad
accounts, reasons about how they are built (budget structure, placements, audiences, creative,
attribution) and commits to a conclusion about what to change and why. Then it carries that conclusion
into the next piece of work.
The word that matters is reasoning . A media buyer's value was never pulling the
numbers; it was knowing which number matters today, why it moved, and what to do about it. An AI media
buyer automates that judgment without dropping the context at the handoff to a report, plan or account
move.
In one line
A dashboard hands you data. An AI media buyer hands you a decision.
What it is not
The category gets muddy because very different things get called “AI for ads”. Four of them are
worth separating:
Not a reporting dashboard. A dashboard renders your data and leaves the analysis
to you. Adding a chat box changes the interface, not the category: you now get the same summary in
sentences, and the decision is still yours to make, alone, at 8am.
Not platform automation. Meta Advantage+ and Google Performance Max are the platforms' own AI. They are genuinely good
at optimising the auction inside one platform, but no platform tool will tell you to move budget to
a competing platform, and each optimises toward what its own pixel can see. Your cost of goods, your
return rate and your margin are not in that set. An AI media buyer sits on your side of the
table.
Not a rules engine. “If CPA > X, pause” is automation without judgment. It
fires on a threshold; it can't tell you why CPA moved or whether pausing is the right
call.
Not a creative generator. Reading creative and making creative are different
products. Reading it (the hook, the angle, where viewers leave) is part of the job; producing the
asset is not.
AI media buyer vs dashboard vs platform AI vs rules
The fastest way to place the category is side by side, across the capabilities that actually
matter:
Capability Reporting dashboard Platform AI (Advantage+, Performance Max) Rules engine AI media buyer
Reasons about why a metric moved No No No Yes
Reads Meta and Google side by side Partly One platform No Yes
Works for the advertiser, not the auction Yes No Yes Yes
Reads analytics and store data beyond the platform Partly No No Yes
Turns the conclusion into the next piece of work No Inside one platform One prescribed action Yes
Keeps the decision, before-state and result together No No Partial Yes
Explains its confidence and flags bad data No No No Yes
The column on the right is the reason the category exists: judgment that continues into
finished work, on the advertiser's side.
How the category got here: manual, rules, platform AI, AI media buyer
The job didn't appear overnight. It is the fourth step in a twenty-year arc, and each step automated
a different layer while leaving the hardest one, judgment, to a human:
Manual buying. A person set every bid, budget and audience by hand. Total control,
zero scale.
Rules and scripts. “If CPA > X, pause.” Scale arrived, but the rules were blind
to context: they fired on a threshold, never on a reason.
Platform AI. Advantage+ and Performance Max automated bidding and placement, but
optimised toward the platform's auction and hid much of the account structure from the
buyer.
AI media buyer. The first layer that automates the reasoning : it reads
the account, commits to a conclusion, explains it and carries the decision into the next piece of
work. It works for you, not the auction.
What a real one does, day to day
Strip away the marketing and the job becomes one loop with three moves: notice, decide, carry through.
A capable AI media buyer does all three.
It watches, and writes the verdict first
It reads the accounts on a schedule, builds a baseline for each, and works out what changed. What
you open is a short list ranked by money, not a wall of charts. This is the principle behind why we lead with the verdict : conclusion first,
evidence underneath.
It answers, in plain language
You ask “why did Meta ROAS drop yesterday?” and get a strategist's answer with evidence, not a
chart to decode. That includes the awkward truths a dashboard glosses over, like a blended ROAS hiding a placement leak , or a number
that is still inside the attribution window and
shouldn't be trusted yet.
It carries the decision into work
A useful conclusion should not die in chat. It can become a report, a media plan, a field-by-field
campaign build or an account-move card, with the same evidence and brand context still attached.
Three tests you can run on any demo
A definition is only useful if it comes with a test. Each property below is a question you can ask
in a twenty-minute demo, and each one has a failure answer that sounds fine until you look at it.
1. Does it state a position?
A position is a claim someone could be wrong about, with the reasoning attached and a cost per month
next to it. A chart, an alert or “impression share is down 12%” is none of those. Ask it what to do
about a campaign, and see whether the answer contains a verb.
The harder half of the same test is whether the position holds when the obvious move is wrong. On
one live account, asked to analyse 61 Google campaigns carrying $7,825 (₺378,800) over 28 days, the
output was:
Adgent Google budget analysis · one live account, August 2026 · translated from Turkish
“Pacing is 34–86% but impression share is 10–43%. Not a budget problem: a rank wall.”
Neither easy move, cut or raise, was the answer. The position named the layer the problem lives on,
rank, and pointed the work there.
2. Does it ever tell you no?
A system that only says yes isn't reasoning, it's executing. On a real account, ours declined a
target CPA an order of magnitude below anything the account had ever produced, and refused to treat a
pixel with four purchases in thirty days as ready for a conversion campaign. Each time it showed the
account's own numbers as the reason. Automation that can't decline is just a faster way to be
wrong.
3. Does the decision survive the handoff?
Ask what happens after the verdict. If the answer is “copy it into another tool”, the product has
automated analysis but left the operational handoff intact. A complete loop carries the reasoning into
the next artifact and keeps the result available for the next account read.
Account moves make that test concrete. The before-state must be captured when the move happens, not
reconstructed later from a report. On one live Meta account, a country exclusion became a ledger row
with the value it replaced. Adgent then prepared the exact inverse from that same row, and the put-back
landed as its own event 29 seconds later.
22:33:54
Inverse, by the agent owner · team
Geo exclusion, put back Meta · one ad set
LT: excluded LT: no longer excluded
Executed
22:33:25
Proposed in chat owner · team
Geo exclusion Meta · one ad set
LT: not excluded LT: excluded
Executed
Change Ledger, one live account, Meta, 26 August 2026. The two rows are 29 seconds apart.
For supported reversible changes made through Adgent, the ledger can prepare an inverse from the
recorded before-state for approval. Edits made directly in the platform appear in a separate change
log; they cannot be undone from that row.
From decision to account work
A real AI media buyer should not stop at “here is what I found.” The decision may need a client-ready
report, a four-week media plan, a recurring check, a complete campaign build or a specific account move.
The product earns its place when it carries the same reasoning into that next step.
The history matters as much as the handoff. The next account read should know what the team decided,
which move followed and what happened afterward. That is how the system gets more useful over time
without asking the team to rebuild context from old decks, spreadsheets and chat threads.
How to choose an AI media buyer
If you are evaluating tools in this category, five questions separate the real ones from the
dashboards with a chatbot:
Does it reason, or just report? Ask it “why did this move?”. A real one gives a
cause, not a chart.
Can it carry a decision into finished work? Ask to turn the finding into a report,
plan, campaign build or account move, then check whether the reasoning and result stay attached.
Does it read past the platform's own report? Platform-reported ROAS alone isn't
ground truth. It should read sources the platform doesn't own, such as GA4, Search Console and
Merchant Center, and say plainly which store connections are live and which are only planned.
Does it flag what it can't measure? The honest ones say “this number can't be
trusted yet” instead of inventing confidence.
Does it read Meta and Google in one place? Not three separate tools bolted side by
side.
For a wider map of the tools that get sold under this name, see how to choose an AI media buying tool and AI media buyer vs Performance Max vs
dashboard .
Where Adgent sits against this definition
Adgent is a team of AI agents working toward your marketing goals, and buying media is one of the
jobs they do. Stated at the scope we can actually evidence, on the accounts we have driven
first-hand:
Reads Meta and Google Ads, with GA4, Search Console and Merchant Center alongside.

Frequently asked
Q: What is an AI media buyer?
A: Software that reads ad accounts like a senior strategist, explains what changed and why, and carries the decision into the next piece of work. It reasons about account structure instead of only rendering metrics.
Q: How is an AI media buyer different from a dashboard?
A: A dashboard renders data and hands the analysis back to you. An AI media buyer ranks issues by impact, states a position with evidence and turns the decision into a report, plan, campaign build or account move.
Q: Is an AI media buyer the same as Meta Advantage+ or Google Performance Max?
A: No. Those are the platforms' own automation, optimising toward their own auction. An AI media buyer sits on the advertiser's side, reads Meta and Google side by side, and can lean on sources the platform doesn't own, such as GA4, Search Console and Merchant Center.
Q: What happens after an AI media buyer makes a decision?
A: The useful ones carry it forward. Depending on the job, the decision becomes a report, media plan, campaign build, recurring agent or account move, with the evidence and later result still attached.
Q: Does an AI media buyer replace a media buyer?
A: No. It changes what the buyer spends time on. Account reads, anomaly detection and report drafting start from finished work, so the person can focus on strategy, creative direction and the decisions that require business context.
Q: How is an AI media buyer different from programmatic advertising?
A: Programmatic automates buying impressions in real time within an ad exchange. An AI media buyer sits a layer above: it reasons about existing accounts, decides what should change and carries that decision into work. Programmatic is a buying mechanism; an AI media buyer is a decision layer.
Q: What channels does an AI media buyer cover?
A: The useful ones read Meta and Google Ads in one place and pull context from GA4, Search Console and Merchant Center, so the answer rests on more than platform-reported numbers. Adgent connects Meta and Google Ads today; TikTok is not connected.
Q: How does an AI media buyer help an agency?
A: It gives each client account the same daily read, ranked decisions and report workflow. Junior teams start from worked recommendations while senior buyers spend their time on strategy and the calls that matter.
